tactics.name: Reconnaissance
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to gather information about the AI system they can use to plan future operations.

tactics.name: Resource Development
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to establish resources they can use to support operations.

tactics.name: AI Attack Adaptation
tactics.summary: The adversary is adapting capabilities, methods, knowledge, or objectives into attack-ready outputs for a target or current operational conditions.

tactics.name: Initial Access
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to gain access to the AI system.

tactics.name: AI Model Access
tactics.summary: The adversary is attempting to gain some level of access to an AI model.

tactics.name: Execution
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to run malicious code embedded in AI artifacts or software.

tactics.name: Persistence
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to maintain their foothold via AI artifacts or software.

tactics.name: Privilege Escalation
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to gain higher-level permissions.

tactics.name: Defense Evasion
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to avoid being detected by AI-enabled security software.

tactics.name: Credential Access
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to steal account names and passwords.

tactics.name: Discovery
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to figure out your AI environment.

tactics.name: Lateral Movement
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to move through your AI environment.

tactics.name: Collection
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to gather AI artifacts and other related information relevant to their goal.

tactics.name: Command and Control
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to communicate with compromised AI systems to control them.

tactics.name: Exfiltration
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to steal AI artifacts or other information about the AI system.

tactics.name: Impact
tactics.summary: The adversary is trying to manipulate, interrupt, erode confidence in, or destroy your AI systems and data.

AML.T0000.name: Search Open Technical Databases
AML.T0000.summary: Adversaries may search for publicly available research and technical documentation to learn how and where AI is used within a victim organization. The adversary can use this information to identify targets for attack, or to tailor an existing attack to make it more effective.
AML.T0000.description:
Adversaries may search for publicly available research and technical documentation to learn how and where AI is used within a victim organization. The adversary can use this information to identify targets for attack, or to tailor an existing attack to make it more effective. Organizations often use open source model architectures trained on additional proprietary data in production. Knowledge of this underlying architecture allows the adversary to craft more realistic proxy models (Replicate AI Model Behavior). An adversary can search these resources for publications for authors employed at the victim organization.
Research and technical materials may exist as academic papers published in Journals and Conference Proceedings or stored in Pre-Print Repositories, as well as Technical Blogs. Publicly accessible AI services may be identified via Scan Databases.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit the connection between publicly disclosed approaches and the data, models, and algorithms used in production.
mitigations.AML.M0039: Decoy assets are catalogued by the same internet scan databases (e.g., Shodan, Censys) that adversaries query to locate exposed AI infrastructure. Adversarial engagement that originates from those platforms can grant defenders visibility into those discovery channels.

AML.T0000.000.name: Journals and Conference Proceedings
AML.T0000.000.summary: Many of the publications accepted at premier artificial intelligence conferences and journals come from commercial labs. Some journals and conferences are open access, others may require paying for access or a membership.
AML.T0000.000.description: Many of the publications accepted at premier artificial intelligence conferences and journals come from commercial labs. Some journals and conferences are open access, others may require paying for access or a membership. These publications will often describe in detail all aspects of a particular approach for reproducibility. This information can be used by adversaries to implement the paper.

AML.T0000.001.name: Pre-Print Repositories
AML.T0000.001.summary: Pre-Print repositories, such as arXiv, contain the latest academic research papers that haven't been peer reviewed. They may contain research notes, or technical reports that aren't typically published in journals or conference proceedings.
AML.T0000.001.description: Pre-Print repositories, such as arXiv, contain the latest academic research papers that haven't been peer reviewed. They may contain research notes, or technical reports that aren't typically published in journals or conference proceedings. Pre-print repositories also serve as a central location to share papers that have been accepted to journals. Searching pre-print repositories provides adversaries with a relatively up-to-date view of what researchers in the victim organization are working on.

AML.T0000.002.name: Technical Blogs
AML.T0000.002.summary: Research labs at academic institutions and company R&D divisions often have blogs that highlight their use of artificial intelligence and its application to the organization's unique problems. Individual researchers also frequently document their work in blog posts.
AML.T0000.002.description: Research labs at academic institutions and company R&D divisions often have blogs that highlight their use of artificial intelligence and its application to the organization's unique problems. Individual researchers also frequently document their work in blog posts. An adversary may search for posts made by the target victim organization or its employees. In comparison to Journals and Conference Proceedings and Pre-Print Repositories this material will often contain more practical aspects of the AI system. This could include underlying technologies and frameworks used, and possibly some information about the API access and use case. This will help the adversary better understand how that organization is using AI internally and the details of their approach that could aid in tailoring an attack.

AML.T0000.003.name: Scan Databases
AML.T0000.003.summary: Adversaries may search public internet-scan services to identify a victim's exposed AI infrastructure.
AML.T0000.003.description:
Adversaries may search public internet-scan services to identify a victim's exposed AI infrastructure. These services, such as Shodan and Censys, continuously scan the internet and publish the active IP addresses, hostnames, open ports, and service banners, which adversaries can query without interacting with the target directly.
Information gathered this way may also reveal candidates for follow-on Active Scanning to confirm that services remain reachable, to probe for misconfigurations or unauthorized endpoints. It may also inform later initial access attempts such as Exploit Public-Facing Application. Unlike Active Scanning, this technique relies on third-party scan data and involves no direct interaction with the victim system.

mitigations.AML.M0039: Decoy assets are catalogued by the same internet scan databases (e.g., Shodan, Censys) that adversaries query to locate exposed AI infrastructure. Adversarial engagement that originates from those platforms can grant defenders visibility into those discovery channels.

AML.T0001.name: Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis
AML.T0001.summary: Much like the Search Open Technical Databases, there is often ample research available on the vulnerabilities of common AI models. Once a target has been identified, an adversary will likely try to identify any pre-existing work that has been done for this class of models.
AML.T0001.description: Much like the Search Open Technical Databases, there is often ample research available on the vulnerabilities of common AI models. Once a target has been identified, an adversary will likely try to identify any pre-existing work that has been done for this class of models. This will include not only reading academic papers that may identify the particulars of a successful attack, but also identifying pre-existing implementations of those attacks. The adversary may obtain Adversarial AI Attack Implementations or develop their own Adversarial AI Attacks if necessary.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit disclosure of the production AI stack and system-specific technical details that let adversaries connect public vulnerability research to the deployed target.

AML.T0002.name: Acquire Public AI Artifacts
AML.T0002.summary: Adversaries may search public sources, including cloud storage, public-facing services, and software or data repositories, to identify AI artifacts. These AI artifacts may include the software stack used to train and deploy models, training and testing data, model configurations and parameters.
AML.T0002.description:
Adversaries may search public sources, including cloud storage, public-facing services, and software or data repositories, to identify AI artifacts. These AI artifacts may include the software stack used to train and deploy models, training and testing data, model configurations and parameters. An adversary will be particularly interested in artifacts hosted by or associated with the victim organization as they may represent what that organization uses in a production environment. Adversaries may identify artifact repositories via other resources associated with the victim organization (e.g. Search Victim-Owned Websites or Search Open Technical Databases). These AI artifacts often provide adversaries with details of the AI task and approach.
AI artifacts can aid in an adversary's ability to Replicate AI Model Behavior. If these artifacts include pieces of the actual model in production, they can be used to directly Craft Adversarial Data. Acquiring some artifacts requires registration (providing user details such as an email address or name), AWS keys, or written requests, and may require the adversary to Establish Accounts.
Artifacts might be hosted on victim-controlled infrastructure, providing the victim with some information on who has accessed that data.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit the release of sensitive information in the metadata of deployed systems and publicly available applications.

AML.T0002.000.name: Datasets
AML.T0002.000.summary: Adversaries may collect public datasets to use in their operations. Datasets used by the victim organization or datasets that are representative of the data used by the victim organization may be valuable to adversaries. Datasets can be stored in cloud storage, or on victim-owned websites.
AML.T0002.000.description:
Adversaries may collect public datasets to use in their operations. Datasets used by the victim organization or datasets that are representative of the data used by the victim organization may be valuable to adversaries. Datasets can be stored in cloud storage, or on victim-owned websites. Some datasets require the adversary to Establish Accounts for access.
Acquired datasets help the adversary advance their operations, stage attacks, and tailor attacks to the victim organization.

mitigations.AML.M0001: Limiting the release of datasets can reduce an adversary's ability to target production models trained on the same or similar data.

AML.T0002.001.name: Models
AML.T0002.001.summary: Adversaries may acquire public models to use in their operations. Adversaries may seek models used by the victim organization or models that are representative of those used by the victim organization.
AML.T0002.001.description:
Adversaries may acquire public models to use in their operations. Adversaries may seek models used by the victim organization or models that are representative of those used by the victim organization. Representative models may include model architectures, or pre-trained models which define the architecture as well as model parameters from training on a dataset. The adversary may search public sources for common model architecture configuration file formats such as YAML or Python configuration files, and common model storage file formats such as ONNX (.onnx), HDF5 (.h5), Pickle (.pkl), PyTorch (.pth), or TensorFlow (.pb, .tflite).
Acquired models are useful in advancing the adversary's operations and are frequently used to tailor attacks to the victim model.

mitigations.AML.M0001: Limiting the release of model architectures and checkpoints can reduce an adversary's ability to target those models.

AML.T0002.002.name: AI Agent Configuration
AML.T0002.002.summary: Adversaries may acquire publicly accessible AI agent configuration files to understand agent capabilities, gain unauthorized access to tools and data sources, or identify credentials for further attacks.
AML.T0002.002.description:
Adversaries may acquire publicly accessible AI agent configuration files to understand agent capabilities, gain unauthorized access to tools and data sources, or identify credentials for further attacks. Configuration files define what tools an agent can use, credentials for external services, system prompts, and behavioral settings, making them valuable resources for adversaries targeting AI agent deployments.
Once configuration files are acquired, adversaries may perform Discover AI Agent Configuration to gain additional insights they can use in their operation or Credentials from AI Agent Configuration to harvest secrets.
AI agent configuration files come in multiple forms depending on the platform and agent framework. Agent configuration files adversaries may target include: - System prompts: Files containing agent instructions, behavioral guidelines, and internal logic. - Tool configuration: Files defining tools the agent can utilize, including Model Context Protocol (MCP) configs (e.g., `mcp.json`, `claude_desktop_config.json`), IDE-specific configs (e.g., `.claude/settings.json`, `.vscode/tasks.json`), and framework-specific settings that define external tool and data source integrations. - Skills and workflows: Files defining agent capabilities, behaviors, or workflows. Often a combination of instructions, scripts, and resources. - Environment and deployment configs: Files that control agent deployment and runtime behavior, often environment variables or framework-specific configs.

AML.T0003.name: Search Victim-Owned Websites
AML.T0003.summary: Adversaries may search websites owned by the victim for information that can be used during targeting. Victim-owned websites may contain technical details about their AI-enabled products or services.
AML.T0003.description:
Adversaries may search websites owned by the victim for information that can be used during targeting. Victim-owned websites may contain technical details about their AI-enabled products or services. Victim-owned websites may contain a variety of details, including names of departments/divisions, physical locations, and data about key employees such as names, roles, and contact info. These sites may also have details highlighting business operations and relationships.
Adversaries may search victim-owned websites to gather actionable information. This information may help adversaries tailor their attacks (e.g. Adversarial AI Attacks or Manual Modification). Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance (e.g. Search Open Technical Databases or Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis)

mitigations.AML.M0000: Restrict release of technical information on ML-enabled products and organizational information on the teams supporting ML-enabled products.

AML.T0004.name: Search Application Repositories
AML.T0004.summary: Adversaries may search open application repositories during targeting. Examples of these include Google Play, the iOS App store, the macOS App Store, and the Microsoft Store.
AML.T0004.description:
Adversaries may search open application repositories during targeting. Examples of these include Google Play, the iOS App store, the macOS App Store, and the Microsoft Store.
Adversaries may craft search queries seeking applications that contain AI-enabled components. Frequently, the next step is to Acquire Public AI Artifacts.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit the release of sensitive information in the metadata of deployed systems and publicly available applications.

AML.T0005.name: Replicate AI Model Behavior
AML.T0005.summary: Adversaries may replicate an AI model's behavior or selected capabilities by training or adapting another model to approximate the target's responses, decision regions, or other characteristics.
AML.T0005.description:
Adversaries may replicate an AI model's behavior or selected capabilities by training or adapting another model to approximate the target's responses, decision regions, or other characteristics. The result may be a surrogate for attack development, a functional replica, or a student model incorporating selected target capabilities.
Replication may cover a whole model or only the behaviors relevant to the adversary's objective. Models may be developed from gathered artifacts, collected model outputs, or adaptation of an existing model. How closely the model must reproduce the target's behavior depends on the adversary's goals.
Replicate AI Model Behavior supports adversaries' ability to achieve Resource Development when producing a reusable model capability and AI Attack Adaptation when tailoring a model for a particular target or operation.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limiting release of technical information about a model and training data can reduce an adversary's ability to create an accurate proxy model.
mitigations.AML.M0001: Limiting the release of model artifacts can reduce an adversary's ability to create an accurate proxy model.
mitigations.AML.M0002: Obfuscating model outputs can reduce an adversary's ability to produce an accurate proxy model.
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit inference queries to reduce the labeled outputs available for training a proxy model.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Access controls on models APIs can reduce an adversary's ability to produce an accurate proxy model.
mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected replication activity to reduce the usefulness of collected outputs for reproducing the target model's behavior or capabilities.

AML.T0005.000.name: Replicate Behavior from Gathered AI Artifacts
AML.T0005.000.summary: Adversaries may replicate AI model behavior by training or fine-tuning another model from gathered AI artifacts, such as representative datasets, published architectures, training objectives, documented hyperparameters, or pretrained components.
AML.T0005.000.description:
Adversaries may replicate AI model behavior by training or fine-tuning another model from gathered AI artifacts, such as representative datasets, published architectures, training objectives, documented hyperparameters, or pretrained components.
Artifacts may approximate the target without direct interaction with it. The adversary may reproduce a reported training approach, recreate a dataset, or combine public and privately acquired components. Adversaries may obtain these components via Acquire Public AI Artifacts or gather them from victim environments via AI Artifact Collection

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limiting release of technical information about a model and training data can reduce an adversary's ability to create an accurate proxy model.
mitigations.AML.M0001: Limiting the release of model artifacts can reduce an adversary's ability to create an accurate proxy model.

AML.T0005.001.name: Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs
AML.T0005.001.summary: Adversaries may replicate an AI model's behavior or selected capabilities by training or adapting another model using outputs or other sources of supervision obtained from the target.
AML.T0005.001.description:
Adversaries may replicate an AI model's behavior or selected capabilities by training or adapting another model using outputs or other sources of supervision obtained from the target. Supervisory material may include labels, scores, probabilities, generated responses, reasoning explanations, evaluations, reward or preference signals, and tool-use or agent interaction trajectories.
The adversary may use supervised learning, knowledge distillation, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or related methods. Target-generated material may be filtered, combined with other data, or acquired from multiple teacher models. The resulting model may reproduce selected capabilities rather than the target's full behavior, architecture, parameters, or output ontology.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Obfuscating model outputs restricts an adversary's ability to create an accurate proxy model by querying a model and observing its outputs.
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit inference queries to reduce the labeled outputs available for training a proxy model.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if a proxy training dataset has been exfiltrated.
mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected replication activity to reduce the usefulness of collected outputs for reproducing the target model's behavior or capabilities.

AML.T0005.002.name: Adapt Existing Model to Replicate Behavior
AML.T0005.002.summary: Adversaries may select an existing AI model whose behavior resembles a target and adapt it to more closely reproduce the capabilities or responses of interest. They may fine-tune the model or adjust its prompts and inference settings to improve that similarity.
AML.T0005.002.description:
Adversaries may select an existing AI model whose behavior resembles a target and adapt it to more closely reproduce the capabilities or responses of interest. They may fine-tune the model or adjust its prompts and inference settings to improve that similarity.
The resulting model may serve as a surrogate for attack development or provide a reusable capability that replicates selected target behavior.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limiting release of technical information about a model and training data can reduce an adversary's ability to create an accurate proxy model.

AML.T0006.name: Active Scanning
AML.T0006.summary: Adversaries may actively scan for publicly reachable AI systems and resources for targeting. They may identify resources or systems that are misconfigured or are known vulnerable versions. This is distinct from other reconnaissance techniques that do not involve direct interaction with the victim system.
AML.T0006.description:
Adversaries may actively scan for publicly reachable AI systems and resources for targeting. They may identify resources or systems that are misconfigured or are known vulnerable versions. This is distinct from other reconnaissance techniques that do not involve direct interaction with the victim system.
Since AI systems are often deployed in cloud environments, adversaries can use various enumeration methods to effectively discover AI systems and uncover information about their supporting underlying platforms. For agentic and SaaS-hosted systems, the victim system can include the shared platform and provider control plane on which the victim's agents are deployed.
Adversaries may probe the victim system to gather information and metadata for targeting, or actively scan for specific open ports on a potential victim's network or accessible deployed servers, with the goal of locating different types of deployed AI services. These methods could also include directly scanning a target's assets for publicly available AI agents, or for accessible agentic chat interfaces on SaaS platforms (ex: Copilot Studio Hunter).
Information gained from Active Scanning may yield targets that provide opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance such as Search Open Technical Databases, Search Open Websites/Domains, Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis, or Gather RAG-Indexed Targets.

mitigations.AML.M0019: Require authenticated access to production AI endpoints and monitor queries to limit unauthenticated probing of exposed AI services.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Segment AI agent components so an exposed service does not reveal or provide reachability to additional internal components.
mitigations.AML.M0039: By capturing adversarial fingerprinting behavior, honeypots can help provide early warning of sweeping activity meant to discover exposed AI targets and attack surfaces being explored by adversaries.

AML.T0006.000.name: Enumerate Hosted AI Resources
AML.T0006.000.summary: Adversaries may directly probe an agentic or SaaS platform to enumerate the resources a specific victim has deployed on it.
AML.T0006.000.description: Adversaries may directly probe an agentic or SaaS platform to enumerate the resources a specific victim has deployed on it. Platforms frequently host AI agents behind predictable URL structures derived from identifiers such as environment, tenant, resource-group, or agent names, and default out-of-the-box deployment configurations keep these conventions consistent across victims. Adversaries can learn these conventions from public sources such as vendor documentation, code repositories and actual hosted resources, then fuzz or brute-force the derived namespace to discover live AI agents, endpoints, and associated metadata. Discovered resources can be used to identify targets for further access, collection, or attack adaptation.

mitigations.AML.M0039: By capturing adversarial fingerprinting behavior, honeypots can help provide early warning of sweeping activity meant to discover exposed AI targets and attack surfaces being explored by adversaries.

AML.T0006.001.name: Query Platform Metadata APIs
AML.T0006.001.summary: Adversaries may query documented or undocumented APIs in agentic SaaS hosting platforms to uncover agentic targets.
AML.T0006.001.description:
Adversaries may query documented or undocumented APIs in agentic SaaS hosting platforms to uncover agentic targets. SaaS and agentic platforms can expose provider control-plane or identity APIs that return tenant, environment, or deployment information IDs, including for resources that are misconfigured or unintentionally accessible by unauthenticated users.
Attackers have been seen abusing this type of functionality to perform information gathering on SaaS platforms, for example via AADInternals' OSINT page, an OSINT online tool showcasing an undocumented API reconnaissance method for Entra ID. This undocumented Power Platform API could be used to uncover environment IDs, which may subsequently be used to scan for public agents. Following the identified abuse, required authentication was added to the tool.

mitigations.AML.M0039: By capturing adversarial fingerprinting behavior, honeypots can help provide early warning of sweeping activity meant to discover exposed AI targets and attack surfaces being explored by adversaries.

AML.T0006.002.name: Scan for Exposed AI Infrastructure
AML.T0006.002.summary: Adversaries may scan network ports and services to identify deployed AI backends, model-serving endpoints, and AI agent infrastructure reachable over the internet.
AML.T0006.002.description:
Adversaries may scan network ports and services to identify deployed AI backends, model-serving endpoints, and AI agent infrastructure reachable over the internet. Self-hosted AI runtimes typically listen on predictable, well-known ports and expose standard API paths, allowing adversaries to efficiently locate candidate hosts and infer the platform running on them.
After identifying candidate hosts, adversaries can interact with them directly to confirm live AI services, fingerprint the software stack, and determine version and configuration details. This information can be used to select exploitable targets and tailor subsequent access attempts.

mitigations.AML.M0039: By capturing adversarial fingerprinting behavior, honeypots can help provide early warning of sweeping activity meant to discover exposed AI targets and attack surfaces being explored by adversaries.

AML.T0006.003.name: Probe AI Agent Trigger Channels
AML.T0006.003.summary: Adversaries may send crafted inputs to potential public triggers, such as email addresses, webhooks, or messaging channels, to elicit a response that indicates an invocation of agentic activity.
AML.T0006.003.description: Adversaries may send crafted inputs to potential public triggers, such as email addresses, webhooks, or messaging channels, to elicit a response that indicates an invocation of agentic activity. The nature of the response and its content can often reveal agent-managed accounts and expose the additional agentic attack surface. Identified triggers can be used to directly attack the agent.

mitigations.AML.M0039: By capturing adversarial fingerprinting behavior, honeypots can help provide early warning of sweeping activity meant to discover exposed AI targets and attack surfaces being explored by adversaries.

AML.T0007.name: Discover AI Artifacts
AML.T0007.summary: Adversaries may search private sources to identify AI learning artifacts that exist on the system and gather information about them. These artifacts can include the software stack used to train and deploy models, training and testing data management systems, container registries, software repositories, and model zoos.
AML.T0007.description:
Adversaries may search private sources to identify AI learning artifacts that exist on the system and gather information about them. These artifacts can include the software stack used to train and deploy models, training and testing data management systems, container registries, software repositories, and model zoos.
This information can be used to identify targets for further collection, exfiltration, or disruption, and to tailor and improve attacks.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can limit an adversary's ability to identify AI models, datasets, and other artifacts on a system.
mitigations.AML.M0012: Encrypting AI artifacts can protect against adversary attempts to discover sensitive information.

AML.T0008.name: Acquire Infrastructure
AML.T0008.summary: Adversaries may buy, lease, or rent infrastructure for use throughout their operation. A wide variety of infrastructure exists for hosting and orchestrating adversary operations. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, mobile devices, and third-party web services.
AML.T0008.description:
Adversaries may buy, lease, or rent infrastructure for use throughout their operation. A wide variety of infrastructure exists for hosting and orchestrating adversary operations. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, mobile devices, and third-party web services. Free resources may also be used, but they are typically limited. Infrastructure can also include physical components such as countermeasures that degrade or disrupt AI components or sensors, including printed materials, wearables, or disguises.
Use of these infrastructure solutions allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation. Solutions may help adversary operations blend in with traffic that is seen as normal, such as contact to third-party web services. Depending on the implementation, adversaries may use infrastructure that makes it difficult to physically tie back to them as well as utilize infrastructure that can be rapidly provisioned, modified, and shut down.

mitigations.AML.M0043: Decommission agent-acquired infrastructure when authorization ends to limit its continued use beyond the authorized task.

AML.T0008.000.name: AI Development Workspaces
AML.T0008.000.summary: Developing and staging AI attacks often requires expensive compute resources. Adversaries may need access to one or many GPUs in order to develop an attack.
AML.T0008.000.description: Developing and staging AI attacks often requires expensive compute resources. Adversaries may need access to one or many GPUs in order to develop an attack. They may try to anonymously use free resources such as Google Colaboratory, or cloud resources such as AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud as an efficient way to stand up temporary resources to conduct operations. Multiple workspaces may be used to avoid detection.

AML.T0008.001.name: Consumer Hardware
AML.T0008.001.summary: Adversaries may acquire consumer hardware to conduct their attacks. Owning the hardware provides the adversary with complete control of the environment. These devices can be hard to trace.
AML.T0008.001.description: Adversaries may acquire consumer hardware to conduct their attacks. Owning the hardware provides the adversary with complete control of the environment. These devices can be hard to trace.

AML.T0008.002.name: Domains
AML.T0008.002.summary: Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses. They can be purchased or, in some cases, acquired for free.
AML.T0008.002.description:
Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses. They can be purchased or, in some cases, acquired for free.
Adversaries may use acquired domains for a variety of purposes (see ATT&CK). Large AI datasets are often distributed as a list of URLs to individual datapoints. Adversaries may acquire expired domains that are included in these datasets and replace individual datapoints with poisoned examples (Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts: Datasets).

AML.T0008.003.name: Physical Countermeasures
AML.T0008.003.summary: Adversaries may acquire or manufacture physical countermeasures to aid or support their attack.
AML.T0008.003.description:
Adversaries may acquire or manufacture physical countermeasures to aid or support their attack.
These components may be used to disrupt or degrade the model, such as adversarial patterns printed on stickers or T-shirts, disguises, or decoys. They may also be used to disrupt or degrade the sensors used in capturing data, such as laser pointers, light bulbs, or other tools.

AML.T0008.004.name: Serverless
AML.T0008.004.summary: Adversaries may purchase and configure serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting.
AML.T0008.004.description:
Adversaries may purchase and configure serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting. By utilizing serverless infrastructure, adversaries can make it more difficult to attribute infrastructure used during operations back to them.
Once acquired, the serverless runtime environment can be leveraged to either respond directly to infected machines or to proxy traffic to an adversary-owned command and control server. As traffic generated by these functions will appear to come from subdomains of common cloud providers, it may be difficult to distinguish from ordinary traffic to these providers. This can be used to bypass a Content Security Policy that prevent retrieving content from arbitrary locations.

AML.T0008.005.name: AI Service Proxies
AML.T0008.005.summary: Adversaries may acquire proxy infrastructure that mediates access to AI services. Proxies can provide a common interface to multiple upstream accounts or providers while concealing underlying credentials from downstream users.
AML.T0008.005.description:
Adversaries may acquire proxy infrastructure that mediates access to AI services. Proxies can provide a common interface to multiple upstream accounts or providers while concealing underlying credentials from downstream users. Adversaries may purchase access to existing proxy services from commercial operators or gray-market resellers, or deploy publicly available proxy software on their own infrastructure.
Proxy infrastructure may route requests across provider APIs, cloud endpoints, aggregators, and account pools based on service health, availability, quotas, or cost, with failover when access is disrupted. Operators may rotate or replace accounts and mix coordinated requests with unrelated customer traffic, enabling access from restricted regions as well as complicating detection and attribution (See Centralized AI Service Request Routing)..Adversaries may deliberately utilize proxies for Defense Evasion (See Centralized AI Service Request Routing and AI Service Request Metadata Sanitization).
AI service proxy infrastructure may be used as "transfer stations" for gray-market resale. Their upstream suppliers may Establish Accounts through bulk registration, supported by verification and payment intermediaries, while operators pool capacity from promotional credits, discounted access, unused quotas, or shared subscriptions. Proxy infrastructure may also use Valid Accounts obtained through credential theft as observed in LLMjacking campaigns.
Adversaries have used proxy services to route requests and collect responses for model distillation campaigns. Adversaries may collect Outputs from AI Models and use them to Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs.

AML.T0010.name: Supply Chain Compromise
AML.T0010.summary: Adversaries may manipulate products, components, or their development and delivery mechanisms before they reach downstream consumers to compromise data or systems. Manipulation may involve source code, dependencies, development tools, build environments, software updates, distribution channels, or hardware.
AML.T0010.description:
Adversaries may manipulate products, components, or their development and delivery mechanisms before they reach downstream consumers to compromise data or systems. Manipulation may involve source code, dependencies, development tools, build environments, software updates, distribution channels, or hardware.
In AI environments, targets may include Hardware, Software, Data Repositories, Model Repositories, Container Registries, and AI Agent Tools. Compromised components may introduce malicious executable behavior, alter model behavior, or provide unauthorized access when incorporated into downstream systems.
Autonomous AI agents may also select and conduct supply-chain attacks against software or services outside the AI supply chain. An agent may develop a malicious contribution, submit it through an established development workflow, and attempt to persuade maintainers to approve and distribute it.

mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify AI artifacts and associated software, data, and configuration against protected approval records before incorporating them into downstream systems.
mitigations.AML.M0023: Record component identities, versions, sources, and dependencies across the AI supply chain. Use these records to identify builds and deployments affected by reported compromises and guide replacement or rollback.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Exercise the introduction of controlled untrusted software, data, models, and agent tools through representative acquisition and deployment paths. Remediate weaknesses in provenance, validation, approvals, isolation, and rollback.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on compromised suppliers, components, and distribution channels. Use this intelligence to identify affected dependencies, prevent their introduction into downstream systems, and prioritize investigation and replacement of compromised components.

AML.T0010.000.name: Hardware
AML.T0010.000.summary: Adversaries may target AI systems by disrupting or manipulating the hardware supply chain. AI models often run on specialized hardware such as GPUs, TPUs, or embedded devices, but may also be optimized to operate on CPUs.
AML.T0010.000.description: Adversaries may target AI systems by disrupting or manipulating the hardware supply chain. AI models often run on specialized hardware such as GPUs, TPUs, or embedded devices, but may also be optimized to operate on CPUs.

mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on compromised hardware suppliers and products, including affected models and production batches where known. Use this intelligence to identify affected hardware, prevent its introduction into downstream systems, and prioritize investigation and replacement.

AML.T0010.001.name: Software
AML.T0010.001.summary: Adversaries may target software packages that are commonly used in AI-enabled systems or are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle.
AML.T0010.001.description:
Adversaries may target software packages that are commonly used in AI-enabled systems or are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle. This can include deep learning frameworks used to build AI models (e.g. PyTorch, TensorFlow, Jax), generative AI integration frameworks (e.g. LangChain, LangFlow), inference engines, and AI DevOps tools. They may also target the dependency chains of any of these software packages. Additionally, adversaries may target specific components used by AI software such as configuration files or example usage of AI packages, which may be distributed in Jupyter notebooks.
Adversaries may compromise legitimate packages or publish malicious software to a namesquatted location. They may target package names that are hallucinated by large language models (see: Publish Hallucinated Entities). They may also perform an AI Supply Chain Rug Pull in which they first publish a legitimate package and then publish a malicious version once they reach a critical mass of users.

mitigations.AML.M0013: Enforce properly signed drivers and ML software frameworks.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify software packages and supporting artifacts, including configuration files and notebooks, against approved digests or signed manifests before installation or use. Reject unauthorized substitutions or changes.
mitigations.AML.M0023: Record AI software packages, frameworks, inference engines, and DevOps tools, including versions and dependencies. Use these records to identify deployments affected by reported software compromises and guide replacement or rollback.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Introduce controlled untrusted AI packages, libraries, plugins, or software components. Verify dependency controls, scanning, signing, approval, isolation, and safe installation.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on compromised software packages, dependencies, and releases, including affected versions and distribution locations. Use this intelligence to identify affected software, prevent its introduction into downstream systems, and prioritize investigation and replacement.

AML.T0010.002.name: Data Repository
AML.T0010.002.summary: Adversaries may abuse data repositories or other dataset distribution services to introduce compromised data into downstream AI workflows.
AML.T0010.002.description:
Adversaries may abuse data repositories or other dataset distribution services to introduce compromised data into downstream AI workflows. They may replace or modify published datasets, manipulate versions or references that consumers resolve, or publish malicious datasets under identities or locations that consumers trust.
The repository or distribution service need not itself be compromised. Adversaries may use legitimate publishing functionality or control an upstream account, namespace, or artifact referenced by a downstream workflow. Compromised data may subsequently be downloaded, synchronized, or incorporated into training, fine-tuning, evaluation, or retrieval systems.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent tampering with ML artifacts and prevent unauthorized copying.
mitigations.AML.M0007: Screen acquired datasets for upstream manipulation, comparing them with trusted source records or dataset versions. Quarantine and remediate affected data before training.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify datasets against protected manifests of approved versions and digests before use in training, fine-tuning, evaluation, or retrieval. Reject unauthorized substitutions or changes.
mitigations.AML.M0023: Record dataset sources, releases, and relationships to training, evaluation, and retrieval workflows. Use these records to identify systems exposed to compromised sources or releases and trace downstream effects.
mitigations.AML.M0025: Dataset provenance can protect against supply chain compromise of data.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Introduce controlled untrusted datasets through representative acquisition and ingestion paths. Verify provenance, integrity, sanitization, review, and rejection controls.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on data repositories and distribution services delivering compromised datasets, including affected publishing accounts, dataset versions, and references. Use this intelligence to identify affected data dependencies, prevent ingestion of compromised datasets, and prioritize investigation of workflows that have already consumed them.

AML.T0010.003.name: Model Repository
AML.T0010.003.summary: Adversaries may abuse model repositories or other model distribution services to introduce compromised models into downstream AI systems. They may replace published artifacts, manipulate model versions or references that consumers resolve, or publish malicious models under identities or locations that consumers trust.
AML.T0010.003.description:
Adversaries may abuse model repositories or other model distribution services to introduce compromised models into downstream AI systems. They may replace published artifacts, manipulate model versions or references that consumers resolve, or publish malicious models under identities or locations that consumers trust.
The repository or distribution service need not itself be compromised. Adversaries may use legitimate publishing functionality or control an upstream account, namespace, or artifact referenced by a downstream workflow. Consumers may retrieve the compromised model for inference, fine-tuning, or incorporation into another application.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent tampering with ML artifacts and prevent unauthorized copying.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate acquired models for unexpected outputs, backdoor behavior, and sensitive information disclosure before deployment. Reject or quarantine models that fail acceptance criteria and revalidate replacements.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Pin models to approved versions and digests, and verify all model files and bundled components before loading. Obtain expected values from authenticated sources or protected approval records.
mitigations.AML.M0017: An adversary could repackage the application with a malicious version of the model.
mitigations.AML.M0023: Record model publishers, repositories, versions, available digests, and bundled components. Use these records to trace compromised releases to fine-tuned derivatives and consuming applications and guide investigation, replacement, or rollback.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Introduce a controlled untrusted or modified model through representative acquisition and deployment paths. Verify provenance, scanning, signing, approval, isolation, and rollback.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on model repositories and distribution services delivering compromised models, including affected publishing accounts, model versions, and references. Use this intelligence to identify affected model dependencies, prevent integration of compromised models, and prioritize investigation of systems that have already incorporated them.

AML.T0010.004.name: Container Registry
AML.T0010.004.summary: An adversary may compromise a victim's container registry by pushing a manipulated container image and overwriting an existing container name and/or tag. Users of the container registry as well as automated CI/CD pipelines may pull the adversary's container image, compromising their AI Supply Chain.
AML.T0010.004.description:
An adversary may compromise a victim's container registry by pushing a manipulated container image and overwriting an existing container name and/or tag. Users of the container registry as well as automated CI/CD pipelines may pull the adversary's container image, compromising their AI Supply Chain. This can affect development and deployment environments.
Container images may include AI models, so the compromised image could have an AI model which was manipulated by the adversary (See Manipulate AI Model).

mitigations.AML.M0014: Pin container images to approved digests and verify their authenticity before deployment. Reject substitutions introduced through mutable image tags.
mitigations.AML.M0023: Record container image digests, registries, included AI components, and consuming workloads. Use these records to identify deployments running compromised images.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on container registries distributing compromised images, including affected repositories, tags, and image digests. Use this intelligence to identify affected image dependencies, prevent deployment of compromised images, and prioritize investigation and replacement of affected containers.

AML.T0010.005.name: AI Agent Tool
AML.T0010.005.summary: Adversaries may target AI agent tools as a means to compromise a victim's AI supply chain. Tools add capabilities to AI agents, allowing them to interact with other services, connect to data sources, access internet resources, run system tools, and execute code.
AML.T0010.005.description:
Adversaries may target AI agent tools as a means to compromise a victim's AI supply chain. Tools add capabilities to AI agents, allowing them to interact with other services, connect to data sources, access internet resources, run system tools, and execute code. They are an attractive target for adversaries because compromising an AI agent can provide them with broad access and permissions on the victim's system via the agent's other tools.
Poisoned AI agent tools may contain malicious definitions or instructions, hidden executable logic, or deliberately poisoned runtime responses (See AI Agent Tool Poisoning). These changes may manipulate the agent's behavior, modify how other tools are invoked, introduce hidden side effects, or provide unauthorized access to data and services. Adversaries have successfully used a poisoned MCP server to exfiltrate private user data.
Agent tools have exploded in popularity, with thousands of MCP servers available publicly. They are often released on open-source software repositories such as GitHub, indexed on hubs specific to MCP servers, and published to package registries such as NPM. AI agents can also be connected to remotely-hosted tools. This creates an environment where malicious tools can proliferate rapidly and safeguards are often not in place.

mitigations.AML.M0023: Record agent tool packages and remote integrations, including providers, available versions, endpoints, and consuming agents. Use these records to identify agents exposed to compromised tools and guide disabling, replacement, or reconnection to a safe version.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Introduce a controlled untrusted agent tool or tool definition. Verify source authorization, integrity, review, permission boundaries, and safe activation.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on compromised AI agent tool dependencies, including affected packages, versions, and remote services. Use this intelligence to identify affected integrations, prevent adoption of compromised tools, and prioritize disabling affected integrations and investigating prior tool activity.

AML.T0011.name: User Execution
AML.T0011.summary: An adversary may rely upon a user to load, execute, interpret, or otherwise use a malicious or unsafe artifact. In AI systems, user execution may include loading a model or causing an inference runtime to process executable or behavior-shaping components bundled with an AI artifact.
AML.T0011.description:
An adversary may rely upon a user to load, execute, interpret, or otherwise use a malicious or unsafe artifact. In AI systems, user execution may include loading a model or causing an inference runtime to process executable or behavior-shaping components bundled with an AI artifact. The resulting effect may include host code execution or malicious AI behavior.
Users may inadvertently execute unsafe code introduced via Supply Chain Compromise.
Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to execute malicious code by, for example, opening a malicious document file or link.

mitigations.AML.M0011: Restricting binaries from loading external libraries can limit their ability to execute malicious code.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify artifacts against protected approval records before deserialization, loading, interpretation, or inference. Reject unauthorized changes before executable or behavior-shaping components are processed.
mitigations.AML.M0016: Vulnerability scanning can help identify malicious binaries and prevent user execution.
mitigations.AML.M0018: Training users to be able to identify attempts at manipulation will make them less susceptible to performing techniques that cause the execution of malicious code.

AML.T0011.000.name: Unsafe AI Artifacts
AML.T0011.000.summary: Adversaries may develop new AI artifacts or manipulate existing AI artifacts that have a deleterious effect when loaded, executed, interpreted, or used for inference by a victim. The unsafe artifacts may continue to work as expected from the victim's perspective.
AML.T0011.000.description:
Adversaries may develop new AI artifacts or manipulate existing AI artifacts that have a deleterious effect when loaded, executed, interpreted, or used for inference by a victim. The unsafe artifacts may continue to work as expected from the victim's perspective.
Unsafe AI artifacts may include serialized models, model packages, and bundled components such as prompt or chat templates, tokenizer metadata, configuration, pre-processing logic, post-processing logic, or other executable or behavior-shaping metadata.
An unsafe artifact may exploit deserialization or another software vulnerability to execute code on the host. However, exploitation of a software vulnerability is not required. An artifact may instead use functionality intentionally supported by an AI runtime to alter model context, model outputs, safety behavior, or agent actions.
Adversaries may introduce unsafe artifacts through a Supply Chain Compromise. Execution may occur when a user loads the artifact, starts an inference runtime, submits an inference request, or otherwise causes the artifact's bundled logic to be processed.

mitigations.AML.M0011: Restrict library loading by ML artifacts.
mitigations.AML.M0013: Prevent execution of ML artifacts that are not properly signed.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify artifacts against protected approval records before deserialization, loading, or inference. Reject unauthorized changes before executable components are processed.
mitigations.AML.M0016: Vulnerability scanning can help identify malicious AI artifacts, such as models or data, and prevent user execution.
mitigations.AML.M0018: Train users to identify attempts of manipulation to prevent them from running unsafe code which when executed could develop unsafe artifacts. These artifacts may have a detrimental effect on the system.

AML.T0011.001.name: Malicious Package
AML.T0011.001.summary: Adversaries may develop malicious software packages that when imported by a user have a deleterious effect. Malicious packages may behave as expected to the user. They may be introduced via Supply Chain Compromise.
AML.T0011.001.description: Adversaries may develop malicious software packages that when imported by a user have a deleterious effect. Malicious packages may behave as expected to the user. They may be introduced via Supply Chain Compromise. They may not present as obviously malicious to the user and may appear to be useful for an AI-related task.

mitigations.AML.M0011: Restricting packages from loading external libraries can limit their ability to execute malicious code.
mitigations.AML.M0013: Code signing provides a guarantee that the software package has not been manipulated after signing took place.
mitigations.AML.M0016: Vulnerability scanning can help identify malicious packages and prevent user execution.
mitigations.AML.M0018: Train users to identify attempts of manipulation to prevent them from running unsafe code from external packages.

AML.T0011.002.name: Poisoned AI Agent Tool
AML.T0011.002.summary: A victim may invoke a poisoned tool when interacting with an AI agent. Invocation may expose the agent to poisoned definitions or responses, execute malicious tool implementation logic, or cause the agent to invoke additional tools.
AML.T0011.002.description:
A victim may invoke a poisoned tool when interacting with an AI agent. Invocation may expose the agent to poisoned definitions or responses, execute malicious tool implementation logic, or cause the agent to invoke additional tools. Poisoned tools may be introduced through AI software, installed packages, skills, or connections to remotely hosted services.
Poisoned AI agent tools may be introduced into the victim's environment via Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool.

AML.T0011.003.name: Malicious Link
AML.T0011.003.summary: An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to click on a link that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from Spearphishing Link.
AML.T0011.003.description:
An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to click on a link that will lead to code execution. This user action will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from Spearphishing Link. Clicking on a link may also lead to other execution techniques such as exploitation of a browser or application vulnerability via Exploitation for Client Execution. Links may also lead users to download files that require execution via Malicious File.
There are many ways an adversary can leverage malicious links to gain access to a victim system via an AI system. For example, an AI Agent that is configured to not validate website origin headers will accept connections from any website, allowing adversaries to access otherwise inaccessible networks.

AML.T0012.name: Valid Accounts
AML.T0012.summary: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access. Credentials may take the form of usernames and passwords of individual user accounts or API keys that provide access to various AI resources and services.
AML.T0012.description:
Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access. Credentials may take the form of usernames and passwords of individual user accounts or API keys that provide access to various AI resources and services.
Compromised credentials may provide access to additional AI artifacts and allow the adversary to perform Discover AI Artifacts. Compromised credentials may also grant an adversary increased privileges such as write access to AI artifacts used during development or production.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Restrict model registries and training data to approved identities so compromised accounts expose only explicitly authorized AI assets.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Authenticate production AI endpoints and monitor model queries for misuse of otherwise valid credentials.
mitigations.AML.M0043: Revoke credentials and disable unneeded accounts to limit reuse of agent-associated access after its authorized purpose ends.

AML.T0013.name: Discover AI Model Ontology
AML.T0013.summary: Adversaries may discover the ontology of an AI model's output space, for example, the types of objects a model can detect. The adversary may discover the ontology by repeated queries to the model, forcing it to enumerate its output space.
AML.T0013.description:
Adversaries may discover the ontology of an AI model's output space, for example, the types of objects a model can detect. The adversary may discover the ontology by repeated queries to the model, forcing it to enumerate its output space. Or the ontology may be discovered in a configuration file or in documentation about the model.
The model ontology helps the adversary understand how the model is being used by the victim. It is useful to the adversary in creating targeted attacks.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Suggested approaches: - Restrict the number of results shown - Limit specificity of output class ontology - Use randomized smoothing techniques - Reduce the precision of numerical outputs
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit inference queries to reduce an adversary's ability to discover the model's full output ontology.

AML.T0014.name: Discover AI Model Family
AML.T0014.summary: Adversaries may discover the general family of a model. General information about the model may be revealed in documentation, or the adversary may use carefully constructed examples and analyze the model's responses to categorize it.
AML.T0014.description:
Adversaries may discover the general family of a model. General information about the model may be revealed in documentation, or the adversary may use carefully constructed examples and analyze the model's responses to categorize it.
Knowledge of the model family can help the adversary identify means of attacking the model and help tailor the attack.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Suggested approaches: - Restrict the number of results shown - Limit specificity of output class ontology - Use randomized smoothing techniques - Reduce the precision of numerical outputs
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit inference queries to reduce an adversary's ability to infer the family of AI model.
mitigations.AML.M0006: Use multiple different models to fool adversaries of which type of model is used and how the model used.

AML.T0015.name: Evade AI Model
AML.T0015.summary: Adversaries can Craft Adversarial Data that prevents an AI model from correctly identifying the contents of the data or Generate Deepfakes that fools an AI model expecting authentic data.
AML.T0015.description:
Adversaries can Craft Adversarial Data that prevents an AI model from correctly identifying the contents of the data or Generate Deepfakes that fools an AI model expecting authentic data.
This technique can be used to evade a downstream task where AI is utilized. The adversary may evade AI-based virus/malware detection or network scanning towards the goal of a traditional cyber attack. AI model evasion through deepfake generation may also provide initial access to systems that use AI-based biometric authentication.

mitigations.AML.M0003: Hardened models are more difficult to evade.
mitigations.AML.M0006: Using multiple different models increases robustness to attack.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models against representative adversarial inputs for misclassification or missed detection under realistic operating conditions. Use failures against robustness acceptance criteria to guide model selection, remediation, or deployment restrictions.
mitigations.AML.M0009: Using a variety of sensors can make it more difficult for an attacker to compromise and produce malicious results.
mitigations.AML.M0010: Preprocessing model inputs can prevent malicious data from going through the machine learning pipeline.
mitigations.AML.M0015: Prevent an attacker from introducing adversarial data into the system.
mitigations.AML.M0034: Deepfake detection can be used to identify and block generated content.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Execute representative digital, multimodal, and physical-domain evasion attacks. Use successful attacks to improve model robustness, preprocessing, adversarial-input detection, human oversight, and monitoring.

AML.T0016.name: Obtain Capabilities
AML.T0016.summary: Adversaries may search for and obtain software capabilities for use in their operations. Capabilities may be specific to AI-based attacks Adversarial AI Attack Implementations or generic software tools repurposed for malicious intent (Software Tools).
AML.T0016.description: Adversaries may search for and obtain software capabilities for use in their operations. Capabilities may be specific to AI-based attacks Adversarial AI Attack Implementations or generic software tools repurposed for malicious intent (Software Tools). In both instances, an adversary may modify or customize the capability to aid in targeting a particular AI-enabled system.

mitigations.AML.M0001: Limit public release of production model artifacts that adversaries could acquire and adapt as operational capabilities.

AML.T0016.000.name: Adversarial AI Attack Implementations
AML.T0016.000.summary: Adversaries may search for existing open source implementations of AI attacks. The research community often publishes their code for reproducibility and to further future research.
AML.T0016.000.description: Adversaries may search for existing open source implementations of AI attacks. The research community often publishes their code for reproducibility and to further future research. Libraries intended for research purposes, such as CleverHans, the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox, and FoolBox, can be weaponized by an adversary. Adversaries may also obtain and use tools that were not originally designed for adversarial AI attacks as part of their attack.

AML.T0016.001.name: Software Tools
AML.T0016.001.summary: Adversaries may search for and obtain software tools to support their operations. Software designed for legitimate use may be repurposed by an adversary for malicious intent. An adversary may modify or customize software tools to achieve their purpose.
AML.T0016.001.description: Adversaries may search for and obtain software tools to support their operations. Software designed for legitimate use may be repurposed by an adversary for malicious intent. An adversary may modify or customize software tools to achieve their purpose. Software tools used to support attacks on AI systems are not necessarily AI-based themselves.

AML.T0016.002.name: Generative AI
AML.T0016.002.summary: Adversaries may search for and obtain generative AI models or tools, such as large language models (LLMs), to assist them in various steps of their operation.
AML.T0016.002.description:
Adversaries may search for and obtain generative AI models or tools, such as large language models (LLMs), to assist them in various steps of their operation. Generative AI can be used in a variety of malicious ways, such as to generate malware, to Generate Deepfakes, to Generate Malicious Commands, for Retrieval Content Crafting, or to generate Phishing content.
Adversaries may obtain open source models and serve them locally using frameworks such as Ollama or vLLM. They may host them using cloud infrastructure. Or, they may leverage AI service providers such as HuggingFace.
They may need to jailbreak the model (see LLM Jailbreak) to bypass any restrictions put in place to limit the types of responses it can generate. They may also need to break the terms of service of the model's developer.
Generative AI models may also be "uncensored" meaning they are designed to generate content without any restrictions such as guardrails or content filters. Uncensored GenAI is ripe for abuse by cybercriminals. Models may be fine-tuned to remove alignment and guardrails or be subjected to targeted manipulations to bypass refusal resulting in uncensored variants of the model. Uncensored models may be built for offensive and defensive cybersecurity, which can be abused by an adversary. There are also models that are expressly designed and advertised for malicious use.

mitigations.AML.M0001: Limit public release of production model artifacts that adversaries could acquire and adapt as operational capabilities.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Align generative models to resist and adversary's malicious requests and attempts to remove safety behavior.

AML.T0016.003.name: Exploits
AML.T0016.003.summary: Adversaries may search for and obtain exploits to support their operations. An exploit takes advantage of a bug or vulnerability in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur on computer hardware or software.
AML.T0016.003.description: Adversaries may search for and obtain exploits to support their operations. An exploit takes advantage of a bug or vulnerability in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur on computer hardware or software. Exploits may be downloaded from public repositories, acquired from private sources, purchased, stolen, or obtained from vulnerability research and exploit-sharing communities. An obtained exploit may be used without modification or serve as input to later adaptation or development.

AML.T0016.004.name: AI Agent Tools
AML.T0016.004.summary: Adversaries may search for and obtain tools that extend the capabilities of an AI agent. These capabilities may allow an agent to interact with operating systems, browsers, networks, cloud services, data stores, software repositories, identity systems, or other external resources.
AML.T0016.004.description:
Adversaries may search for and obtain tools that extend the capabilities of an AI agent. These capabilities may allow an agent to interact with operating systems, browsers, networks, cloud services, data stores, software repositories, identity systems, or other external resources.
AI agent tools may be distributed as Model Context Protocol servers, plugins, skills, connectors, function libraries, computer-use adapters, execution brokers, remote APIs, or similar integrations. Adversaries may obtain legitimate tools and configure them for malicious use, acquire modified or purpose-built tools, or combine multiple integrations into an operational toolset.
Agent tools may expose model-visible descriptions and executable interfaces that influence which capabilities an agent selects and how it invokes them. Obtaining these tools may give an agent access to resources, credentials, or actions that are unavailable through model inference alone.

AML.T0017.name: Develop Capabilities
AML.T0017.summary: Adversaries may develop their own capabilities to support operations. This process encompasses identifying requirements, building or adapting solutions, validating or packaging capabilities, and preparing them for deployment.
AML.T0017.description:
Adversaries may develop their own capabilities to support operations. This process encompasses identifying requirements, building or adapting solutions, validating or packaging capabilities, and preparing them for deployment. Capabilities used to support attacks on AI-enabled systems are not necessarily AI-based themselves. Adversaries may also use autonomous AI agents to iteratively develop capabilities, including exploit methods for known or previously unknown software vulnerabilities.
Examples include creating adversarial AI attacks, developing websites containing malicious instructions for AI agents, crafting malicious AI artifacts, building malware, or implementing software exploits.

AML.T0017.000.name: Adversarial AI Attacks
AML.T0017.000.summary: Adversaries may develop their own adversarial attacks. They may leverage existing libraries as a starting point (Adversarial AI Attack Implementations). They may implement ideas described in public research papers or develop custom made attacks for the victim model.
AML.T0017.000.description: Adversaries may develop their own adversarial attacks. They may leverage existing libraries as a starting point (Adversarial AI Attack Implementations). They may implement ideas described in public research papers or develop custom made attacks for the victim model.

AML.T0017.001.name: Autonomous Exploit Development
AML.T0017.001.summary: An autonomous AI agent may identify a software vulnerability and develop or materially adapt an exploit capability with limited human direction. The agent may analyze source code, documentation, service behavior, and error responses to infer a vulnerability and the conditions required to exploit it.
AML.T0017.001.description:
An autonomous AI agent may identify a software vulnerability and develop or materially adapt an exploit capability with limited human direction. The agent may analyze source code, documentation, service behavior, and error responses to infer a vulnerability and the conditions required to exploit it.
The agent may formulate and test vulnerability hypotheses, generate probes or payloads, interpret the results, and revise its approach through repeated action-observation cycles. It may combine multiple weaknesses into an exploit chain or package the resulting capability for later use. Validation may establish that the exploit produces the intended access, code execution, or other technical effect. The vulnerability may be publicly known or previously unknown.

mitigations.AML.M0035: Exercise autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploit development against authorized systems. Use demonstrated exploits to prioritize remediation, verify compensating controls, and improve detection of probing and exploit validation.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on adversary use of autonomous agents to develop exploits, including targeted software, identified vulnerabilities, and reported exploit capabilities. Use this intelligence to identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation and compensating controls, and update adversarial evaluations and detection procedures.

AML.T0017.002.name: AI Agent Tools
AML.T0017.002.summary: Adversaries may develop or materially adapt tools, integrations, or tool servers designed to extend the capabilities of an AI agent.
AML.T0017.002.description:
Adversaries may develop or materially adapt tools, integrations, or tool servers designed to extend the capabilities of an AI agent. These capabilities may allow an agent to interact with operating systems, browsers, networks, cloud services, data stores, software repositories, identity systems, or other external resources.
AI agent tools may be implemented as Model Context Protocol servers, plugins, skills, connectors, function libraries, computer-use adapters, execution brokers, remote APIs, or similar model-callable interfaces. Development may include creating executable functionality, model-visible tool descriptions, procedural instructions, input schemas, authentication methods, permission handling, or packaging needed to make a capability available to an agent.

AML.T0017.003.name: Malware
AML.T0017.003.summary: Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations. This may include creating or modifying malicious scripts, executables, libraries, or software packages to enable unauthorized access, execution, credential theft, collection, exfiltration, or disruption.
AML.T0017.003.description:
Adversaries may develop malware to support their operations. This may include creating or modifying malicious scripts, executables, libraries, or software packages to enable unauthorized access, execution, credential theft, collection, exfiltration, or disruption. Malware may be developed as a standalone capability or embedded within otherwise legitimate-looking software, such as a package that performs malicious actions when installed or imported.
Adversaries may use AI models or autonomous AI agents to generate malicious code, adapt existing implementations, and iteratively test and refine functionality. AI agents may translate high-level operational objectives into malware requirements. Development may include preparing the malicious code as an installable package for subsequent staging and delivery.

AML.T0018.name: Manipulate AI Model
AML.T0018.summary: Adversaries may manipulate an AI model artifact or its bundled components to change AI system behavior, introduce malicious code, or establish persistent malicious functionality. This may include modifying model weights, model architecture, or prompt-construction logic.
AML.T0018.description:
Adversaries may manipulate an AI model artifact or its bundled components to change AI system behavior, introduce malicious code, or establish persistent malicious functionality. This may include modifying model weights, model architecture, or prompt-construction logic.
Manipulated artifacts may retain expected behavior under ordinary conditions while activating malicious behavior only for selected inputs, contexts, or deployment conditions.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent tampering with AI artifacts and prevent unauthorized modification.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models against trusted baselines and representative adversarial inputs for behavior consistent with manipulation. Investigate unexplained regressions or input-dependent behavior and restrict deployment until findings are resolved.
mitigations.AML.M0013: Code signing provides a guarantee that the model has not been manipulated after signing took place.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Attempt controlled modification or substitution of models, weights, adapters, and related configuration. Remediate weaknesses in authorization, artifact integrity, deployment approval, monitoring, and recovery.

AML.T0018.000.name: Poison AI Model
AML.T0018.000.summary: Adversaries may manipulate an AI model's weights to change it's behavior or performance, resulting in a poisoned model. Adversaries may poison a model by directly manipulating its weights, training the model on poisoned data, further fine-tuning the model, or otherwise interfering with its training process.
AML.T0018.000.description:
Adversaries may manipulate an AI model's weights to change it's behavior or performance, resulting in a poisoned model. Adversaries may poison a model by directly manipulating its weights, training the model on poisoned data, further fine-tuning the model, or otherwise interfering with its training process.
The change in behavior of poisoned models may be limited to targeted categories in predictive AI models, or targeted topics, concepts, or facts in generative AI models, or aim for a general performance degradation.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent tampering with ML artifacts and prevent unauthorized copying.
mitigations.AML.M0007: Screen training data for poisoning that could introduce malicious model behavior. Quarantine and remediate affected data before training.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate trained and acquired models using clean evaluation data and targeted tests for backdoors, prediction bias, and other poisoning effects. Include measures beyond aggregate accuracy, which may remain normal in poisoned models.
mitigations.AML.M0013: Code signing provides a guarantee that the model has not been manipulated after signing took place.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify model weights and checkpoints against protected approval records before loading or deployment. Reject unauthorized substitutions or changes made after approval.
mitigations.AML.M0023: Record relationships between base models, checkpoints, fine-tuned derivatives, and deployed applications. Use these records to trace poisoned model versions to potentially affected derivatives and deployments and guide evaluation, replacement, or retraining.
