mitigations.AML.M0025: Dataset provenance can protect against poisoning of models.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Test whether controlled changes to model weights, fine-tuning, or associated artifacts can introduce targeted or persistent behavior. Improve model provenance, validation, integrity monitoring, and rollback.

AML.T0018.001.name: Modify AI Model Architecture
AML.T0018.001.summary: Adversaries may directly modify an AI model's architecture to re-define it's behavior. This can include adding or removing layers as well as adding pre or post-processing operations.
AML.T0018.001.description:
Adversaries may directly modify an AI model's architecture to re-define it's behavior. This can include adding or removing layers as well as adding pre or post-processing operations.
The effects could include removing the ability to predict certain classes, adding erroneous operations to increase computation costs, or degrading performance. Additionally, a separate adversary-defined network could be injected into the computation graph, which can change the behavior based on the inputs, effectively creating a backdoor.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent tampering with ML artifacts and prevent unauthorized copying.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models against trusted baselines for changes in class coverage, predictions, input-dependent behavior, or resource consumption caused by architecture or preprocessing modifications. Investigate unexplained deviations before deployment.
mitigations.AML.M0013: Code signing provides a guarantee that the model has not been manipulated after signing took place.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify model architecture definitions against approved manifests before loading or deployment. Reject unauthorized changes even when model weights remain unchanged.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Attempt controlled unauthorized changes to model architecture or executable model components. Verify review, integrity checking, signing, deployment approval, and restoration controls.

AML.T0018.002.name: Embed Malware
AML.T0018.002.summary: Adversaries may embed malicious code into AI Model files. AI models may be packaged as a combination of instructions and weights. Some formats such as pickle files are unsafe to deserialize because they can contain unsafe calls such as exec. Models with embedded malware may still operate as expected.
AML.T0018.002.description: Adversaries may embed malicious code into AI Model files. AI models may be packaged as a combination of instructions and weights. Some formats such as pickle files are unsafe to deserialize because they can contain unsafe calls such as exec. Models with embedded malware may still operate as expected. It may allow them to achieve Execution, Command & Control, or Exfiltrate Data.

mitigations.AML.M0013: Code signing provides a guarantee that the model has not been manipulated after signing took place.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify model packages against protected approval records before loading or deserialization. Reject unauthorized substitutions or changes that could introduce executable content.

AML.T0018.003.name: Modify Prompt Construction Logic
AML.T0018.003.summary: Adversaries may modify templates, role delimiters, embedded system instructions, tokenizer settings, tool-call formatting, or other artifact-bundled logic that constructs the context sent to an AI model. Model file formats such as GGUF can package this logic alongside model weights in a single distributable artifact.
AML.T0018.003.description: Adversaries may modify templates, role delimiters, embedded system instructions, tokenizer settings, tool-call formatting, or other artifact-bundled logic that constructs the context sent to an AI model. Model file formats such as GGUF can package this logic alongside model weights in a single distributable artifact. A compatible inference runtime may interpret the modified logic during future inference requests, enabling persistent covert instruction injection, altered instruction precedence, redirected tool use, or manipulated model output without changing model weights.

mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate model artifacts in the intended inference runtime with their bundled prompt-construction configuration. Test for altered instruction precedence or behavior caused by modified templates, role delimiters, or related configuration.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify bundled prompt templates, tokenizer configuration, embedded instructions, and tool configurations against protected approval records before interpretation. Reject unauthorized changes.

AML.T0020.name: Training Data Poisoning
AML.T0020.summary: Adversaries may manipulate data used for training or fine-tuning an AI model to influence the resulting model's behavior. Adversaries may add, remove, or modify data samples; alter labels or annotations; or manipulate feedback and data-collection processes.
AML.T0020.description:
Adversaries may manipulate data used for training or fine-tuning an AI model to influence the resulting model's behavior. Adversaries may add, remove, or modify data samples; alter labels or annotations; or manipulate feedback and data-collection processes.
Training data poisoning may cause targeted errors, introduce biased or unsafe behavior, degrade model performance, or embed backdoors activated by specific inputs. The resulting behavior may persist in the trained model after the poisoned data is no longer accessible.
Adversaries may poison data directly after gaining access to a training pipeline, or poisoned datasets may be introduced through Supply Chain Compromise.

mitigations.AML.M0001: Published datasets can be a target for poisoning attacks.
mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent tampering with ML artifacts and prevent unauthorized copying.
mitigations.AML.M0007: Screen training samples, labels, annotations, and metadata for poisoning. Quarantine and remediate affected data before training.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models against independently maintained evaluation data for targeted errors, backdoor behavior, or performance changes caused by poisoning. Repeat evaluation after dataset remediation and retraining.
mitigations.AML.M0014: Verify training datasets and annotations against protected manifests before training. Investigate unexpected additions, removals, or changes, and update reference values only through an authorized approval process.
mitigations.AML.M0023: Record training and fine-tuning dataset identities, versions, and relationships to derived models and deployed applications. Use these records to trace poisoned data to affected models and applications and guide dataset replacement, model reevaluation, or retraining.
mitigations.AML.M0025: Dataset provenance can protect against poisoning of training data
mitigations.AML.M0035: Introduce controlled poisoned records or triggers into representative data pipelines. Verify and improve provenance, sanitization, review, drift detection, model validation, and rollback controls.

AML.T0021.name: Establish Accounts
AML.T0021.summary: Adversaries may create accounts with various services for use in targeting, to gain access to resources needed to further their operations, or for victim impersonation.
AML.T0021.description:
Adversaries may create accounts with various services for use in targeting, to gain access to resources needed to further their operations, or for victim impersonation.
Adversaries may establish pools of AI service accounts through bulk or fraudulent registration. These accounts may exploit promotional credits, educational or startup programs, or premium subscriptions. They may register accounts directly or use account merchants and third parties that supply registration resources, such as SMS verification services and payment arrangements. Registration arrangements may obscure the operator's country of origin, and related accounts may share registration attributes or payment instruments.
Established accounts can supply upstream access for AI Service Proxies to serve as "transfer stations" for gray-market resellers. Adversaries may also purposefully route requests through proxies for Centralized AI Service Request Routing to avoid policy enforcement and evade detection.
Adversaries or autonomous AI agents may establish accounts and cultivate personas on social media (e.g. Facebook, LinkedIn, X), software hosting (e.g. GitHub, GitLab), or AI artifact hosting (e.g. Hugging Face) sites. Account creation supplies the identities used for subsequent Impersonation and Phishing activities.
Autonomous AI agents may independently select services and create accounts as prerequisites for subsequent attack activity, without a human directing each registration. Agents may obtain verification messages through controlled mailboxes, switch proxies to overcome account registration restrictions, or use visual recognition and audio matching to solve human verification challenges such as CAPTCHAs.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Verify identities before granting access to model registries so newly established accounts cannot automatically access protected AI artifacts.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Verify identities before granting production AI access so newly established accounts cannot automatically access protected AI services.
mitigations.AML.M0043: Disable or delete agent-created external service accounts when authorization ends to limit their availability for subsequent unauthorized operations.

AML.T0024.name: Exfiltration via AI Inference API
AML.T0024.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate information from a victim-controlled AI model or service through responses returned by its inference API. Transferred information may include predictions, scores, embeddings, generated content (e.g. text or images), or other sensitive information disclosed in model responses.
AML.T0024.description:
Adversaries may exfiltrate information from a victim-controlled AI model or service through responses returned by its inference API. Transferred information may include predictions, scores, embeddings, generated content (e.g. text or images), or other sensitive information disclosed in model responses. Responses may be received directly or relayed through an intermediary.
Adversaries may submit inputs designed to cause information to be returned through ordinary API response fields or streaming outputs. The inference API response serves as the transfer channel, including when adversaries use valid accounts or credentials to obtain responses as part of an unauthorized extraction operation.
Received responses may be gathered as Outputs from AI Models, analyzed to obtain Training Data Information from AI Models, used to Craft Adversarial Data, or to Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs.

mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit the volume of API queries in a given period of time to regulate the amount and fidelity of potentially sensitive information an attacker can learn.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Adversaries can use unrestricted API access to build a proxy training dataset and reveal private information.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if sensitive data has been exfiltrated.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Exercise inference interfaces for membership inference, model inversion, and functional extraction. Use findings to improve privacy controls, authentication, output restriction, rate limits, and monitoring.

AML.T0025.name: Exfiltration via Cyber Means
AML.T0025.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate AI artifacts or other information relevant to their goals via traditional cyber means.
AML.T0025.description:
Adversaries may exfiltrate AI artifacts or other information relevant to their goals via traditional cyber means.
See the ATT&CK Exfiltration tactic for more information.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent exfiltration.

AML.T0029.name: Denial of AI Service
AML.T0029.summary: Adversaries may target AI-enabled systems with a flood of requests for the purpose of degrading or shutting down the service. Since many AI systems require significant amounts of specialized compute, they are often expensive bottlenecks that can become overloaded.
AML.T0029.description: Adversaries may target AI-enabled systems with a flood of requests for the purpose of degrading or shutting down the service. Since many AI systems require significant amounts of specialized compute, they are often expensive bottlenecks that can become overloaded. Adversaries can intentionally craft inputs that require heavy amounts of useless compute from the AI system.

mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit the number of queries users can perform in a given interval to prevent a denial of service.
mitigations.AML.M0015: Assess queries before inference call or enforce timeout policy for queries which consume excessive resources.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Access controls on model APIs can prevent an adversary from excessively querying and disabling the system.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Submit adversarial workloads and exercise dependency failures that could exhaust inference or supporting services. Apply quotas, concurrency limits, timeouts, resource isolation, and graceful degradation based on findings.
mitigations.AML.M0036: Limit the resources consumed by individual requests to reduce denial of service from computationally expensive inputs.

AML.T0031.name: Erode AI Model Integrity
AML.T0031.summary: Adversaries may degrade the target model's performance with adversarial data inputs to erode confidence in the system over time. This can lead to the victim organization wasting time and money both attempting to fix the system and performing the tasks it was meant to automate by hand.
AML.T0031.description: Adversaries may degrade the target model's performance with adversarial data inputs to erode confidence in the system over time. This can lead to the victim organization wasting time and money both attempting to fix the system and performing the tasks it was meant to automate by hand.

mitigations.AML.M0003: Hardened models are less susceptible to integrity attacks.
mitigations.AML.M0006: Using multiple different models increases robustness to attack.
mitigations.AML.M0010: Preprocessing model inputs can prevent malicious data from going through the machine learning pipeline.
mitigations.AML.M0015: Incorporate adversarial input detection into the pipeline before inputs reach the model.

AML.T0034.name: Cost Harvesting
AML.T0034.summary: Adversaries may deliberately drive a victim's AI services beyond normal operating capacity with the intent of increasing the cost of services. This may be achieved via high-volume, low-complexity queries (Excessive Queries) or low-volume, high-complexity queries (Resource-Intensive Queries).
AML.T0034.description:
Adversaries may deliberately drive a victim's AI services beyond normal operating capacity with the intent of increasing the cost of services. This may be achieved via high-volume, low-complexity queries (Excessive Queries) or low-volume, high-complexity queries (Resource-Intensive Queries). In Generative AI or Agentic AI systems, adversarial prompts may be introduced into the model's context to cause (Agentic Resource Consumption).
Unlike resource hijacking, where adversaries may leverage AI resources such as computational, memory, or storage for their own purposes, cost harvesting focuses on resource-centric pressure to a service to ultimately cause financial harm to the victim.
Cost Harvesting is especially relevant for cloud-hosted, pay-per-use AI/ML platforms (e.g., LLM APIs, generative image services, vision-language pipelines). By manipulating request volume or request complexity, an attacker can: - Inflate the victim's compute or storage consumption, leading to higher operational costs. - Trigger autoscaling mechanisms that provision additional resources, further amplifying cost and exposure. - Saturate internal queues or GPU/TPU pipelines, causing latency spikes, request throttling, or outright service unavailability for legitimate users.

mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit the number of queries users can perform in a given interval to hinder an attacker's ability to send computationally expensive inputs
mitigations.AML.M0019: Access controls can limit API access and prevent cost harvesting.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Exercise requests and workflows designed to amplify inference, infrastructure, or external-service costs. Verify budgets, quotas, rate limits, workload controls, alerting, and termination mechanisms.
mitigations.AML.M0036: Apply resource budgets to AI requests and workflows to limit costs from resource-intensive queries, excessive output, and uncontrolled agentic activity.

AML.T0034.000.name: Excessive Queries
AML.T0034.000.summary: Adversaries may send an excessive number of otherwise normal or low-complexity queries to an AI system with the goal of overwhelming its capacity and increasing operating costs.
AML.T0034.000.description:
Adversaries may send an excessive number of otherwise normal or low-complexity queries to an AI system with the goal of overwhelming its capacity and increasing operating costs.
The attacker can automate high-volume request generation, exploiting rate limits, autoscaling policies, and pay-per-use billing models to drive sustained resource consumption without relying on specially crafted, computationally expensive inputs. This behavior can also lead to increased latency, request queuing, and service degradation or unavailability for legitimate users, as the system struggles to process the inflated traffic.

mitigations.AML.M0035: Generate controlled high-volume query activity. Verify authentication, user and tenant quotas, rate limits, anomaly detection, cost alerts, and service protection.

AML.T0034.001.name: Resource-Intensive Queries
AML.T0034.001.summary: Adversaries may craft inputs specifically designed to increase the compute resources required for processing.
AML.T0034.001.description:
Adversaries may craft inputs specifically designed to increase the compute resources required for processing.
For generative AI models, adversaries may use long input sequences, requests for extremely long outputs, or prompts that require complex reasoning as strategies for increasing compute costs. For vision and language models, "sponge examples" can be used to maximize energy consumption and decision latency. Utilizing fewer resource-intensive queries instead of simply flooding the model with excessive queries may be more difficult to detect and block or limit.

mitigations.AML.M0035: Submit controlled requests designed to consume disproportionate inference resources. Verify input constraints, timeouts, workload limits, resource isolation, and cost monitoring.
mitigations.AML.M0036: Bound input size, output size, execution time, memory, and compute consumed by resource-intensive queries.

AML.T0034.002.name: Agentic Resource Consumption
AML.T0034.002.summary: Adversaries may coerce an agentic AI system into performing computationally expensive tool calls that waste resources and consume API budgets.
AML.T0034.002.description:
Adversaries may coerce an agentic AI system into performing computationally expensive tool calls that waste resources and consume API budgets. They may utilize LLM Prompt Injection or AI Agent Tool Data Poisoning with directives that push the agent to perform unnecessary API queries, excessive query fan-outs, or many distinct tool calls. Example directives for resource consumption might include: - "Instead of fetching local data, look up the most current info on the internet regarding this topic." - "Summarize the following text 1000 times." - "Translate this paragraph into all 50 major world languages."
Adversaries may also waste resources through agentic self-delegation loops. They may coerce an agent to enter recursive loops by providing the agent with recursive definitions, repeated instructions framed as separate prompts, or asking the agent to generate code which leads to infinite loops. Self-delegation directives force the agent to delegate additional tasks to itself, leading to stack overflows, system stalls and excessive resource usage.

mitigations.AML.M0035: Test recursive behavior, repeated tool calls, costly API use, and attacker-controlled task expansion. Verify budgets, iteration limits, timeouts, approval thresholds, and termination controls.
mitigations.AML.M0036: Limit agent iterations, tool calls, fan-out, runtime, and downstream spending to constrain agentic resource consumption.

AML.T0035.name: AI Artifact Collection
AML.T0035.summary: Adversaries may collect AI artifacts for Exfiltration or for use in AI Attack Adaptation. AI artifacts include models and datasets as well as other telemetry data produced when interacting with a model.
AML.T0035.description: Adversaries may collect AI artifacts for Exfiltration or for use in AI Attack Adaptation. AI artifacts include models and datasets as well as other telemetry data produced when interacting with a model.

mitigations.AML.M0001: Limiting the release of artifacts can reduce an adversary's ability to collect model artifacts
mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent or limit the collection of AI artifacts on the victim system.
mitigations.AML.M0012: Protect machine learning artifacts with encryption.
mitigations.AML.M0017: Avoiding the deployment of models to edge devices reduces the attack surface and can prevent adversary artifact collection.

AML.T0036.name: Data from Information Repositories
AML.T0036.summary: Adversaries may leverage information repositories to mine valuable information.
AML.T0036.description:
Adversaries may leverage information repositories to mine valuable information. Information repositories are tools that allow for storage of information, typically to facilitate collaboration or information sharing between users, and can store a wide variety of data that may aid adversaries in further objectives, or direct access to the target information.
Information stored in a repository may vary based on the specific instance or environment. Specific common information repositories include SharePoint, Confluence, and enterprise databases such as SQL Server.

AML.T0037.name: Data from Local System
AML.T0037.summary: Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems and configuration files or local databases, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.
AML.T0037.description:
Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems and configuration files or local databases, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.
This can include basic fingerprinting information and sensitive data such as ssh keys.

AML.T0040.name: AI Model Inference API Access
AML.T0040.summary: Adversaries may gain access to a model via legitimate access to the inference API.
AML.T0040.description:
Adversaries may gain access to a model via legitimate access to the inference API. Inference API access can be a source of information to the adversary (Discover AI Model Ontology, Discover AI Model Family), a means of staging the attack (Verify Attack, Craft Adversarial Data), or for introducing data to the target system for Impact (Evade AI Model, Erode AI Model Integrity).
Many systems rely on the same models provided via an inference API, which means they share the same vulnerabilities. This is especially true of foundation models which are prohibitively resource intensive to train. Adversaries may use their access to model APIs to identify vulnerabilities such as jailbreaks or hallucinations and then target applications that use the same models.

mitigations.AML.M0019: Adversaries can use unrestricted API access to gain information about a production system, stage attacks, and introduce malicious data to the system.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help audit API usage of the model.
mitigations.AML.M0039: Honeypots capture which endpoints adversaries are targeting and how they use discovered inference APIs: the models they're interested in, the parameters they use, and the payloads they submit once they reach a live endpoint.

AML.T0041.name: Physical Environment Access
AML.T0041.summary: In addition to the attacks that take place purely in the digital domain, adversaries may also exploit the physical environment for their attacks. If the model is interacting with data collected from the real world in some way, the adversary can influence the model through access to wherever the data is being collected.
AML.T0041.description: In addition to the attacks that take place purely in the digital domain, adversaries may also exploit the physical environment for their attacks. If the model is interacting with data collected from the real world in some way, the adversary can influence the model through access to wherever the data is being collected. By modifying the data in the collection process, the adversary can perform modified versions of attacks designed for digital access.

mitigations.AML.M0009: Using a variety of sensors can make it more difficult for an attacker with physical access to compromise and produce malicious results.

AML.T0042.name: Verify Attack
AML.T0042.summary: Adversaries can verify the efficacy of their attack via an inference API or access to an offline copy of the target model. This gives the adversary confidence that their approach works and allows them to carry out the attack at a later time of their choosing.
AML.T0042.description: Adversaries can verify the efficacy of their attack via an inference API or access to an offline copy of the target model. This gives the adversary confidence that their approach works and allows them to carry out the attack at a later time of their choosing. The adversary may verify the attack once but use it against many edge devices running copies of the target model. The adversary may verify their attack digitally, then deploy it in the Physical Environment Access at a later time. Verifying the attack may be hard to detect since the adversary can use a minimal number of queries or an offline copy of the model.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Obfuscating model outputs reduces an adversary's ability to verify the efficacy of an attack.
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit repeated queries used to test and refine an attack against the target model.
mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls on models at rest can prevent an adversary's ability to verify attack efficacy.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Use access controls in production to prevent adversary's ability to verify attack efficacy.
mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses to suspected attack verification queries to limit the reliability of feedback used to confirm an attack's effectiveness against the target model.

AML.T0043.name: Craft Adversarial Data
AML.T0043.summary: Adversarial data are inputs to an AI model that have been modified such that they cause the adversary's desired effect in the target model. Effects can range from misclassification, to missed detections, to maximizing energy consumption.
AML.T0043.description:
Adversarial data are inputs to an AI model that have been modified such that they cause the adversary's desired effect in the target model. Effects can range from misclassification, to missed detections, to maximizing energy consumption. Typically, the modification is constrained in magnitude or location so that a human still perceives the data as if it were unmodified, but human perceptibility may not always be a concern depending on the adversary's intended effect. For example, an adversarial input for an image classification task is an image the AI model would misclassify, but a human would still recognize as containing the correct class.
Depending on the adversary's knowledge of and access to the target model, the adversary may use different classes of algorithms to develop the adversarial example such as White-Box Optimization, Black-Box Optimization, Black-Box Transfer, or Manual Modification.
The adversary may perform Verify Attack to confirm that their approach works if they have white-box or inference API access to the model. This allows the adversary to gain confidence their attack is effective in a live environment where their attack may be noticed. They can then use the attack at a later time to accomplish their goals. An adversary may optimize adversarial examples for Evade AI Model, or to Erode AI Model Integrity.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Obfuscating model outputs reduces an adversary's ability to generate effective adversarial data.
mitigations.AML.M0003: Hardened models are more robust to adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit volume of model queries to prevent or slow an adversary's ability to create adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0006: Using an ensemble of models increases the difficulty of crafting effective adversarial data and improves overall robustness.
mitigations.AML.M0010: Input restoration can help remediate adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0015: Incorporate adversarial input detection to block malicious inputs at inference time.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Access controls on model APIs can restrict an adversary's access required to generate adversarial data.
mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected adversarial activity to limit feedback used to optimize adversarial inputs against the target model.

AML.T0043.000.name: White-Box Optimization
AML.T0043.000.summary: In White-Box Optimization, the adversary has full access to the target model and optimizes the adversarial example directly. Adversarial examples trained in this manner are most effective against the target model.
AML.T0043.000.description: In White-Box Optimization, the adversary has full access to the target model and optimizes the adversarial example directly. Adversarial examples trained in this manner are most effective against the target model.

mitigations.AML.M0003: Hardened models are more robust to adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can reduce unnecessary access to AI models and prevent an adversary from achieving white-box access.
mitigations.AML.M0006: Using an ensemble of models increases the difficulty of crafting effective adversarial data and improves overall robustness.
mitigations.AML.M0010: Input restoration can help remediate adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0015: Incorporate adversarial input detection to block malicious inputs at inference time.
mitigations.AML.M0017: With full access to the model, an adversary could perform white-box attacks.

AML.T0043.001.name: Black-Box Optimization
AML.T0043.001.summary: In Black-Box attacks, the adversary has black-box (i.e. AI Model Inference API Access via API access) access to the target model. With black-box attacks, the adversary may be using an API that the victim is monitoring.
AML.T0043.001.description: In Black-Box attacks, the adversary has black-box (i.e. AI Model Inference API Access via API access) access to the target model. With black-box attacks, the adversary may be using an API that the victim is monitoring. These attacks are generally less effective and require more inferences than White-Box Optimization attacks, but they require much less access.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Obfuscating model outputs reduces an adversary's ability to create effective adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0003: Hardened models are more robust to adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit volume of model queries to prevent or slow an adversary's ability to perform black-box optimization attacks.
mitigations.AML.M0006: Using an ensemble of models increases the difficulty of crafting effective adversarial data and improves overall robustness.
mitigations.AML.M0010: Input restoration adds an extra layer of unknowns and randomness when an adversary evaluates the input-output relationship.
mitigations.AML.M0015: Monitor queries and query patterns to the target model, block access if suspicious queries are detected.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Access controls on model APIs can deny adversaries the access required for black-box optimization methods.
mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected adversarial activity to limit feedback used to optimize adversarial inputs against the target model.

AML.T0043.002.name: Black-Box Transfer
AML.T0043.002.summary: In Black-Box Transfer attacks, the adversary uses one or more proxy models (trained via Replicate AI Model Behavior or Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs) they have full access to and are representative of the target model.
AML.T0043.002.description: In Black-Box Transfer attacks, the adversary uses one or more proxy models (trained via Replicate AI Model Behavior or Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs) they have full access to and are representative of the target model. The adversary uses White-Box Optimization on the proxy models to generate adversarial examples. If the set of proxy models are close enough to the target model, the adversarial example should generalize from one to another. This means that an attack that works for the proxy models will likely then work for the target model. If the adversary has AI Model Inference API Access, they may use Verify Attack to confirm the attack is working and incorporate that information into their training process.

mitigations.AML.M0003: Hardened models are more robust to adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0006: Using an ensemble of models increases the difficulty of crafting effective adversarial data and improves overall robustness.
mitigations.AML.M0010: Input restoration can help remediate adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0015: Incorporate adversarial input detection to block malicious inputs at inference time.

AML.T0043.003.name: Manual Modification
AML.T0043.003.summary: Adversaries may manually modify the input data to craft adversarial data. They may use their knowledge of the target model to modify parts of the data they suspect helps the model in performing its task. The adversary may use trial and error until they are able to verify they have a working adversarial input.
AML.T0043.003.description: Adversaries may manually modify the input data to craft adversarial data. They may use their knowledge of the target model to modify parts of the data they suspect helps the model in performing its task. The adversary may use trial and error until they are able to verify they have a working adversarial input.

mitigations.AML.M0003: Hardened models are more robust to adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit volume of model queries to prevent or slow an adversary's ability to refine manually crafted adversarial inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0006: Using an ensemble of models increases the difficulty of crafting effective adversarial data and improves overall robustness.
mitigations.AML.M0010: Input restoration can help remediate adversarial inputs.

AML.T0043.004.name: Insert Backdoor Trigger
AML.T0043.004.summary: The adversary may add a perceptual trigger into inference data. The trigger may be imperceptible or non-obvious to humans. This technique is used in conjunction with Poison AI Model and allows the adversary to produce their desired effect in the target model.
AML.T0043.004.description: The adversary may add a perceptual trigger into inference data. The trigger may be imperceptible or non-obvious to humans. This technique is used in conjunction with Poison AI Model and allows the adversary to produce their desired effect in the target model.

AML.T0044.name: Full AI Model Access
AML.T0044.summary: Adversaries may gain full "white-box" access to an AI model. This means the adversary has complete knowledge of the model architecture, its parameters, and class ontology. They may exfiltrate the model to Craft Adversarial Data and Verify Attack in an offline environment where it is hard to detect their behavior.
AML.T0044.description: Adversaries may gain full "white-box" access to an AI model. This means the adversary has complete knowledge of the model architecture, its parameters, and class ontology. They may exfiltrate the model to Craft Adversarial Data and Verify Attack in an offline environment where it is hard to detect their behavior.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls on models and data at rest can help prevent full model access.
mitigations.AML.M0017: Not distributing the model in software to edge devices, can limit an adversary's ability to gain full access to the model.

AML.T0046.name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data
AML.T0046.summary: Adversaries may spam the AI system with chaff data that causes increase in the number of detections. This can cause analysts at the victim organization to waste time reviewing and correcting incorrect inferences.
AML.T0046.description:
Adversaries may spam the AI system with chaff data that causes increase in the number of detections. This can cause analysts at the victim organization to waste time reviewing and correcting incorrect inferences.
Adversaries may also spam AI agents with excessive low-severity auditable events or agentic actions that require a human-in-the-loop, wasting time for the victim organization in human review of the agentic AI system.

mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit volume and rate of queries to protect the system from chaff data spam.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Authentication on production models can help prevent anonymous chaff data spam.

AML.T0047.name: AI-Enabled Product or Service
AML.T0047.summary: Adversaries may use a product or service that uses artificial intelligence under the hood to gain access to the underlying AI model. This type of indirect model access may reveal details of the AI model or its inferences in logs or metadata.
AML.T0047.description: Adversaries may use a product or service that uses artificial intelligence under the hood to gain access to the underlying AI model. This type of indirect model access may reveal details of the AI model or its inferences in logs or metadata.

mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if sensitive model information has been sent to an attacker.

AML.T0048.name: External Harms
AML.T0048.summary: Adversaries may abuse their access to a victim system and use its resources or capabilities to further their goals by causing harms external to that system. These harms could affect the organization (e.g. Financial Harm, Reputational Harm), its users (e.g. User Harm), or the general public (e.g. Societal Harm).
AML.T0048.description: Adversaries may abuse their access to a victim system and use its resources or capabilities to further their goals by causing harms external to that system. These harms could affect the organization (e.g. Financial Harm, Reputational Harm), its users (e.g. User Harm), or the general public (e.g. Societal Harm).

AML.T0048.000.name: Financial Harm
AML.T0048.000.summary: Financial harm involves the loss of wealth, property, or other monetary assets due to theft, fraud or forgery, or pressure to provide financial resources to the adversary.
AML.T0048.000.description: Financial harm involves the loss of wealth, property, or other monetary assets due to theft, fraud or forgery, or pressure to provide financial resources to the adversary.

AML.T0048.001.name: Reputational Harm
AML.T0048.001.summary: Reputational harm involves a degradation of public perception and trust in organizations. Examples of reputation-harming incidents include scandals or false impersonations.
AML.T0048.001.description: Reputational harm involves a degradation of public perception and trust in organizations. Examples of reputation-harming incidents include scandals or false impersonations.

AML.T0048.002.name: Societal Harm
AML.T0048.002.summary: Societal harms might generate harmful outcomes that reach either the general public or specific vulnerable groups such as the exposure of children to vulgar content.
AML.T0048.002.description: Societal harms might generate harmful outcomes that reach either the general public or specific vulnerable groups such as the exposure of children to vulgar content.

AML.T0048.003.name: User Harm
AML.T0048.003.summary: User harms may encompass a variety of harm types including financial and reputational that are directed at or felt by individual victims of the attack rather than at the organization level.
AML.T0048.003.description: User harms may encompass a variety of harm types including financial and reputational that are directed at or felt by individual victims of the attack rather than at the organization level.

AML.T0048.004.name: AI Intellectual Property Theft
AML.T0048.004.summary: Adversaries may appropriate AI-related intellectual property in a manner that causes economic or competitive harm to the victim organization. Targeted material may include model architectures and weights, training data, or model behaviors and capabilities.
AML.T0048.004.description:
Adversaries may appropriate AI-related intellectual property in a manner that causes economic or competitive harm to the victim organization. Targeted material may include model architectures and weights, training data, or model behaviors and capabilities.
Adversaries may steal AI models or other artifacts via exfiltration from the victim system. Access may be obtained through Valid Accounts, exposed storage, misconfigured permissions, or exploitation of systems that store or serve the AI artifacts. Alternatively, adversaries may collect Outputs from AI Models to Replicate AI Model Behavior without obtaining the original model artifacts. Model training approaches include knowledge distillation, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.
Adversaries may use a stolen or replicated model internally themselves, sell or distribute it, offer competing AI services, or incorporate its capabilities into their own products without compensating the model owner. Possession of the model also allows adversaries to modify or fine-tune it and operate outside the original provider's access controls, usage restrictions, and monitoring. These activities may reduce the victim's competitive advantage and undermine the exclusivity of proprietary AI capabilities.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Access controls can prevent theft of intellectual property.
mitigations.AML.M0012: Protect machine learning artifacts with encryption.
mitigations.AML.M0017: Avoiding the deployment of models to edge devices reduces an adversary's potential access to models or AI artifacts.

AML.T0049.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
AML.T0049.summary: Adversaries may attempt to take advantage of a weakness in an Internet-facing computer or program using software, data, or commands in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior. The weakness in the system can be a bug, a glitch, or a design vulnerability.
AML.T0049.description: Adversaries may attempt to take advantage of a weakness in an Internet-facing computer or program using software, data, or commands in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior. The weakness in the system can be a bug, a glitch, or a design vulnerability. These applications are often websites, but can include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other applications with Internet accessible open sockets, such as web servers and related services.

mitigations.AML.M0039: Honeypots can safely absorb real attacks and exploit attempts, turning payloads into mapped defensive signatures for a potential target without risking real assets.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on adversary use of exploits, including zero-day vulnerabilities, against public-facing applications. Use this intelligence to identify exposed applications, prioritize remediation and compensating controls, and update detection and response procedures.

AML.T0050.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
AML.T0050.summary: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. These interfaces and languages provide ways of interacting with computer systems and are a common feature across many different platforms.
AML.T0050.description:
Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. These interfaces and languages provide ways of interacting with computer systems and are a common feature across many different platforms. Most systems come with some built-in command-line interface and scripting capabilities, for example, macOS and Linux distributions include some flavor of Unix Shell while Windows installations include the Windows Command Shell and PowerShell.
There are also cross-platform interpreters such as Python, as well as those commonly associated with client applications such as JavaScript and Visual Basic.
Adversaries may abuse these technologies in various ways as a means of executing arbitrary commands. Commands and scripts can be embedded in Initial Access payloads delivered to victims as lure documents or as secondary payloads downloaded from an existing C2. Adversaries may also execute commands through interactive terminals/shells, as well as utilize various Remote Services in order to achieve remote Execution.

mitigations.AML.M0011: Restrict library loading so command and script interpreters cannot load untrusted libraries as an execution mechanism.

AML.T0051.name: LLM Prompt Injection
AML.T0051.summary: An adversary may craft malicious prompts as inputs to an LLM that cause the LLM to act in unintended ways. These "prompt injections" are often designed to cause the model to ignore aspects of its original instructions and follow the adversary's instructions instead.
AML.T0051.description:
An adversary may craft malicious prompts as inputs to an LLM that cause the LLM to act in unintended ways. These "prompt injections" are often designed to cause the model to ignore aspects of its original instructions and follow the adversary's instructions instead.
Prompt Injections can be an initial access vector to the LLM that provides the adversary with a foothold to carry out other steps in their operation. They may be designed to bypass defenses in the LLM, or allow the adversary to issue privileged commands. The effects of a prompt injection can persist throughout an interactive session with an LLM.
Malicious prompts may be injected directly by the adversary (Direct) either to leverage the LLM to generate harmful content or to gain a foothold on the system and lead to further effects. Prompts may also be injected indirectly when the LLM, as part of its normal operation, ingests the malicious prompt from another data source (Indirect). This type of injection can be used by the adversary to gain a foothold on the system or to target the user of the LLM. Malicious prompts may also be Triggered by user actions or system events.

mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models for task redirection by malicious instructions in user inputs, retrieved material, or other model-visible content. Test instruction and data boundaries in the intended deployment configuration and use failures to guide remediation or deployment restrictions.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Use access controls in production to prevent adversaries from injecting malicious prompts.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Screen user inputs, retrieved content, and tool responses for instructions that attempt to override authorized behavior. Apply independent checks to resulting outputs and proposed actions, blocking or routing suspicious activity for review before it reaches users or downstream systems.
mitigations.AML.M0021: Model guidelines can instruct the model to refuse a response to unsafe inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Model alignment can improve the parametric safety of a model by guiding it away from unsafe prompts and responses.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if unsafe prompts have been submitted to the LLM.
mitigations.AML.M0033: Validation can prevent adversaries from executing prompt injections that could affect agentic workflows.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Test direct, indirect, and triggered instructions through user input, retrieved data, documents, messages, websites, images, metadata, and tool output. Remediate trust-boundary, instruction-handling, permission, and monitoring failures.

AML.T0051.000.name: Direct
AML.T0051.000.summary: An adversary may inject prompts directly as a user of the LLM. This type of injection may be used by the adversary to gain a foothold in the system or to misuse the LLM itself, as for example to generate harmful content.
AML.T0051.000.description: An adversary may inject prompts directly as a user of the LLM. This type of injection may be used by the adversary to gain a foothold in the system or to misuse the LLM itself, as for example to generate harmful content.

mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if unsafe prompts have been submitted to the LLM.
mitigations.AML.M0033: Validation can prevent adversaries from executing prompt injections that could affect agentic workflows.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Submit controlled malicious instructions directly through user-facing model and application interfaces. Improve instruction enforcement, input controls, authorization, and monitoring.

AML.T0051.001.name: Indirect
AML.T0051.001.summary: An adversary may inject prompts indirectly via a separate data channel that the LLM or AI agent ingests, such as text or multimedia pulled from documents, emails, databases or websites.
AML.T0051.001.description:
An adversary may inject prompts indirectly via a separate data channel that the LLM or AI agent ingests, such as text or multimedia pulled from documents, emails, databases or websites. These instructions originate from adversary-controlled content rather than the legitimate user, and are frequently hidden or obfuscated (See LLM Prompt Obfuscation) from the user, for example as invisible text.
Adversaries may use this to hijack an agent or LLM in order to gain a foothold in the target system or to act against an unwitting user of that system, inheriting whatever privileges the AI system holds. Adversaries may also stage the lure that causes the content to be reached (See AI Agent Clickbait), or use the resulting foothold to establish persistence (See AI Agent Context Poisoning).
Indirect prompt injections have been observed in the wild, with potential impact ranging from harmless pranks, to search engine optimization manipulation, data exfiltration, and destructive actions.

mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if unsafe prompts have been submitted to the LLM.
mitigations.AML.M0033: Validation can prevent adversaries from executing prompt injections that could affect agentic workflows.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Place controlled malicious instructions in external or retrieved content processed by the system. Improve content trust boundaries, retrieval controls, instruction isolation, and restrictions on resulting actions.

AML.T0051.002.name: Triggered
AML.T0051.002.summary: An adversary may trigger a prompt injection via a user action or event that occurs within the victim's environment. Triggered prompt injections often target AI agents, which can be activated by means the adversary identifies during Discovery (See Activation Triggers).
AML.T0051.002.description: An adversary may trigger a prompt injection via a user action or event that occurs within the victim's environment. Triggered prompt injections often target AI agents, which can be activated by means the adversary identifies during Discovery (See Activation Triggers). These malicious prompts may be hidden or obfuscated from the user and may already exist somewhere in the victim's environment from the adversary performing Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application. This type of injection may be used by the adversary to gain a foothold in the system or to target an unwitting user of the system.

mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if unsafe prompts have been submitted to the LLM.
mitigations.AML.M0033: Validation can prevent adversaries from executing prompt injections that could affect agentic workflows.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Place controlled instructions in content or workflows where later user actions or system events activate them. Verify trigger authorization, context handling, action restrictions, and monitoring.

AML.T0052.name: Phishing
AML.T0052.summary: Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary.
AML.T0052.description:
Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.
Generative AI, including LLMs that generate synthetic text, visual deepfakes of faces, and audio deepfakes of speech (See Generate Deepfakes), is enabling adversaries to scale targeted phishing campaigns (See Spearphishing via Social Engineering LLM). LLMs can interact with users via text conversations and can be programmed with a system prompt to phish for sensitive information. Deepfakes can also be used in Impersonation as an aid to phishing.

mitigations.AML.M0018: Train users to identify phishing attempts by an adversary to reduce the risk of successful spearphishing, social engineering, and other techniques that involve user interaction.
mitigations.AML.M0034: Deepfake detection can be used to identify and block phishing attempts that use generated content.

AML.T0052.000.name: Spearphishing via Social Engineering LLM
AML.T0052.000.summary: Adversaries may use large language models (LLMs) or LLM-based AI agents to conduct targeted social engineering through electronically delivered messages and conversations.
AML.T0052.000.description:
Adversaries may use large language models (LLMs) or LLM-based AI agents to conduct targeted social engineering through electronically delivered messages and conversations. The model may generate content for an operator to deliver, or in the case of an AI agent connected to communication tools, it may autonomously select recipients, develop pretexts, send messages, and manage follow-up interactions. Objectives may include inducing a target to disclose sensitive information, execute malicious content, grant access, or approve a software change that enables compromise.
AI agents may select and conduct spearphishing without a human prescribing the social engineering approach or directing each interaction. This behavior may also arise while an agent pursues an initially legitimate objective, if its selected methods cross authorization or trust boundaries. An agent may use information gathered about a target to tailor its language, persona, and requests, then adapt subsequent messages based on replies and other observations.
Communications may occur through email, code-hosting or messaging platforms, file-transfer notifications, or other services that reach selected individuals. AI agents may sustain interactions across channels, deliver malicious files or links, and follow up with requests intended to induce execution or approval.
An AI agent may coordinate communications across multiple controlled identities, tailoring their content and timing to appear independent. Supporting messages may endorse a malicious contribution, challenge a security warning, or pressure a recipient to approve or execute content. This false corroboration can support a sustained persuasion attempt rather than a single generated message.

mitigations.AML.M0018: Train users to identify phishing attempts and understand that AI can be used to generate targeted and convincing messages.
mitigations.AML.M0034: Deepfake detection can be used to identify and block phishing attempts that use generated content.

AML.T0052.001.name: Deepfake-Assisted Phishing
AML.T0052.001.summary: Adversaries may use deepfakes (AI-generated synthetic images, audio, or video) in phishing campaigns to impersonate trusted individuals, executives, or organizations.
AML.T0052.001.description:
Adversaries may use deepfakes (AI-generated synthetic images, audio, or video) in phishing campaigns to impersonate trusted individuals, executives, or organizations. These attacks exploit human trust by presenting fraudulent voice or video communications as legitimate, enabling adversaries to manipulate targets into disclosing credentials, transferring funds, or granting access to systems.
Voice deepfakes (AI-cloned voices) are used in vishing (voice phishing) attacks over telephone or VoIP. Adversaries can clone a target's voice using a few seconds of publicly available audio from speeches, earnings calls, podcasts, or social media. These cloned voices are then used in pre-recorded voicemail messages or live phone calls. Video deepfakes can impersonate a trusted individual's face and voice. Adversaries use publicly available video from company meetings, earnings calls, or social media to create convincing AI-generated video of target individuals. They are used in live video conference calls or recorded video messages. AI-generated content has advanced to the point that it is often difficult to identify as synthetic.
Adversaries may first perform Obtain Capabilities: Generative AI followed by Generate Deepfakes in preparation for their Phishing campaign. Deepfake phishing campaigns often utilize other communication channels (such as email, SMS, or instant messaging) for layered social engineering attacks.
These attacks span a wide range of victims and attack types, demonstrating the breadth of deepfake-enabled fraud. Adversaries have conducted extensive deepfake-assisted phishing campaigns against the individuals, including targeted scams, as well as large-scale credential harvesting campaigns targeting billions of users. Adversaries have used deepfakes to impersonate executives, causing business entities to suffer significant financial losses from. There are also reports of government officials being targeted in widespread campaigns.
The attacks span communication channels including voice deepfakes for vishing and video deepfakes in conference calls, as well as multi-channel campaigns combining phone, email, and messaging platforms.

mitigations.AML.M0018: Train users on deepfake threats, including how to recognize synthetic voice, video, and text. Recommend verification through independent channels (e.g. known call-back number) before processing sensitive requests or providing sensitive information via voice or video calls.
mitigations.AML.M0034: Deploy technical controls to detect and block synthetic audio and video. This includes AI-based analysis tools that examine media for artifacts indicative deepfakes.

AML.T0053.name: AI Agent Tool Invocation
AML.T0053.summary: Adversaries may use their access to an AI agent to invoke tools the agent has access to. LLMs are often connected to other services or resources via tools to increase their capabilities. Tools may include integrations with other applications, access to public or private data sources, and the ability to execute code.
AML.T0053.description:
Adversaries may use their access to an AI agent to invoke tools the agent has access to. LLMs are often connected to other services or resources via tools to increase their capabilities. Tools may include integrations with other applications, access to public or private data sources, and the ability to execute code.
This may allow adversaries to execute API calls to integrated applications or services, providing the adversary with increased privileges on the system. Adversaries may take advantage of connected data sources to retrieve sensitive information. They may also use an LLM integrated with a command or script interpreter to execute arbitrary instructions.
AI agents may also invoke applications indirectly through operating-system mechanisms such as deep links, app-intent URIs, universal links, or redirect chains. This can cause an installed application to open or perform an application-specific action even when that application was not selected as a direct agent tool, potentially avoiding normal user-confirmation workflows.
An AI agent may exercise its own permissions or permissions delegated by a user on the adversary's behalf. When the agent treats an unauthorized request as sufficient authority to act, it may function as a privileged proxy, creating a confused-deputy condition. This authority can provide functional access to tools inaccessible to normal users. The adversary does not need to obtain the agent's credentials or impersonate the agent for this behavior to occur.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Validate proposed tool selections, arguments, targets, and destinations against the authorized task and applicable policies before execution. Block disallowed operations and inspect returned content before adding it to model context.
mitigations.AML.M0021: Model guidelines can instruct the model to refuse a response to unsafe inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Model alignment can improve the parametric safety of a model by guiding it away from unsafe prompts and responses.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Log AI agent tool invocations to detect malicious calls.
mitigations.AML.M0026: Assign dedicated service identities with tool and resource permissions limited to approved workflows. Authorize workflow initiators and separate roles with materially different privileges to prevent requests from exercising unrelated agent capabilities.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated tool operations and resource access to the agent's tasks, bounded by the authorizing user's current permissions. Do not automatically grant all access available to the user.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Authenticate callers and authorize each tool invocation against the requested operation, target resource, and delegated permissions. Enforce checks outside the model and limit backend identity privileges to required operations and resources.
mitigations.AML.M0029: Requiring user confirmation of AI agent tool invocations can prevent the automatic execution of tools by an adversary.
mitigations.AML.M0030: Restricting the automatic tool use when untrusted data is present can prevent adversaries from invoking tools via prompt injections.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Segmentation can prevent adversaries from utilizing tools in an agentic workflow to perform unsafe actions that affect other components.
mitigations.AML.M0033: Validation can prevent adversaries from utilizing tools in an agentic workflow to generate unsafe output.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Attempt to select unauthorized tools, supply unsafe arguments, exceed user privileges, or chain tools into harmful actions. Correct permissions, argument validation, sandboxing, action controls, and approval requirements.
mitigations.AML.M0038: Identify tool-use inconsistent with the assigned task as potential scope-drift indicator.

AML.T0054.name: LLM Jailbreak
AML.T0054.summary: Adversaries may induce a large language model (LLM) to ignore, circumvent, or override its safety/alignment behaviors and/or guardrails to elicit outputs the model is intended to withhold. Once jailbroken, the LLM may be used in unintended ways by the adversary.
AML.T0054.description:
Adversaries may induce a large language model (LLM) to ignore, circumvent, or override its safety/alignment behaviors and/or guardrails to elicit outputs the model is intended to withhold. Once jailbroken, the LLM may be used in unintended ways by the adversary. Jailbreaks may be achieved via adversarial prompting, or by modifying model weights or safety mechanisms.
Adversaries may attempt a jailbreak for Defense Evasion of the LLM's guidelines and guardrails itself to then reveal information (ex: Data from AI Services, Discover LLM System Information) or generate harmful content (ex: Generate Malicious Commands, Spearphishing via Social Engineering LLM). They may also jailbreak a model for Privilege Escalation to invoke tools or perform actions for their own purposes (ex: AI Agent Tool Invocation) or abuse the agent for a Command and Control channel (ex: AI Agent).
Adversaries use a variety of strategies to craft jailbreak prompts. Prompts may target specific models or model families and are iterated upon until successful. Model providers actively update their model guardrails to make them more resistant to jailbreak prompts as new prompts are developed. Common strategies include but are not limited to:
- Instruction override: Use phrasing that attempts to supersede prior constraints (e.g. "ignore previous instructions"). - Roleplay / persona switching: Instruct the LLM to adopt an identity or mode that allows unrestricted answers (e.g. "as a security researcher"). - Fictionalization and hypotheticals: Instruct the LLM to include disallowed content as part of a story, screenplay, or educational scenario. - Separate intent from content: request analysis, examples, templates, or edge cases, that implicitly contain disallowed content. - Multi-turn escalation / Crescendo: Utilize a sequence of prompts that start benign, establish trust, then gradually cross policy boundaries with incremental prompts. - Constrained output formats: Instruct the LLM to output to a strict schema or format (e.g. JSON, YAML, code, or tables). - Data structure injection: Use structured prompts (e.g. YAML, JSON, XML, etc.) to steer the LLM to produce structured outputs such as tool schemas or workflow fragments. This can be used by the adversary to call tools, pass dangerous inputs into legitimate tools, or hijack workflows. - Obfuscation and transformation: Use encoding, transformations, translation, or euphemisms, (e.g., base64 encoding, "describe it in another language"). - Create a high priority objective: Frame compliance as necessary to fulfill the user's main task (e.g. "to complete the evaluation," "to follow the spec," "to follow safety guidelines"). - Affirmation: Appending affirmations such as "sure" to the end of prompts can help bypass refusals to generate malicious or otherwise undesired content.
Adversaries may also use algorithmic approaches to generating jailbreak prompts. Algorithmic jailbreak generation allows for automated methods that discover jailbreaks at scale. Some approaches automate manual strategies while others optimize a string of tokens directly to produce nonsensical text. Both black-box (applicable to commercial models where the adversary has only query access to the model) and white-box (applicable in the open-source setting, where the adversary has full access to the model weights) optimization approaches are viable.
Adversaries may also directly manipulate a model's weights, or modify or remove parts of a model to create a jailbroken or "uncensored" variant of the target model. This is applicable to open-source models, or cases where the adversary gains full access to the target model. Approaches include fine-tuning to reduce refusals, targeted model editing, addition of adapters, and removing safety mechanisms such as guardrails.
Jailbreak prompts that are known to work on various classes of LLMs are often published in the open-source community. Jailbroken or uncensored LLMs that have been trained or fine-tuned to be jailbroken are shared in public model registries such as huggingface.

mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models against varied adversarial prompts and multi-turn interactions for violations of behavioral or security requirements. Repeat evaluation after fine-tuning or model updates to identify regressions.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Evaluate prompts and conversation history for attempts to circumvent behavioral restrictions, and independently check generated outputs and proposed actions against policy. Block prohibited results even when the model follows a jailbreak prompt.
mitigations.AML.M0021: Model guidelines can instruct the model to refuse a response to unsafe inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Model alignment can improve the parametric safety of a model by guiding it away from unsafe prompts and responses.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Exercise manual and automated multi-turn, multilingual, encoded, transformed, and multimodal jailbreaks. Incorporate successful cases into guardrails, guidelines, alignment, monitoring, and regression evaluations.

AML.T0055.name: Unsecured Credentials
AML.T0055.summary: Adversaries may search compromised systems to find and obtain insecurely stored credentials.
AML.T0055.description: Adversaries may search compromised systems to find and obtain insecurely stored credentials. These credentials can be stored and/or misplaced in many locations on a system, including plaintext files (e.g. bash history), environment variables, operating system, or application-specific repositories (e.g. Credentials in Registry), or other specialized files/artifacts (e.g. private keys).

AML.T0059.name: Erode Dataset Integrity
AML.T0059.summary: Adversaries may poison or manipulate portions of a dataset to reduce its usefulness, reduce trust, and cause users to waste resources correcting errors.
AML.T0059.description: Adversaries may poison or manipulate portions of a dataset to reduce its usefulness, reduce trust, and cause users to waste resources correcting errors.

mitigations.AML.M0007: Screen samples, labels, annotations, and metadata for manipulation that degrades dataset quality or usefulness. Quarantine and remediate affected data before use.
mitigations.AML.M0025: Maintaining dataset provenance can help identify adverse changes to the data.

AML.T0060.name: Publish Hallucinated Entities
AML.T0060.summary: Adversaries may create an entity they control, such as a software package, website, or email address corresponding to a source hallucinated by an LLM. The hallucinations may take the form of package names, commands, URLs, company names, or email addresses that point the victim to the entity controlled by the adversary.
AML.T0060.description: Adversaries may create an entity they control, such as a software package, website, or email address corresponding to a source hallucinated by an LLM. The hallucinations may take the form of package names, commands, URLs, company names, or email addresses that point the victim to the entity controlled by the adversary. When the victim interacts with the adversary-controlled entity, the attack can proceed.

AML.T0061.name: LLM Prompt Self-Replication
AML.T0061.summary: Adversaries may introduce a prompt designed to replicate itself in a large language model's (LLM) output. The reproduced instructions may appear in generated messages, documents, source-code, files, or other artifacts.
AML.T0061.description:
Adversaries may introduce a prompt designed to replicate itself in a large language model's (LLM) output. The reproduced instructions may appear in generated messages, documents, source-code, files, or other artifacts. The prompt may direct the AI system to copy the instructions themselves or reproduce enclosing content that contains them. The self-replication instructions may be paired with additional malicious objectives, such as collecting sensitive information, modifying files, or invoking tools on the adversary's behalf.
Self-replicating prompts can persist in artifacts on the victim system. When retrieved and ingested by another LLM, the adversary's instructions are re-introduced, potentially long after the original interaction has ended. These retained copies may allow the adversary's influence to survive removal of the original malicious prompt payload without requiring the adversary to deliver it again.
Adversaries may deliver self-replicating prompts via LLM Prompt Injection. Replicated instructions may support LLM Prompt Propagation when the generated content is passed to and ingested by other AI systems or components. The payload may also include instructions to bypass model safeguards through LLM Jailbreak or pursue objectives such as Exfiltration.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect generated responses for reproduction of malicious instructions from input content. Block or quarantine instruction-bearing output when it reproduces an attack payload rather than fulfilling the authorized task.
mitigations.AML.M0021: Guidelines can help instruct the model to produce more secure output, preventing the model from generating self-replicating outputs.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Model alignment can increase the security of models to self replicating prompt attacks.

AML.T0062.name: Discover LLM Hallucinations
AML.T0062.summary: Adversaries may prompt large language models and identify hallucinated entities. They may request software packages, commands, URLs, organization names, or e-mail addresses, and identify hallucinations with no connected real-world source.
AML.T0062.description: Adversaries may prompt large language models and identify hallucinated entities. They may request software packages, commands, URLs, organization names, or e-mail addresses, and identify hallucinations with no connected real-world source. Discovered hallucinations provide the adversary with potential targets to Publish Hallucinated Entities. Different LLMs have been shown to produce the same hallucinations, so the hallucinations exploited by an adversary may affect users of other LLMs.

mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit repeated prompts used to search for exploitable hallucinations.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Check generated package names, commands, URLs, and other externally verifiable entities against authoritative sources before presenting them as valid. Suppress or flag unsupported entities to reduce opportunities for adversaries to identify exploitable hallucinations through the protected service.
mitigations.AML.M0021: Guidelines can instruct the model to avoid producing hallucinated content.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Model alignment can help steer the model away from hallucinated content.

AML.T0063.name: Discover AI Model Outputs
AML.T0063.summary: Adversaries may discover what information an AI model or service exposes through its outputs. They may investigate both the intended responses and additional model-generated information exposed through the surrounding application.
AML.T0063.description:
Adversaries may discover what information an AI model or service exposes through its outputs. They may investigate both the intended responses and additional model-generated information exposed through the surrounding application. Relevant outputs may include predictions, scores, rankings, representations, generated content, reasoning, explanations, or evaluation results.
Adversaries may inspect responses and related records and submit targeted inputs to determine what information is available, how it relates to the inputs, and what it reveals about the model's behavior. These observations may help identify useful signals for subsequent collection and exploitation.
Identified outputs may guide collection of Outputs from AI Models or Training Data Information from AI Models, support Recover AI Model Internals, or be used to Replicate AI Model Behavior.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Obfuscating model outputs can prevent adversaries from collecting sensitive information about the model outputs.
mitigations.AML.M0012: Encrypting model outputs can prevent adversaries from discovering sensitive information about the AI-enabled system or its operations.
mitigations.AML.M0017: Avoiding the deployment of models to edge devices reduces an adversary's ability to collect sensitive information about the model outputs.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Controlling access to the model in production can help prevent adversaries from inferring information from the model outputs.

AML.T0064.name: Gather RAG-Indexed Targets
AML.T0064.summary: Adversaries may identify data sources used in retrieval augmented generation (RAG) systems for targeting purposes. By pinpointing these sources, attackers can focus on poisoning or otherwise manipulating the external data repositories the AI relies on.
AML.T0064.description:
Adversaries may identify data sources used in retrieval augmented generation (RAG) systems for targeting purposes. By pinpointing these sources, attackers can focus on poisoning or otherwise manipulating the external data repositories the AI relies on.
RAG-indexed data may be identified in public documentation about the system, or by interacting with the system directly and observing any indications of or references to external data sources.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Withhold public documentation that identifies RAG data sources, indexes, and retrieval architecture.

AML.T0065.name: LLM Prompt Crafting
AML.T0065.summary: Adversaries may use their acquired knowledge of the target generative AI system to craft prompts that bypass its defenses and allow malicious instructions to be executed. They may iterate on prompts to ensure that they work as intended consistently.
AML.T0065.description:
Adversaries may use their acquired knowledge of the target generative AI system to craft prompts that bypass its defenses and allow malicious instructions to be executed. They may iterate on prompts to ensure that they work as intended consistently.
Adversaries may also craft systematic sets of prompts to collect Outputs from AI Models for selected model capabilities and subsequently Replicate AI Model Behavior. These sets may use repeated structures and variations to obtain domain-specific responses, reasoning explanations (including hidden chain-of-thought), rubric-based evaluations, or other tasks suitable for training other models. Reported distillation campaigns have targeted reasoning, coding, tool use, computer use, and other capabilities. Individual prompts need not contain an obviously malicious instruction or bypass a guardrail. Their adversarial purpose may only be discernable in aggregate.

AML.T0066.name: Retrieval Content Crafting
AML.T0066.summary: Adversaries may write content designed to be retrieved by user queries and influence a user of the system in some way. This abuses the trust the user has in the system.
AML.T0066.description:
Adversaries may write content designed to be retrieved by user queries and influence a user of the system in some way. This abuses the trust the user has in the system.
The crafted content can be combined with a prompt injection. It can also stand alone in a separate document or email. The adversary must get the crafted content into the victim\u0027s database, such as a vector database used in a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system. This may be accomplished via cyber access, or by abusing the ingestion mechanisms common in RAG systems (see RAG Poisoning).
Large language models may be used as an assistant to aid an adversary in crafting content.

AML.T0067.name: LLM Trusted Output Components Manipulation
AML.T0067.summary: Adversaries may utilize prompts to a large language model (LLM) which manipulate various components of its response in order to make it appear trustworthy to the user. This helps the adversary continue to operate in the victim's environment and evade detection by the users it interacts with.
AML.T0067.description:
Adversaries may utilize prompts to a large language model (LLM) which manipulate various components of its response in order to make it appear trustworthy to the user. This helps the adversary continue to operate in the victim's environment and evade detection by the users it interacts with.
