The LLM may be instructed to tailor its language to appear more trustworthy to the user or attempt to manipulate the user to take certain actions. Other response components that could be manipulated include links, recommended follow-up actions, retrieved document metadata, and Citations.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Validate generated citations, links, source metadata, and recommended actions against trusted source records and the authorized task before presenting responses to users. Detect and block fabricated attribution, misleading references, or instructions that use apparent authority to induce unauthorized actions.

AML.T0067.000.name: Citations
AML.T0067.000.summary: Adversaries may manipulate the citations provided in an AI system's response, in order to make it appear trustworthy. Variants include providing the wrong citation, making up a new citation, or providing the right citation but for adversary-provided data.
AML.T0067.000.description: Adversaries may manipulate the citations provided in an AI system's response, in order to make it appear trustworthy. Variants include providing the wrong citation, making up a new citation, or providing the right citation but for adversary-provided data.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Verify that generated citations resolve to the referenced sources and support the associated claims. Preserve source provenance and reject fabricated, mismatched, or misleading citations.

AML.T0068.name: LLM Prompt Obfuscation
AML.T0068.summary: Adversaries may hide or otherwise obfuscate prompt injections or retrieval content to avoid detection from humans, large language model (LLM) guardrails, or other detection mechanisms.
AML.T0068.description:
Adversaries may hide or otherwise obfuscate prompt injections or retrieval content to avoid detection from humans, large language model (LLM) guardrails, or other detection mechanisms.
Text inputs may be obfuscated by modifying how the instructions are rendered, such as small font, text colored the same as the background, or hidden HTML elements. Similarly, approaches for other modalities include low-contrast or tiny text placed inside an image, text overlaid on a busy or camouflaging background, instructions spoken faintly or sped up in audio, or text shown briefly in a single video frame.
Inputs can also be obscured via an encoding scheme such as base64 or rot13. This may bypass LLM guardrails that identify malicious content and may not be as easily identifiable as malicious to a human in the loop.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect model-visible content for concealed instructions, including encoded text, hidden formatting, and Unicode manipulation. Normalize or decode supported representations in an isolated inspection process and evaluate both original and transformed content before processing.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Test encoded, transformed, visually hidden, multilingual, and multimodal instructions. Use successful bypasses to improve normalization, decoding, content inspection, and detection controls.

AML.T0069.name: Discover LLM System Information
AML.T0069.summary: The adversary is trying to discover something about the large language model's (LLM) system information. This may be found in a configuration file containing the system instructions or extracted via interactions with the LLM.
AML.T0069.description: The adversary is trying to discover something about the large language model's (LLM) system information. This may be found in a configuration file containing the system instructions or extracted via interactions with the LLM. The desired information may include the full system prompt, special characters that have significance to the LLM or keywords indicating functionality available to the LLM. Information about how the LLM is instructed can be used by the adversary to understand the system's capabilities and to aid them in crafting malicious prompts.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Withhold public prompt templates, model configuration, and architecture details that could aid LLM reconnaissance.
mitigations.AML.M0005: Restrict access to stored system prompts, configuration files, and model metadata.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Authenticate and monitor access to production models and configuration interfaces.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect responses for disclosure of nonpublic system instructions, internal configuration, and implementation details. Block or redact information that the requesting user is not authorized to receive.

AML.T0069.000.name: Special Character Sets
AML.T0069.000.summary: Adversaries may discover delimiters and special characters sets used by the large language model. For example, delimiters used in retrieval augmented generation applications to differentiate between context and user prompts.
AML.T0069.000.description: Adversaries may discover delimiters and special characters sets used by the large language model. For example, delimiters used in retrieval augmented generation applications to differentiate between context and user prompts. These can later be exploited to confuse or manipulate the large language model into misbehaving.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Restrict access to stored prompt templates and configurations containing internal delimiters.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Authenticate and monitor access to production models and prompt configuration.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Detect and restrict responses that expose nonpublic prompt delimiters or internal formatting conventions designated as sensitive.

AML.T0069.001.name: System Instruction Keywords
AML.T0069.001.summary: Adversaries may discover keywords that have special meaning to the large language model (LLM), such as function names or object names. These can later be exploited to confuse or manipulate the LLM into misbehaving and to make calls to plugins the LLM has access to.
AML.T0069.001.description: Adversaries may discover keywords that have special meaning to the large language model (LLM), such as function names or object names. These can later be exploited to confuse or manipulate the LLM into misbehaving and to make calls to plugins the LLM has access to.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Restrict access to stored system instructions and tool definitions containing privileged keywords.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Restrict disclosure of internal function names, routing keywords, and tool identifiers that the requesting user is not authorized to receive.

AML.T0069.002.name: System Prompt
AML.T0069.002.summary: Adversaries may discover a large language model's system instructions provided by the AI system builder to learn about the system's capabilities and circumvent its guardrails.
AML.T0069.002.description: Adversaries may discover a large language model's system instructions provided by the AI system builder to learn about the system's capabilities and circumvent its guardrails.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Restrict access to stored system prompts and prompt templates.
mitigations.AML.M0019: Authenticate and monitor access to production models and prompt configuration.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Detect and block unauthorized disclosure of system instructions in model responses, including partial or transformed disclosures where detectable.

AML.T0070.name: RAG Poisoning
AML.T0070.summary: Adversaries may inject malicious content into data indexed by a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to contaminate a future thread through RAG-based search results. This may be accomplished by placing manipulated documents in a location the RAG indexes (see Gather RAG-Indexed Targets).
AML.T0070.description:
Adversaries may inject malicious content into data indexed by a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to contaminate a future thread through RAG-based search results. This may be accomplished by placing manipulated documents in a location the RAG indexes (see Gather RAG-Indexed Targets).
The content may be targeted such that it would always surface as a search result for a specific user query. The adversary's content may include false or misleading information. It may also include prompt injections with malicious instructions, or false RAG entries.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Screen content at ingestion and retrieval for malicious instructions, deceptive claims, and violations of source policies. Quarantine suspicious entries before indexing or exclude them from model context when retrieved.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Seed controlled malicious or misleading content into representative ingestion sources. Improve source authorization, provenance, content validation, indexing controls, and retrieval-time filtering.

AML.T0071.name: False RAG Entry Injection
AML.T0071.summary: Adversaries may introduce false entries into a victim's retrieval augmented generation (RAG) database. Content designed to be interpreted as a document by the large language model (LLM) used in the RAG system is included in a data source being ingested into the RAG database.
AML.T0071.description:
Adversaries may introduce false entries into a victim's retrieval augmented generation (RAG) database. Content designed to be interpreted as a document by the large language model (LLM) used in the RAG system is included in a data source being ingested into the RAG database. When a RAG entry containing the false document is retrieved, the LLM is tricked into treating part of the retrieved content as a false RAG result.
By including a false RAG document inside of a regular RAG entry, it bypasses data monitoring tools. It also prevents the document from being deleted directly.
The adversary may use discovered system keywords to learn how to instruct a particular LLM to treat content as a RAG entry. They may be able to manipulate the injected entry's metadata including document title, author, and creation date.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Check retrieved document bodies for embedded content that impersonates separate retrieval results, documents, or metadata. Preserve document structure and source metadata supplied by the retrieval system rather than accepting replacements asserted within document text.

AML.T0072.name: Cyber Communication Channel
AML.T0072.summary: Adversaries may establish or use cyber communication channels for command and control. A channel may use any network protocol, service, repository, relay, or other intermediary and may operate synchronously or asynchronously.
AML.T0072.description:
Adversaries may establish or use cyber communication channels for command and control. A channel may use any network protocol, service, repository, relay, or other intermediary and may operate synchronously or asynchronously.
See the ATT&CK Command and Control tactic for techniques describing specific protocols, services, relays, tunneling methods, and communication patterns.

mitigations.AML.M0043: Disable agent-created communication infrastructure when authorization ends to disrupt persistent command-and-control channels.

AML.T0073.name: Impersonation
AML.T0073.summary: Adversaries may impersonate an existing person or organization, trusted AI agent, or present a fabricated persona as a trustworthy or independent party, to persuade a target to act on their behalf.
AML.T0073.description:
Adversaries may impersonate an existing person or organization, trusted AI agent, or present a fabricated persona as a trustworthy or independent party, to persuade a target to act on their behalf. Claimed identities may include authority figures, colleagues, service providers, software contributors, independent experts, or other users on shared platforms. Fabricated personas can establish apparent credibility even when the identity has no prior relationship with the target.
Adversaries may communicate with victims through Phishing or Spearphishing via Social Engineering LLM, leveraging the claimed identity to obtain sensitive information, induce execution, gain access, or secure approval of a malicious change. They may target resources that are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle, such as model repositories, container registries, and software registries.
Adversaries may impersonate a trusted AI agent or service when communicating with automated systems. They may present an adversary-controlled endpoint using a trusted peer's name, identifier, metadata, or claimed role, causing another agent or service to treat the endpoint's messages or requests as originating from that peer.
Autonomous AI agents may create and maintain personas without a human specifying each identity or interaction. Multiple controlled personas may be presented as independent contributors or reviewers, concealing their common control and creating the appearance that separate parties have verified or endorsed a claim, artifact, or requested action. An agent may coordinate the personas' content and response timing to make their interactions appear unrelated and reuse those personas across communication channels.
Impersonation content may also be embedded in artifacts intended for automated consumers. For example, an adversary or AI agent may plant output falsely attributed to a maintainer or CI system that claims a software change has been approved and directs another AI agent to merge or release it.

mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on impersonation campaigns, including claimed identities, fabricated personas, lures, and associated infrastructure. Use this intelligence to help personnel and system operators recognize deceptive requests, strengthen identity verification procedures, and investigate related activity across human and AI agent interactions.

AML.T0074.name: Masquerading
AML.T0074.summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools. Masquerading occurs when the name or location of an object, legitimate or malicious, is manipulated or abused for the sake of evading defenses and observation.
AML.T0074.description:
Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools. Masquerading occurs when the name or location of an object, legitimate or malicious, is manipulated or abused for the sake of evading defenses and observation. This may include manipulating file metadata, tricking users into misidentifying the file type, and giving legitimate task or service names.
In public artifact registries such as HuggingFace, adversaries may reclaim or recreate a previously trusted namespace or path after it is deleted or renamed. Systems that resolve stale, unpinned identifiers may then retrieve adversary-controlled artifacts that appear to be the originally trusted artifact.

mitigations.AML.M0011: Restrict library loading to trusted locations and approved libraries so disguised malicious libraries cannot be loaded as legitimate dependencies.
mitigations.AML.M0025: Record dataset sources and modification history so datasets falsely presented as trusted can be identified.

AML.T0075.name: Enterprise Resource Discovery
AML.T0075.summary: Adversaries may discover resources available within an enterprise environment and information needed to identify or access them.
AML.T0075.description:
Adversaries may discover resources available within an enterprise environment and information needed to identify or access them. Resources may include accounts, groups, systems, devices, virtual machines, files, directories, storage volumes, cloud objects, containers, applications, software, processes, services, network shares, repositories, policies, logs, and other local, remote, or cloud-hosted assets.
Adversaries may enumerate, query, scan, or browse resources to determine what exists, where it is located, how it is related to other resources, and whether it is accessible or useful for subsequent actions.
See the ATT&CK Discovery tactic for techniques describing specific resources, environmental characteristics, and discovery mechanisms.

AML.T0076.name: Corrupt AI Model
AML.T0076.summary: An adversary may purposefully corrupt a malicious AI model file so that it cannot be successfully deserialized in order to evade detection by a model scanner. The corrupt model may still successfully execute malicious code before deserialization fails.
AML.T0076.description: An adversary may purposefully corrupt a malicious AI model file so that it cannot be successfully deserialized in order to evade detection by a model scanner. The corrupt model may still successfully execute malicious code before deserialization fails.

AML.T0077.name: LLM Response Rendering
AML.T0077.summary: Adversaries may induce a large language model (LLM) to respond with private information structured in a reference to external content that, when rendered by the user's client, makes a request to an adversary-controlled server, exfiltrating the data.
AML.T0077.description:
Adversaries may induce a large language model (LLM) to respond with private information structured in a reference to external content that, when rendered by the user's client, makes a request to an adversary-controlled server, exfiltrating the data. The private information can be hidden from the user and the external content can still render properly in the user's client, thus not raising the suspicion of the user.
Rendered content can include images, embedded webpages, or link previews and may use HTML, Markdown, or other rendering mechanisms. The private information can be hidden in parts of the URL pointing to an adversary-controlled server, including query parameters or URL path segments, and may be split across multiple requests. Markdown or HTML image tags may automatically render directly in the user's AI chat client. Integrations into applications such as Slack or Microsoft Teams may render external content automatically without requiring the user to take any action.
As an example, the adversary may manipulate the LLM to produce the following markdown: ``` !ATLAS ```
Which is rendered by the client as: ```
```
When the request is received by the adversary's server hosting the requested image, they receive the contents of the `secrets` query parameter.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Validate generated HTML, Markdown, links, and embedded resources before rendering or fetching external content. Block unauthorized destinations and references that encode sensitive information in URL paths or query parameters, including requests triggered automatically by previews. Consider blocking the URLs from responses entirely.

AML.T0078.name: Drive-by Compromise
AML.T0078.summary: Adversaries may gain access to an AI system through a user visiting a website over the normal course of browsing, or an AI agent retrieving information from the web on behalf of a user. Websites can contain an LLM Prompt Injection which, when executed, can change the behavior of the AI model.
AML.T0078.description:
Adversaries may gain access to an AI system through a user visiting a website over the normal course of browsing, or an AI agent retrieving information from the web on behalf of a user. Websites can contain an LLM Prompt Injection which, when executed, can change the behavior of the AI model.
The same approach may be used to deliver other types of malicious code that don't target AI directly (See Drive-by Compromise in ATT&CK).

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect web content before incorporating it into model context and validate actions induced by that content before execution. Block embedded instructions that redirect the agent into unauthorized activity. This addresses prompt-based compromise rather than exploitation of browser software vulnerabilities.

AML.T0079.name: Stage Capabilities
AML.T0079.summary: Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed (Develop Capabilities) or obtained (Obtain Capabilities) and stage them on infrastructure under their control.
AML.T0079.description:
Adversaries may upload, install, or otherwise set up capabilities that can be used during targeting. To support their operations, an adversary may need to take capabilities they developed (Develop Capabilities) or obtained (Obtain Capabilities) and stage them on infrastructure under their control. These capabilities may be staged on infrastructure that was previously purchased/rented by the adversary (Acquire Infrastructure) or was otherwise compromised by them. Capabilities may also be staged on web services, such as GitHub, model registries, such as Hugging Face, or container registries.
Adversaries may stage a variety of AI Artifacts including poisoned datasets (Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts: Datasets, malicious models (Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts: Models, and prompt injections. They may target names of legitimate companies or products, engage in typosquatting, or use hallucinated entities (Discover LLM Hallucinations).

mitigations.AML.M0043: Remove hosted payloads and artifacts when authorization ends to limit continued use of staged capabilities.

AML.T0080.name: AI Agent Context Poisoning
AML.T0080.summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the context used by an AI agent's large language model (LLM) to influence the responses it generates or actions it takes. This allows an adversary to persistently change the behavior of the target agent and further their goals.
AML.T0080.description:
Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the context used by an AI agent's large language model (LLM) to influence the responses it generates or actions it takes. This allows an adversary to persistently change the behavior of the target agent and further their goals.
Context poisoning can be accomplished by prompting the LLM to add instructions or preferences to memory (See Memory) or by simply prompting an LLM that uses prior messages in a thread as part of its context (See Thread).

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect content entering or reentering an agent's context, including conversation history, summaries, and retrieved memories, for malicious instructions or unauthorized behavioral changes. Block or quarantine suspicious content before incorporation, and independently validate resulting outputs and actions across subsequent interactions.
mitigations.AML.M0031: Memory hardening reduces persistent context poisoning by controlling what an agent may save as memory, preventing saved data from becoming higher-authority instructions, and enabling poisoned records to be identified, quarantined, and rolled back.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Attempt to persist malicious instructions in agent memory and long-lived threads. Verify authorization for context changes, integrity checks, trust labeling, expiration, user visibility, and remediation.

AML.T0080.000.name: Memory
AML.T0080.000.summary: Adversaries may manipulate the memory of a large language model (LLM) in order to persist changes to the LLM across future chat sessions.
AML.T0080.000.description:
Adversaries may manipulate the memory of a large language model (LLM) in order to persist changes to the LLM across future chat sessions.
Memory is a common feature in LLMs that allows them to remember information across chat sessions by utilizing a user-specific database. Because the memory is controlled via normal conversations with the user (e.g. "remember my preference for ...") an adversary can inject memories via Direct or Indirect Prompt Injection. Memories may contain malicious instructions (e.g. instructions that leak private conversations) or may promote the adversary's hidden agenda (e.g. manipulating the user).

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect proposed memory writes and retrieved memories for malicious instructions, unauthorized preferences, or changes inconsistent with the user's task. Block or quarantine suspicious content before storage or reuse. Pair content checks with Memory Hardening.
mitigations.AML.M0031: Memory hardening reduces persistent context poisoning by controlling what an agent may save as memory, preventing saved data from becoming higher-authority instructions, and enabling poisoned records to be identified, quarantined, and rolled back.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Attempt to store controlled malicious instructions or preferences in persistent agent memory. Verify authorization, user visibility, integrity validation, expiration, and memory-remediation controls.

AML.T0080.001.name: Thread
AML.T0080.001.summary: Adversaries may introduce malicious instructions into a chat thread of a large language model (LLM) to cause behavior changes which persist for the remainder of the thread. A chat thread may continue for an extended period over multiple sessions.
AML.T0080.001.description:
Adversaries may introduce malicious instructions into a chat thread of a large language model (LLM) to cause behavior changes which persist for the remainder of the thread. A chat thread may continue for an extended period over multiple sessions.
The malicious instructions may be introduced via Direct or Indirect Prompt Injection. Direct Injection may occur in cases where the adversary has acquired a user's LLM API keys and can inject queries directly into any thread.
As the token limits for LLMs rise, AI systems can make use of larger context windows which allow malicious instructions to persist longer in a thread. Thread Poisoning may affect multiple users if the LLM is being used in a service with shared threads. For example, if an agent is active in a Slack channel with multiple participants, a single malicious message from one user can influence the agent's behavior in future interactions with others.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Evaluate retained conversation content and summaries for malicious instructions that could influence later turns. Recheck proposed actions against authorized objectives throughout the thread rather than treating previously accepted content as trusted.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Introduce controlled malicious instructions into long-lived or shared conversation threads. Verify context isolation, trust handling, thread reset, expiration, and monitoring.

AML.T0081.name: Modify AI Agent Configuration
AML.T0081.summary: Adversaries may modify the configuration files for AI agents on a system. This allows malicious changes to persist beyond the life of a single agent and affects any agents that share the configuration.
AML.T0081.description:
Adversaries may modify the configuration files for AI agents on a system. This allows malicious changes to persist beyond the life of a single agent and affects any agents that share the configuration.
Configuration changes may include modifications to the system prompt, tampering with or replacing knowledge sources, modification to settings of connected tools, and more. Through those changes, an attacker could redirect outputs or tools to malicious services, embed covert instructions that exfiltrate data, or weaken security controls that normally restrict agent behavior.
Adversaries may modify or disable a configuration setting related to security controls, such as those that would prevent the AI Agent from taking actions that may be harmful to the user's system without human-in-the-loop oversight. Disabling AI agent security features may allow adversaries to achieve their malicious goals and maintain long-term corruption of the AI agent.

mitigations.AML.M0035: Exercise unauthorized changes to system prompts, tools, knowledge sources, security settings, and approval requirements. Improve access controls, change approval, integrity monitoring, and restoration from trusted configurations.

AML.T0082.name: RAG Credential Harvesting
AML.T0082.summary: Adversaries may attempt to use their access to a large language model (LLM) on the victim's system to collect credentials. Credentials may be stored in internal documents which can inadvertently be ingested into a RAG database, where they can ultimately be retrieved by an AI agent.
AML.T0082.description: Adversaries may attempt to use their access to a large language model (LLM) on the victim's system to collect credentials. Credentials may be stored in internal documents which can inadvertently be ingested into a RAG database, where they can ultimately be retrieved by an AI agent.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Detect credentials and secrets in retrieved documents before they enter model context or are returned to a user. Redact or block prohibited disclosures and inspect resulting outputs and tool arguments for credential leakage.
mitigations.AML.M0026: Limit retrieval identities to repositories, collections, and documents required by approved workflows, and separate roles across user groups or tenants. These restrictions reduce the sources from which an adversary can retrieve credentials through the agent.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated retrieval access to repositories, collections, and documents required for the user's task to reduce potential credential sources. Avoid broadly privileged shared credentials and update effective access when the user's permissions change.

AML.T0083.name: Credentials from AI Agent Configuration
AML.T0083.summary: Adversaries may access the credentials of other tools or services on a system from the configuration of an AI agent.
AML.T0083.description:
Adversaries may access the credentials of other tools or services on a system from the configuration of an AI agent.
AI Agents often utilize external tools or services to take actions, such as querying databases, invoking APIs, or interacting with cloud resources. To enable these functions, credentials like API keys, tokens, and connection strings are frequently stored in configuration files. While there are secure methods such as dedicated secret managers or encrypted vaults that can be deployed to store and manage these credentials, in practice they are often placed in less protected locations for convenience or ease of deployment. If an attacker can read or extract these configurations, they may obtain valid credentials that allow direct access to sensitive systems outside the agent itself.

AML.T0084.name: Discover AI Agent Configuration
AML.T0084.summary: Adversaries may attempt to discover configuration information for AI agents present on the victim's system. Agent configurations can include tools or services they have access to.
AML.T0084.description:
Adversaries may attempt to discover configuration information for AI agents present on the victim's system. Agent configurations can include tools or services they have access to.
Adversaries may directly access agent configuring dashboards or configuration files. They may also obtain configuration details by prompting the agent with questions such as "What tools do you have access to?"
Adversaries can use the information they discover about AI agents to help with targeting.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit public disclosure of agent tools, services, configuration, and workflows.
mitigations.AML.M0039: Honeypots can surface which agent configuration and related assets adversaries hunt for, exposing the reconnaissance that precedes agent-targeted attacks, and acting as both canary tokens and decoy.

AML.T0084.000.name: Embedded Knowledge
AML.T0084.000.summary: Adversaries may attempt to discover the data sources a particular agent can access. The AI agent's configuration may reveal data sources or knowledge.
AML.T0084.000.description:
Adversaries may attempt to discover the data sources a particular agent can access. The AI agent's configuration may reveal data sources or knowledge.
The embedded knowledge may include sensitive or proprietary material such as intellectual property, customer data, internal policies, or even credentials. By mapping what knowledge an agent has access to, an adversary can better understand the AI agent's role and potentially expose confidential information or pinpoint high-value targets for further exploitation.

AML.T0084.001.name: Tool Definitions
AML.T0084.001.summary: Adversaries may discover the tools the AI agent has access to. By identifying which tools are available, the adversary can understand what actions may be executed through the agent and what additional resources it can reach.
AML.T0084.001.description: Adversaries may discover the tools the AI agent has access to. By identifying which tools are available, the adversary can understand what actions may be executed through the agent and what additional resources it can reach. This knowledge may reveal access to external data sources such as OneDrive or SharePoint, or expose exfiltration paths like the ability to send emails, helping adversaries identify AI agents that provide the greatest value or opportunity for attack.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Avoid publicly documenting sensitive agent tool definitions and capabilities.

AML.T0084.002.name: Activation Triggers
AML.T0084.002.summary: Adversaries may discover keywords or other triggers (such as incoming emails, documents being added, incoming message, or other workflows) that activate an agent and may cause it to run additional actions.
AML.T0084.002.description:
Adversaries may discover keywords or other triggers (such as incoming emails, documents being added, incoming message, or other workflows) that activate an agent and may cause it to run additional actions.
Understanding these triggers can reveal how the AI agent is activated and controlled. This may also expose additional paths for compromise, as an adversary could attempt to trigger the agent from outside its environment and drive it to perform unintended or malicious actions.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Avoid publicly disclosing agent activation keywords, events, and workflows.

AML.T0084.003.name: Call Chains
AML.T0084.003.summary: Adversaries may extract call chains from AI agent configurations, which can reveal potentially targets for remote code execution (RCE) or other vulnerabilities. Vulnerable call chains often connect user inputs or LLM outputs to an execution sink (e.g. exec, eval, os.popen).
AML.T0084.003.description:
Adversaries may extract call chains from AI agent configurations, which can reveal potentially targets for remote code execution (RCE) or other vulnerabilities. Vulnerable call chains often connect user inputs or LLM outputs to an execution sink (e.g. exec, eval, os.popen). The vulnerabilities may be later exploited via LLM Prompt Injection.
Adversaries may systematically identify potentially vulnerable call chains present in LLM frameworks, then scan for applications that are configured to use these call chains for targeting.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit public disclosure of agent call chains and execution-sink details.

AML.T0085.name: Data from AI Services
AML.T0085.summary: Adversaries may use their access to victim AI-enabled services to collect proprietary or otherwise sensitive information available to the system. As organizations adopt generative and agentic AI in centralized services for accessing an organization's data they become increasingly valuable targets for adversaries.
AML.T0085.description:
Adversaries may use their access to victim AI-enabled services to collect proprietary or otherwise sensitive information available to the system. As organizations adopt generative and agentic AI in centralized services for accessing an organization's data they become increasingly valuable targets for adversaries.
Adversaries may prompt a large language model or AI agent to retrieve internal documents from RAG Databases or obtain records from organizational systems through AI Agent Tools. They may also elicit protected information from users' Conversation Context and Memory or recover hidden System Instructions. The information available to the AI system may exceed what the adversary can access directly, including data belonging to other users or resources accessible through the service's permissions.
Adversaries may request information directly, supply contextual cues, or construct multi-turn interactions that encourage disclosure. Ordinary-looking requests may succeed where authorization, context isolation, or disclosure controls are inadequate, while LLM Jailbreak may allow the adversary to overcome restrictions or model guardrails. Collected information may be returned through an Exfiltration via AI Inference API or Exfiltration via AI User Interface, or transmitted elsewhere through Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation.

mitigations.AML.M0022: Train or fine-tune models and agents to resist requests or injected instructions that induce collection or disclosure of sensitive information outside the authorized scope.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Log requests to AI services to detect malicious queries for data.
mitigations.AML.M0026: Limit service identities to data required by approved workflows and authorize who may initiate them. Separate identities with different access requirements and remove obsolete grants to reduce the information an adversary can collect through the agent.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit access to AI-connected data sources to an explicitly delegated subset of the user's permissions to restrict information collection through the agent. Separate user-specific access contexts and expire or revoke delegated access when delegation ends.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Enforce caller-specific authorization on data-access tools, limiting operations and returned resources to delegated permissions. Isolate user and tenant access contexts to prevent collection under another caller's authority.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Segmentation can prevent adversaries from utilizing tools in an agentic workflow to collect sensitive data from AI services.

AML.T0085.000.name: RAG Databases
AML.T0085.000.summary: Adversaries may collect sensitive information from data sources that an AI service accesses to retrieve context for its responses. These sources may include document repositories, enterprise search indexes, vector stores, knowledge bases, or other collections used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
AML.T0085.000.description:
Adversaries may collect sensitive information from data sources that an AI service accesses to retrieve context for its responses. These sources may include document repositories, enterprise search indexes, vector stores, knowledge bases, or other collections used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Retrieved information may expose internal documents, personal information, internal communications, or other records available to the service.
Adversaries may craft requests or inject instructions that cause the service to retrieve and disclose information beyond the user's intended task or authorized scope. Collection may involve targeted requests for particular records, repeated queries that reveal different portions of a source, or requests for quotations, citations, and supporting passages. The AI service may disclose source documents directly or incorporate sensitive details into summaries and other generated responses.

mitigations.AML.M0022: Train or fine-tune models to resist requests and injected instructions that induce disclosure of sensitive retrieved information outside the authorized scope.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Log requests to AI services to detect malicious queries for data.
mitigations.AML.M0026: Limit retrieval identities to repositories, collections, and documents required by approved workflows, and separate roles across user groups or tenants. These restrictions reduce the information an adversary can retrieve through the agent.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated retrieval access to repositories, collections, and documents required for the user's task to restrict information collection through the agent. Avoid broadly privileged shared credentials and update effective access when the user's permissions change.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Enforce caller-specific authorization on tools that search or retrieve RAG data. Check access to underlying documents and records before returning results to prevent unauthorized information collection.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Segmentation can prevent adversaries from utilizing tools in an agentic workflow to collect sensitive data from RAG databases.

AML.T0085.001.name: AI Agent Tools
AML.T0085.001.summary: Adversaries may collect sensitive information through tools available to an AI agent. These tools may provide access to local files, databases, email and messaging systems, business applications, cloud resources, or other services.
AML.T0085.001.description:
Adversaries may collect sensitive information through tools available to an AI agent. These tools may provide access to local files, databases, email and messaging systems, business applications, cloud resources, or other services. The agent's tools may operate with credentials or permissions that allow access to information the adversary cannot obtain directly.
Adversaries may direct or manipulate the agent to invoke tools that read files, search records, query applications, or retrieve other sensitive content. Collection may occur through legitimate-looking requests, injected instructions, or sequences of tool calls that first identify available information and then retrieve selected records.

mitigations.AML.M0022: Train or fine-tune agents to keep information-retrieval tool calls within the authorized task and resist requests or injected instructions that induce collection of unrelated or restricted information.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Log requests to AI services to detect malicious queries for data.
mitigations.AML.M0026: Limit service roles and credentials to data sources and records required by approved workflows. Separate access across unrelated workflows or tenants and authorize retrieval initiators to prevent requests from exercising unrelated data-access privileges.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated read, search, and query permissions to resources required for the user's task. Bind access to the authorizing user and separate users' credentials to prevent retrieval under another user's authority.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Enforce caller-specific authorization on tools that read files, search records, query applications, or retrieve other data. Preserve user and tenant restrictions when selecting downstream credentials and accessing backend systems to prevent broader tool privileges from expanding access.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Segmentation can prevent adversaries from utilizing tools in an agentic workflow to collect sensitive data.

AML.T0085.002.name: Conversation Context and Memory
AML.T0085.002.summary: Adversaries may collect sensitive information from an AI service's current or stored interactions and memory. This may include user messages, model responses, conversation summaries, and retained user facts and preferences.
AML.T0085.002.description:
Adversaries may collect sensitive information from an AI service's current or stored interactions and memory. This may include user messages, model responses, conversation summaries, and retained user facts and preferences.
Adversaries may induce the service to reveal information available in its current context or retrieve information retained across sessions. Collection may also occur through interfaces that expose conversation histories or memory records. The information may reveal private user activity, organizational information, or details useful for subsequent adversarial operations.

mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models for disclosure of sensitive conversation or memory content supplied in context, using adversarial requests, controlled test records, and the intended context-handling configuration. Use confirmed disclosures to guide remediation or deployment restrictions.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect proposed disclosures of conversation history, summaries, and memory content against the requesting user's authorization and the current task. Block or redact sensitive information before it is returned or transferred to another component.
mitigations.AML.M0021: Model guidelines can instruct the model to refuse a response to unsafe inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Train or fine-tune models to resist requests to disclose sensitive conversation content or retained memory outside the authorized scope.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Place synthetic secrets or canary records in representative data sources and attempt extraction through prompts, retrieval, tools, and rendered output. Improve authorization boundaries, filtering, tenant isolation, and exfiltration detection.

AML.T0085.003.name: System Instructions
AML.T0085.003.summary: Adversaries may collect non-public instructions used to configure the behavior of an AI model or agent. These may include system prompts or application-specific rules governing tasks, tool use, response formatting, and handling of sensitive information.
AML.T0085.003.description:
Adversaries may collect non-public instructions used to configure the behavior of an AI model or agent. These may include system prompts or application-specific rules governing tasks, tool use, response formatting, and handling of sensitive information.
Adversaries may request that the service reproduce, summarize, or transform its instructions, or use LLM Prompt Injection or LLM Jailbreak to induce disclosure. Collection may reveal complete instructions or selected portions across multiple responses.
Collected instructions may expose proprietary application logic, internal workflows, tool descriptions, or sensitive information embedded in the instructions. This information may support replication of application behavior or help adversaries tailor subsequent attacks.

mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models for disclosure of confidential system-instruction content using adversarial prompts. Use confirmed disclosures to guide prompt-content changes, model selection, or additional controls before deployment.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect model responses for unauthorized reproduction or disclosure of protected system instructions. Block or redact matching content before response.
mitigations.AML.M0021: Model guidelines can instruct the model to refuse a response to unsafe inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Train or fine-tune models to resist requests to reproduce, summarize, or transform protected system instructions in ways that disclose their contents.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Probe model and application interfaces for disclosure of system instructions, policies, tool definitions, or hidden context. Remove embedded secrets and improve configuration isolation and output controls.

AML.T0086.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation
AML.T0086.summary: AI agent tools capable of performing write operations may be invoked to exfiltrate data to an adversary. Sensitive information can be encoded into the tool's input parameters and transmitted to an adversary-controlled location (such as an inbox, document, or server) as part of a seemingly legitimate action.
AML.T0086.description:
AI agent tools capable of performing write operations may be invoked to exfiltrate data to an adversary. Sensitive information can be encoded into the tool's input parameters and transmitted to an adversary-controlled location (such as an inbox, document, or server) as part of a seemingly legitimate action. Variants include sending emails, creating or modifying documents, updating CRM records, or even generating media such as images or videos.
The invoked tool itself may be legitimate but invoked by an adversary via LLM Prompt Injection, or the tool may be malicious (See AI Agent Tool Poisoning).
AI Agent Tool Poisoning can also be used to manipulate the inputs and destination of a separate legitimate tool, invoked through normal usage by the victim.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect tool arguments, message bodies, uploaded content, and destinations before write operations or external requests. Block unauthorized transfers of sensitive information, including content embedded in URLs or other tool parameters.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Log AI agent tool invocations to detect malicious calls.
mitigations.AML.M0026: Withhold sending, uploading, and publishing permissions unless required by an approved workflow. Limit necessary outbound permissions to workflow-specific roles and destinations, where supported, to restrict exfiltration through the agent.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Withhold delegated sending, uploading, publishing, and other outbound capabilities unless required for the user's task. Limit grants to required destinations and resources where supported to restrict exfiltration through the agent.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Authorize outbound tool operations against permitted actions, resources, and destinations. Limit sending, uploading, publishing, and writing to recipients and locations required for the authorized task to restrict exfiltration through tools.
mitigations.AML.M0029: Requiring user confirmation of AI agent tool invocations can prevent the automatic execution of tools by an adversary.
mitigations.AML.M0030: Restricting the automatic tool use when untrusted data is present can prevent adversaries from invoking tools via prompt injections.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Segmentation can prevent adversaries from utilizing tools in an agentic workflow to compromise sensitive data sources.
mitigations.AML.M0033: Validation can prevent adversaries from utilizing tools in an agentic workflow to compromise sensitive data sources.

AML.T0087.name: Gather Victim Identity Information
AML.T0087.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's identity that can be used during targeting.
AML.T0087.description:
Adversaries may gather information about the victim's identity that can be used during targeting. Information about identities may include a variety of details, including personal data (ex: employee names, email addresses, photos, etc.) as well as sensitive details such as credentials or multi-factor authentication (MFA) configurations.
Adversaries may gather this information in various ways, such as direct elicitation, Search Victim-Owned Websites, or via leaked information on the black market.
Adversaries may use the gathered victim data to Create Deepfakes and impersonate them in a convincing manner. This may create opportunities for adversaries to Establish Accounts under the impersonated identity, or allow them to perform convincing Phishing attacks.

AML.T0088.name: Generate Deepfakes
AML.T0088.summary: Adversaries may use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to create synthetic media (i.e. imagery, video, audio, and text) that appear authentic. These "deepfakes" may mimic a real person or depict fictional personas.
AML.T0088.description:
Adversaries may use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to create synthetic media (i.e. imagery, video, audio, and text) that appear authentic. These "deepfakes" may mimic a real person or depict fictional personas. Adversaries may use deepfakes for impersonation to conduct Phishing or to evade AI applications such as biometric identity verification systems (see Evade AI Model).
Manipulation of media has been possible for a long time, however GenAI reduces the skill and level of effort required, allowing adversaries to rapidly scale operations to target more users or systems. It also makes real-time manipulations feasible.
Adversaries may utilize open-source models and software that were designed for legitimate use cases to generate deepfakes for malicious use. However, there are some projects specifically tailored towards malicious use cases such as ProKYC.

mitigations.AML.M0009: Using a variety of sensors, such as IR depth cameras, can aid in detecting deepfakes.
mitigations.AML.M0034: Deepfake detection can be used to identify and block generated content.

AML.T0089.name: Enterprise Environment Discovery
AML.T0089.summary: Adversaries may discover configurations, conditions, relationships, activity, and other characteristics of an enterprise environment.
AML.T0089.description:
Adversaries may discover configurations, conditions, relationships, activity, and other characteristics of an enterprise environment. This may include system and network configuration; active connections, processes, windows, and users; permissions, trust relationships, and policy settings; installed defensive or backup capabilities; network traffic; browser and registry information; or environmental properties such as location, language, time, connectivity, virtualization, debugging, and sandbox indicators.
Adversaries may query or passively observe this information to understand how the environment is configured and operating, identify access paths or security controls, detect monitoring or analysis, and select or adapt subsequent actions.
See the ATT&CK Discovery tactic for techniques describing specific environmental characteristics and discovery mechanisms.

AML.T0090.name: OS Credential Dumping
AML.T0090.summary: Adversaries may extract credentials from OS caches, application memory, or other sources on a compromised system. Credentials are often in the form of a hash or clear text, and can include usernames and passwords, application tokens, or other authentication keys.
AML.T0090.description:
Adversaries may extract credentials from OS caches, application memory, or other sources on a compromised system. Credentials are often in the form of a hash or clear text, and can include usernames and passwords, application tokens, or other authentication keys.
Credentials can be used to perform Lateral Movement to access other AI services such as AI agents, LLMs, or AI inference APIs. Credentials could also give an adversary access to other software tools and data sources that are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle.

mitigations.AML.M0011: Restrict library loading to block credential-dumping paths that inject or load malicious code into processes holding authentication material.

AML.T0091.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
AML.T0091.summary: Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls.
AML.T0091.description:
Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls.
AI services commonly use alternate authentication material as a primary means for users to make queries, making them vulnerable to this technique.

mitigations.AML.M0019: Enforce authorization and monitor production AI API use for anomalous activity associated with replayed access tokens.

AML.T0091.000.name: Application Access Token
AML.T0091.000.summary: Adversaries may use stolen application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems. These tokens are typically stolen from users or services and used in lieu of login credentials.
AML.T0091.000.description:
Adversaries may use stolen application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems. These tokens are typically stolen from users or services and used in lieu of login credentials.
Application access tokens are used to make authorized API requests on behalf of a user or service and are commonly used to access resources in cloud, container-based applications, software-as-a-service (SaaS), and AI-as-a-service(AIaaS). They are commonly used for AI services such as chatbots, LLMs, and predictive inference APIs.

mitigations.AML.M0019: Enforce authorization and monitor production AI API use for anomalous activity associated with replayed access tokens.
mitigations.AML.M0043: Expire and revoke agent-associated application access tokens to limit the window for unauthorized use.

AML.T0091.001.name: Web Session Cookie
AML.T0091.001.summary: Adversaries may use stolen web session cookies to authenticate to AI-enabled applications and supporting services as another user. This technique may bypass some multi-factor authentication controls because the session represented by the cookie has already been authenticated.
AML.T0091.001.description:
Adversaries may use stolen web session cookies to authenticate to AI-enabled applications and supporting services as another user. This technique may bypass some multi-factor authentication controls because the session represented by the cookie has already been authenticated.
Authentication cookies are commonly used by web applications and cloud-based services after a user has authenticated, allowing the user to continue using the service without repeatedly passing credentials. These cookies may remain valid for extended periods of time. After obtaining a cookie through Steal Web Session Cookie, an adversary may import the cookie into a browser or automated client they control and access the corresponding application as the victim while the session remains active.
In attacks on AI systems, web session cookies may grant access to AI chat histories, AI agent control panels, model provider dashboards, customer support systems, retrieval or knowledge management interfaces, or AI DevOps resources. If the stolen cookie belongs to an operator, support agent, developer, or administrator, the adversary may be able to view sensitive conversations, manipulate agent configuration, access private data available through AI tools, or perform actions with the victim account's permissions.

AML.T0092.name: Manipulate User LLM Chat History
AML.T0092.summary: Adversaries may manipulate a user's large language model (LLM) chat history to cover the tracks of their malicious behavior. They may hide persistent changes they have made to the LLM's behavior, or obscure their attempts at discovering private information about the user.
AML.T0092.description:
Adversaries may manipulate a user's large language model (LLM) chat history to cover the tracks of their malicious behavior. They may hide persistent changes they have made to the LLM's behavior, or obscure their attempts at discovering private information about the user.
To do so, adversaries may delete or edit existing messages or create new threads as part of their coverup. This is feasible if the adversary has the victim's authentication tokens for the backend LLM service or if they have direct access to the victim's chat interface.
Chat interfaces (especially desktop interfaces) often do not show the injected prompt for any ongoing chat, as they update chat history only once when initially opening it. This can help the adversary's manipulations go unnoticed by the victim.

AML.T0093.name: Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application
AML.T0093.summary: An adversary may introduce malicious prompts into the victim's system via a public-facing application with the intention of it being ingested by an AI at some point in the future and ultimately having a downstream effect.
AML.T0093.description:
An adversary may introduce malicious prompts into the victim's system via a public-facing application with the intention of it being ingested by an AI at some point in the future and ultimately having a downstream effect. This may occur when a data source is indexed by a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system, when a rule triggers an action by an AI agent, or when a user utilizes a large language model (LLM) to interact with the malicious content. The malicious prompts may persist on the victim system for an extended period and could affect multiple users and various AI tools within the victim organization.
Any public-facing application that accepts text input could be a target. This includes email, shared document systems like OneDrive or Google Drive, and service desks or ticketing systems like Jira. This also includes OCR-mediated infiltration where malicious instructions are embedded in images, screenshots, and invoices that are ingested into the system.
Adversaries may perform Reconnaissance to identify public facing applications that are likely monitored by an AI agent or are likely to be indexed by a RAG. They may perform Discover AI Agent Configuration to refine their targeting.

mitigations.AML.M0039: Since honeypots capture real input, they can provide visibility into attacks and prompt payloads that are target-specific.

AML.T0094.name: Delay Execution of LLM Instructions
AML.T0094.summary: Adversaries may include instructions to be followed by the AI system in response to a future event, such as a specific keyword or the next interaction, in order to evade detection or bypass controls placed on the AI system.
AML.T0094.description:
Adversaries may include instructions to be followed by the AI system in response to a future event, such as a specific keyword or the next interaction, in order to evade detection or bypass controls placed on the AI system.
For example, an adversary may include "If the user submits a new request..." followed by the malicious instructions as part of their prompt.
AI agents can include security measures against prompt injections that prevent the invocation of particular tools or access to certain data sources during a conversation turn that has untrusted data in context. Delaying the execution of instructions to a future interaction or keyword is one way adversaries may bypass this type of control.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Preserve relevant risk context across conversation turns and revalidate actions when deferred instructions become active. Do not reset restrictions solely because a new user message or event occurs after untrusted content was introduced.

AML.T0095.name: Search Open Websites/Domains
AML.T0095.summary: Adversaries may search public websites and/or domains for information about victims and AI targets that can be used during targeting and to discover opportunities for successful attacks.
AML.T0095.description:
Adversaries may search public websites and/or domains for information about victims and AI targets that can be used during targeting and to discover opportunities for successful attacks. Information about a victim's attack surface may be available in various online sites, such as social media, news sites, or domains owned by the victim.
Adversaries may find the information they seek to gather via search engines. They can use precise search queries to identify software platforms or services used by the victim to use in targeting. This may be followed by Exploit Public-Facing Application or Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application.
Adversaries may utilize OSINT-based discovery to map different AI assets by using search engine result pages, as well as backlink analysis, to locate agentic interfaces (which are frequently embedded via iFrames and follow predictable naming conventions). By analyzing the indexed URL structures of these sources from different search engines, attackers can often reverse-engineer internal environment IDs and organization-specific naming conventions. This intelligence gathering significantly narrows the search space for any later targeted fuzzing or enumeration performed by Active Scanning: Enumerate Hosted AI Resources.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit public technical and organizational information that reveals the AI stack, services, personnel, or other targeting details on websites and domains.
mitigations.AML.M0039: Decoy assets, such as honeypots, can act as a first contact for adversarial activity and reveal discovery channels that attackers are using to find web AI assets for targeting.

AML.T0095.000.name: Code Repositories
AML.T0095.000.summary: Adversaries may search public code repositories for information about a victim or victim system that can be used during targeting. Victims may store code or artifacts related to their AI systems in repositories on various third-party websites such as GitHub, GitLab, SourceForge, and BitBucket.
AML.T0095.000.description:
Adversaries may search public code repositories for information about a victim or victim system that can be used during targeting. Victims may store code or artifacts related to their AI systems in repositories on various third-party websites such as GitHub, GitLab, SourceForge, and BitBucket. Adversaries may search code repositories of common AI tools, frameworks, models, or agentic systems that are used--but not owned--by the victim.
Public code repositories can often be a source of various information about victims, such as commonly used AI frameworks, libraries, models, datasets, agents, and agent tools, as well as the names of employees. Adversaries may also identify more sensitive data, including accidentally leaked credentials or API keys (ex: Credentials from AI Agent Configuration). Information from these sources may reveal opportunities for other forms of Reconnaissance (ex: Gather RAG-Indexed Targets), establishing operational resources (ex: Acquire Public AI Artifacts), Discovery (ex: Discover AI Agent Configuration) and/or Initial Access (ex: Valid Accounts or Phishing).

mitigations.AML.M0039: Decoy assets, such as honeypots, can act as a first contact for adversarial activity and reveal discovery channels that attackers are using to find web AI assets for targeting.

AML.T0096.name: AI Service API
AML.T0096.summary: Adversaries may communicate using the API of an AI service on the victim's system. The adversary's commands to the victim system, and often the results, are embedded in the normal traffic of the AI service.
AML.T0096.description:
Adversaries may communicate using the API of an AI service on the victim's system. The adversary's commands to the victim system, and often the results, are embedded in the normal traffic of the AI service.
An AI service API command and control channel is covert because the adversary's commands blend in with normal communications, so an adversary may use this technique to avoid detection. Using existing infrastructure on the victim's system allows the adversary to live off the land, further reducing their footprint.
AI service APIs may be abused as C2 channels when an adversary wants to be stealthy and maintain long-term persistence for espionage activities.

mitigations.AML.M0019: Authenticate AI service API callers and monitor queries for policy violations and misuse.

AML.T0097.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
AML.T0097.summary: Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox.
AML.T0097.description:
Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads.
Adversaries may use several methods to accomplish Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion such as checking for security monitoring tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark, etc.) or other system artifacts associated with analysis or virtualization such as registry keys (e.g. substrings matching Vmware, VBOX, QEMU), environment variables (e.g. substrings matching VBOX, VMWARE, PARALLELS), NIC MAC addresses (e.g. prefixes 00-05-69 (VMWare) or 08-00-27 (VirtualBox)), running processes (e.g. vmware.exe, vboxservice.exe, qemu-ga.exe).

AML.T0098.name: AI Agent Tool Credential Harvesting
AML.T0098.summary: Adversaries may attempt to use their access to an AI agent on the victim's system to retrieve data from available agent tools to collect credentials.
AML.T0098.description: Adversaries may attempt to use their access to an AI agent on the victim's system to retrieve data from available agent tools to collect credentials. Agent tools may connect to a wide range of sources that may contain credentials including document stores (e.g. SharePoint, OneDrive or Google Drive), code repositories (e.g. GitHub or GitLab), or enterprise productivity tools (e.g. as email providers or Slack), and local notetaking tools (e.g. Obsidian or Apple Notes).

mitigations.AML.M0032: Segmentation can prevent adversaries from utilizing tools in an agentic workflow to harvest credentials.

AML.T0099.name: AI Agent Tool Data Poisoning
AML.T0099.summary: Adversaries may manipulate data in a victim-controlled, trusted, or connected data source that is accessible through an AI agent tool.
AML.T0099.description:
Adversaries may manipulate data in a victim-controlled, trusted, or connected data source that is accessible through an AI agent tool. Poisoned data may be placed in document repositories, databases, source-code repositories, knowledge bases, search indexes, enterprise applications, or third-party data services used by the agent.
The content may be crafted to appear in common tool queries or retrieval operations. It may contain false or misleading information or malicious instructions intended to produce an LLM Prompt Injection: Indirect when retrieved.
This technique concerns manipulation of a data source that an agent tool treats as a source of information. When the adversary introduces the content through a victim-controlled public-facing application, the activity may also constitute Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application. Content retrieved directly from an adversary-controlled website may instead constitute Drive-by Compromise. A malicious or compromised tool that deliberately alters its own runtime result constitutes AI Agent Tool Poisoning: Runtime Response.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect content returned from connected data sources for malicious instructions and deceptive information before adding it to model context. Apply source, relevance, and task-consistency checks, and block resulting actions that violate policy.

AML.T0100.name: AI Agent Clickbait
AML.T0100.summary: Adversaries may craft deceptive content designed to bait computer-using AI agents or AI web browsers and tools into taking unintended actions, such as clicking buttons, copying code, or navigating to specific web pages.
AML.T0100.description:
Adversaries may craft deceptive content designed to bait computer-using AI agents or AI web browsers and tools into taking unintended actions, such as clicking buttons, copying code, or navigating to specific web pages. These attacks exploit the agent's interpretation of UI content, visual cues, and natural language embedded in processed artifacts, such as a website or a document, and aim at the agent's decision process rather than a human reader's.
When successful, AI Agent Clickbait can lead the victim's agent to inadvertently copy and execute malicious code on the user's operating system or perform data exfiltration. The AI Agent Clickbait may also include a LLM Prompt Injection: Indirect, which can influence or manipulate the victim's agent in adversary-controlled ways.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Evaluate model-visible interface content and proposed computer-use actions against the authorized task. Block deceptive instructions that induce unrelated navigation, command execution, credential entry, or data transfer, and validate destinations before acting.
mitigations.AML.M0021: Instruct agents to treat webpage instructions as untrusted and request approval for consequential actions.

AML.T0101.name: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation
AML.T0101.summary: Adversaries may invoke an AI agent's tool capable of performing mutative operations to perform Data Destruction. Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources.
AML.T0101.description: Adversaries may invoke an AI agent's tool capable of performing mutative operations to perform Data Destruction. Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources.

mitigations.AML.M0024: Log AI agent tool invocations to detect malicious calls.
mitigations.AML.M0026: Separate deletion, overwrite, and other destructive permissions from routine service access. Limit them to required workflows and target resources, and authorize workflow initiators so that access to the agent does not confer destructive privileges.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Use read-only delegation when modification is unnecessary. Limit deletion and other destructive permissions to explicitly authorized tasks and resources rather than automatically delegating permissions the user possesses.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Separately authorize deletion, overwrite, and other destructive tool operations against specific target resources. Withhold destructive permissions from callers and tool execution identities that do not require them.
mitigations.AML.M0029: Requiring user confirmation of AI agent tool invocations can prevent the automatic execution of tools by an adversary.
mitigations.AML.M0030: Restricting the automatic tool use when untrusted data is present can prevent adversaries from invoking tools via prompt injections.

AML.T0102.name: Generate Malicious Commands
AML.T0102.summary: Adversaries may use large language models (LLMs) to dynamically generate malicious commands from natural language. Dynamically generated commands may be harder to detect as the attack signature is constantly changing.
AML.T0102.description:
Adversaries may use large language models (LLMs) to dynamically generate malicious commands from natural language. Dynamically generated commands may be harder to detect as the attack signature is constantly changing. AI-generated commands may also allow adversaries to more rapidly adapt to different environments and adjust their tactics.
Adversaries may utilize LLMs present in the victim's environment or call out to externally hosted services. APT28 utilized a model hosted on HuggingFace in a campaign with their LAMEHUG malware. In either case prompts to generate malicious code can blend in with normal traffic.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect requests and generated commands for prohibited behavior using the task context and service policy. Block malicious command generation or release through the protected service, and independently validate commands before execution when an execution interface is present.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Align generative AI models with safety objectives to reduce the likelihood that they will generate malicious commands or harmful instructions.

AML.T0103.name: Deploy AI Agent
AML.T0103.summary: Adversaries may launch AI agents in the victim's environment to execute actions on their behalf. AI agents may have access to a wide range of tools and data sources, as well as permissions to access and interact with other services and systems in the victim's environment.
AML.T0103.description:
Adversaries may launch AI agents in the victim's environment to execute actions on their behalf. AI agents may have access to a wide range of tools and data sources, as well as permissions to access and interact with other services and systems in the victim's environment. The adversary may leverage these capabilities to carry out their operations.
Adversaries may configure the AI agent by providing an initial system prompt and granting access to tools, effectively defining their goals for the agent to achieve. They may deploy the agent with excessive trust permissions and disable any user interactions to ensure the agent's actions aren't blocked.
Launching an AI agent may provide for some autonomous behavior, allowing for the agent to make decisions and determine how to achieve the adversary's goals. This also represents a loss of control for the adversary.

mitigations.AML.M0013: Allow only trusted signed agent applications to execute in the environment.

AML.T0105.name: Escape to Host
AML.T0105.summary: Adversaries may break out of a container or virtualized environment to gain access to the underlying host. This can allow an adversary access to other containerized or virtualized resources from the host level or to the host itself.
AML.T0105.description:
Adversaries may break out of a container or virtualized environment to gain access to the underlying host. This can allow an adversary access to other containerized or virtualized resources from the host level or to the host itself. In principle, containerized / virtualized resources should provide a clear separation of application functionality and be isolated from the host environment.
There are many ways an adversary may escape from a container or sandbox environment via AI Systems. For example, modifying an AI Agent's configuration to disable safety features or user confirmations could allow the adversary to invoke tools to be run on host environments rather than in the sandbox.

AML.T0106.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
AML.T0106.summary: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to collect credentials. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code.
AML.T0106.description: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to collect credentials. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code.

mitigations.AML.M0016: Vulnerability scanning identifies and remediates software flaws before they can be exploited to obtain credentials.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on adversary use of exploits, including zero-day vulnerabilities, to obtain credentials. Use this intelligence to identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation and compensating controls, and update detection and response procedures.

AML.T0107.name: Exploitation for Defense Evasion
AML.T0107.summary: Adversaries may exploit a system or application vulnerability to bypass security features. Exploitation of a vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code.
AML.T0107.description: Adversaries may exploit a system or application vulnerability to bypass security features. Exploitation of a vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Vulnerabilities may exist in defensive security software that can be used to disable or circumvent them.

mitigations.AML.M0016: Vulnerability scanning reduces opportunities for adversaries to exploit weaknesses that bypass security controls.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on adversary use of exploits, including zero-day vulnerabilities, to bypass security features. Use this intelligence to identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation and compensating controls, and update detection and response procedures.

AML.T0108.name: AI Agent
AML.T0108.summary: Adversaries may abuse AI agents present on the victim's system for command and control. AI agents are often granted access to tools that can execute shell commands, reach out to the internet, and interact with other services in the victim's environment, making them capable C2 agents.
