AML.T0108.description:
Adversaries may abuse AI agents present on the victim's system for command and control. AI agents are often granted access to tools that can execute shell commands, reach out to the internet, and interact with other services in the victim's environment, making them capable C2 agents.
The adversary may modify the behavior of an AI agent for C2 via LLM Prompt Injection and rely on the agent's ability to invoke tools to retrieve and execute the adversary's commands. They may maintain persistent control of an agent via Modify AI Agent Configuration or AI Agent Context Poisoning. They may instruct the agent to not report their actions to the user in an attempt to remain covert.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect agent inputs and proposed actions for attempts to establish unauthorized command retrieval, execution, or result transmission. Block tool operations and communications inconsistent with the agent's authorized task before execution.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Monitor agent prompts, decisions, tool use, and outputs for C2 behavior.

AML.T0109.name: AI Supply Chain Rug Pull
AML.T0109.summary: Adversaries may publish legitimate AI components or software, gain user adoption, then push an update with a malicious variant, leading to Supply Chain Compromise. More scrutiny is often placed on a supply chain dependency when it is first being considered for inclusion in an AI system.
AML.T0109.description:
Adversaries may publish legitimate AI components or software, gain user adoption, then push an update with a malicious variant, leading to Supply Chain Compromise. More scrutiny is often placed on a supply chain dependency when it is first being considered for inclusion in an AI system. Performing a rug pull may allow adversaries to bypass these defenses and be more likely to achieve Initial Access.
Adversaries may Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts, then attempt to gain user trust and increase adoption before performing the rug pull (See AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation).

mitigations.AML.M0014: Pin dependencies and AI artifacts to approved digests and require approval and verification of each update. Prevent mutable references or automatic updates from bypassing this process.
mitigations.AML.M0023: Retain versioned component and dependency records across updates. Use these records to identify deployments that adopted a subsequently identified malicious release and guide replacement or rollback.

AML.T0110.name: AI Agent Tool Poisoning
AML.T0110.summary: Adversaries may poison tools used by AI agents by introducing or modifying malicious content or behavior in a tool's model-visible definition, executable implementation, or runtime responses.
AML.T0110.description:
Adversaries may poison tools used by AI agents by introducing or modifying malicious content or behavior in a tool's model-visible definition, executable implementation, or runtime responses. Tools may include built-in integrations, locally installed packages, remotely hosted services, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and tools, and agent skills or similar capability packages.
A poisoned tool is represented or trusted as performing a benign function, but its definition, implementation, or responses cause agent behavior or tool-mediated effects to differ materially from the represented function. Poisoning may be present when a tool is first published, introduced through a Supply Chain Compromise, or added after adoption through an AI Supply Chain Rug Pull. Once the tool is installed, connected, or otherwise made available to the agent, it may provide the adversary with persistent influence over the agent's actions and external interactions.
Adversaries may poison a tool's model-visible semantic interface, including its descriptions, schemas, parameter documentation, annotations, or agent-readable instructions (See Definition and Instructions). They may introduce hidden executable behavior that changes the effects of otherwise normal tool invocations (See Implementation). They may also cause a malicious or compromised tool to deliberately return content intended to influence the model's subsequent reasoning or actions (See Runtime Response).
Poisoned tools may cause an agent to access sensitive data, alter the inputs or destinations of other tools, execute unauthorized commands, conceal actions from users, or exfiltrate information. Tool poisoning frequently enables other techniques such as LLM Prompt Injection, AI Agent Tool Invocation, and Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation.
Tool poisoning is distinct from malicious data that a benign tool faithfully retrieves from an external or victim-controlled source (See AI Agent Tool Data Poisoning and LLM Prompt Injection: Indirect. Software that merely uses an agent tool package as a delivery vehicle for conventional malware, without subverting the tool's represented interface or operation, may be better described as a malicious package or software supply-chain compromise rather than AI Agent Tool Poisoning.

AML.T0110.000.name: Definition and Instructions
AML.T0110.000.summary: Adversaries may poison the model-visible definition or operational instructions of an AI agent tool to manipulate how an agent interprets, selects, or invokes the tool.
AML.T0110.000.description:
Adversaries may poison the model-visible definition or operational instructions of an AI agent tool to manipulate how an agent interprets, selects, or invokes the tool. The poisoned content may be contained in tool descriptions, docstrings, parameter names, help text, input or output schemas, annotations, examples, manifests, skill instruction files, or other static content used to explain a tool's capabilities to the model.
Malicious instructions in this layer may direct the agent to collect additional data, populate hidden or unnecessary parameters, conceal actions from the user, or invoke other tools. Because an agent may receive a more complete representation of a tool than is shown in the user interface, the model may process malicious instructions that are invisible or only partially visible to a human reviewer.
Definition poisoning may also be used for tool shadowing, in which the definition of one malicious tool contains instructions that alter how the agent selects or invokes another trusted tool. The poisoned tool may not need to be invoked for its definition to influence the agent if definitions from multiple connected tools are included in the same model context.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect tool descriptions, schemas, examples, and operational instructions before exposing them to the model. Reject content that directs unrelated data collection, concealed actions, or manipulation of other tools, and independently validate resulting tool requests.

AML.T0110.001.name: Implementation
AML.T0110.001.summary: Adversaries may poison the executable implementation of an AI agent tool so that normal tool invocation produces unauthorized behavior or hidden side effects.
AML.T0110.001.description:
Adversaries may poison the executable implementation of an AI agent tool so that normal tool invocation produces unauthorized behavior or hidden side effects. The tool may continue to provide its represented functionality while also accessing additional data, modifying requests, changing recipients or destinations, executing unauthorized commands, weakening security controls, or performing covert data exfiltration.
Implementation poisoning does not require the model to interpret or follow malicious instructions. The adversarial effect is produced by executable logic when the agent or user invokes the tool. For example, a poisoned email tool may send the requested message while silently adding an adversary-controlled blind-copy recipient. A file-processing tool may return the requested result while also transmitting the source file to an external service.
Implementation poisoning may be introduced before publication, through compromise of a tool's source repository or build process, or through a malicious update after users have adopted a benign version. Installed copies may continue to exhibit the poisoned behavior even after the malicious package or remote listing is removed.

AML.T0110.002.name: Runtime Response
AML.T0110.002.summary: Adversaries may poison the runtime response channel of a malicious or compromised AI agent tool by deliberately returning content intended to influence the model's subsequent reasoning, decisions, or actions.
AML.T0110.002.description:
Adversaries may poison the runtime response channel of a malicious or compromised AI agent tool by deliberately returning content intended to influence the model's subsequent reasoning, decisions, or actions. Poisoned responses may contain malicious instructions, deceptive data, fabricated errors, embedded resources, or other content designed to be treated as trusted context after an approved tool invocation.
Because tool responses are commonly incorporated into the model's context, an adversary may use them to direct the agent to invoke additional tools, access sensitive information, alter an ongoing workflow, or transmit data to an adversary-controlled destination. Poisoned instructions may be mixed with legitimate results so that the tool appears to operate normally. Responses may use structured or unstructured content, including text, images, resource links, embedded resources, or schema-conforming fields.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Validate tool responses before incorporating them into model context. Detect malicious instructions, fabricated errors, embedded resources, or other content that instructs the agent, and check subsequent actions.

AML.T0111.name: AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation
AML.T0111.summary: AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation is the process of building or leveraging genuinely credible-looking trust signals to increase the perceived legitimacy of AI supply chain components, with the goal of driving adoption of malicious or compromised assets.
AML.T0111.description:
AI Supply Chain Reputation Inflation is the process of building or leveraging genuinely credible-looking trust signals to increase the perceived legitimacy of AI supply chain components, with the goal of driving adoption of malicious or compromised assets.
Adversaries use established developer accounts with a history of legitimate projects and contributions to publish AI models, datasets, packages, and MCP servers that appear trustworthy. They build reputation through real adoption signals such as downloads, GitHub stars, forks, and inclusion in dependency chains, often releasing benign versions before introducing malicious updates via AI Supply Chain Rug Pull.
By relying on authentic history and usage patterns, these components pass both human and automated trust checks, increasing the likelihood they are adopted without scrutiny.

AML.T0112.name: Machine Compromise
AML.T0112.summary: Adversaries may compromise a machine by exploiting or manipulating AI-enabled components on the system. Compromising a victim system allows the adversary to execute arbitrary code, steal credentials, exfiltrate data, and continue to persist on the system.
AML.T0112.description:
Adversaries may compromise a machine by exploiting or manipulating AI-enabled components on the system. Compromising a victim system allows the adversary to execute arbitrary code, steal credentials, exfiltrate data, and continue to persist on the system.
Adversaries may target a Local AI Agent which if compromised grants them the capabilities and permissions of the agent, or AI Artifacts which can contain embedded malware.

AML.T0112.000.name: Local AI Agent
AML.T0112.000.summary: Adversaries may achieve full system compromise by abusing AI agents running locally on a host, such as computer-use agents or AI-driven browsers.
AML.T0112.000.description:
Adversaries may achieve full system compromise by abusing AI agents running locally on a host, such as computer-use agents or AI-driven browsers. These agents are designed to autonomously interact with the operating system, applications, and external services, often with broad permissions to execute commands, access files, manage credentials, and control user workflows.
If an adversary is able to take control of an AI agent's behavior, they effectively gain the same level of access as the agent. This can result in complete control over the machine, including executing arbitrary code, accessing or exfiltrating sensitive data, modifying system configurations, and establishing persistence.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Mediate local agent actions involving command execution, file access, credentials, and system configuration. Validate requested operations against authorized scope and block prohibited actions before they reach the operating system or connected applications.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Monitor local agent commands, file and credential access, tool use, and system changes.

AML.T0112.001.name: AI Artifacts
AML.T0112.001.summary: Adversaries may achieve full system compromise by introducing malicious AI artifacts, such as models or data, that contain embedded malware or other malicious commands. AI artifacts are often stored in model registries or data stores and may affect many systems that pull these resources.
AML.T0112.001.description:
Adversaries may achieve full system compromise by introducing malicious AI artifacts, such as models or data, that contain embedded malware or other malicious commands. AI artifacts are often stored in model registries or data stores and may affect many systems that pull these resources.
Malicious content stored in AI artifacts may be executed as a result of unsafe serialization formats (e.g. Python pickle) or by other bundled scripts or notebooks.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Restrict write access to model registries and AI artifact stores.

AML.T0113.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
AML.T0113.summary: Adversaries may steal web application or service session cookies used to authenticate users to AI-enabled systems, AI services, or supporting enterprise applications.
AML.T0113.description:
Adversaries may steal web application or service session cookies used to authenticate users to AI-enabled systems, AI services, or supporting enterprise applications.
Web applications often use session cookies as authentication tokens after a user has signed in. These cookies may remain valid for extended periods of time, even when the application is not actively being used. In AI systems, session cookies may provide access to chat interfaces, AI agents, AI service consoles, customer support platforms, model management dashboards, or other tools connected to sensitive data and workflows.
Adversaries may obtain session cookies from browser storage, process memory, network traffic, or applications that store authentication material in memory. They may also steal cookies by injecting malicious JavaScript into AI-rendered content, abusing unsafe rendering of LLM outputs, or tricking users or AI operators into opening poisoned content that executes in their browser.
In attacks on AI systems, session cookie theft can allow adversaries to bypass normal authentication flows and gain access to privileged AI-enabled applications without knowing the victim's username, password, or MFA secret. Stolen cookies may then be used with Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie to access the corresponding service as the victim.

AML.T0114.name: AI Service Web Interface
AML.T0114.summary: Adversaries may communicate with compromised systems by abusing the web interface of an AI service as an intermediary command-and-control relay.
AML.T0114.description:
Adversaries may communicate with compromised systems by abusing the web interface of an AI service as an intermediary command-and-control relay. Instead of connecting directly to attacker-controlled infrastructure or using an AI provider's API, malware may open or automate a browser, embedded browser, or WebView component to interact with a public AI assistant.
The malware may prompt the AI assistant to fetch an attacker-controlled URL, include victim data in URL parameters or prompt content, and return attacker-supplied content through the AI assistant's response. The implant can then parse the response and execute embedded instructions.
This technique is especially useful when an AI web interface permits anonymous or unauthenticated browsing, summarization, or URL-fetch behavior. In those cases, adversaries may avoid controls that depend on API keys, service accounts, user identities, or revocable credentials.
This technique allows command-and-control traffic to blend into apparently legitimate AI web traffic to trusted service domains. In this pattern, the AI service acts as a proxy between the compromised system and attacker-controlled infrastructure, shifting detection from API key and account monitoring toward browser automation, prompt content, URL-fetch behavior, and AI service telemetry.

mitigations.AML.M0024: AI telemetry logging can help detect suspicious prompts, browser-based AI service interactions, URL-fetch requests, and AI responses used to relay command-and-control data.

AML.T0115.name: Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts
AML.T0115.summary: Adversaries may create or modify AI artifacts and publish them through public or shared distribution channels to facilitate compromise of downstream AI systems. Poisoned AI artifacts may include datasets, models, and AI agent tools containing malicious content, behaviors, code, or configurations.
AML.T0115.description:
Adversaries may create or modify AI artifacts and publish them through public or shared distribution channels to facilitate compromise of downstream AI systems. Poisoned AI artifacts may include datasets, models, and AI agent tools containing malicious content, behaviors, code, or configurations.
Adversaries may publish novel artifacts or malicious variants of legitimate artifacts through dataset or model repositories, package registries, source code repositories, tool hubs, or remotely hosted services. Victims may subsequently acquire and integrate these artifacts through Supply Chain Compromise.

mitigations.AML.M0007: Dataset publishers and repositories should screen submissions for poisoned samples, annotations, or metadata. Quarantine suspected data before publication and remediate confirmed poisoning.
mitigations.AML.M0016: Model and agent tool registries scan uploaded artifacts for malicious content before listing.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on published poisoned AI artifacts, including identifiers, versions, distribution locations, and evidence of malicious content or behavior. Use this intelligence to block acquisition and use of identified artifacts, investigate existing exposure, and support reporting to distribution platforms for removal.

AML.T0115.000.name: Datasets
AML.T0115.000.summary: Adversaries may publish poisoned datasets intended for training or fine-tuning AI models. The dataset may be newly created or a modified variant of a legitimate dataset and may contain manipulated samples, labels, annotations, or metadata.
AML.T0115.000.description:
Adversaries may publish poisoned datasets intended for training or fine-tuning AI models. The dataset may be newly created or a modified variant of a legitimate dataset and may contain manipulated samples, labels, annotations, or metadata.
Adversaries may distribute poisoned datasets through dataset repositories, code repositories, file-sharing services, or compromised data sources. A victim that incorporates the dataset into a training pipeline may be affected by Training Data Poisoning, potentially through Supply Chain Compromise.

mitigations.AML.M0007: Dataset publishers and repositories should screen submissions for poisoned samples, annotations, or metadata. Quarantine suspected data before publication and remediate confirmed poisoning.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on published poisoned datasets, including identifiers, versions, distribution locations, and evidence of manipulated samples, labels, annotations, or metadata. Use this intelligence to block acquisition and use of identified datasets, investigate training workflows and models that have consumed them, and support reporting to distribution platforms for removal.

AML.T0115.001.name: Models
AML.T0115.001.summary: Adversaries may publish poisoned AI models through model registries, code repositories, or other model distribution channels.
AML.T0115.001.description:
Adversaries may publish poisoned AI models through model registries, code repositories, or other model distribution channels. The model may be newly created or a modified variant of a legitimate model and may contain manipulated weights, configurations, architecture, serialized code, or other components that produce malicious behavior or execute malicious code.
Victims may subsequently download and integrate the model through Supply Chain Compromise.

mitigations.AML.M0008: Model repositories and downstream consumers should evaluate submitted or acquired models for unexpected outputs, backdoor behavior, and sensitive information disclosure before listing or deployment. Reject or quarantine models that fail acceptance criteria.
mitigations.AML.M0016: Model registries scan uploaded models for unsafe serialization, embedded code, malware, and known vulnerabilities before listing.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on published poisoned models, including identifiers, versions, distribution locations, and evidence of malicious content or behavior. Use this intelligence to block acquisition and use of identified models, investigate systems that have loaded or incorporated them, and support reporting to distribution platforms for removal.

AML.T0115.002.name: AI Agent Tools
AML.T0115.002.summary: Adversaries may create and publish poisoned AI agent tools. Poisoned tools may contain malicious model-visible definitions or instructions, hidden executable behavior, or runtime responses designed to manipulate an AI agent.
AML.T0115.002.description:
Adversaries may create and publish poisoned AI agent tools. Poisoned tools may contain malicious model-visible definitions or instructions, hidden executable behavior, or runtime responses designed to manipulate an AI agent. Tools may be published through source code repositories, package registries, agent tool or skill registries, or adversary-controlled remote services. The tool may be newly created or a modified variant of a legitimate tool and may produce malicious behavior when selected, installed, or invoked by a victim's AI agent.
Adversaries may distribute poisoned tools through open-source version control repositories (e.g. GitHub, GitLab), package registries (e.g. npm), or to repositories specifically designed for sharing tools (e.g. OpenClaw Hub). These registries may be largely unregulated and may contain many poisoned tools. Tools may also be published as remotely hosted servers.

mitigations.AML.M0016: Tool registries scan uploaded tool packages and dependencies for malicious code and vulnerabilities before listing.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on published poisoned AI agent tools, including package or service identifiers, versions, distribution locations, and evidence of malicious content or behavior. Use this intelligence to block installation or connection to identified tools, investigate agents that have used them, and support reporting to distribution platforms or service providers for removal.

AML.T0116.name: Autonomous Reconnaissance
AML.T0116.summary: Adversaries may use autonomous AI agents to conduct Reconnaissance activities. Given an objective, target, or partial lead, an agent may autonomously determine what information to obtain and how to investigate it.
AML.T0116.description:
Adversaries may use autonomous AI agents to conduct Reconnaissance activities. Given an objective, target, or partial lead, an agent may autonomously determine what information to obtain and how to investigate it. It may interpret observations, identify gaps in its understanding of the externally observable attack surface, and select subsequent reconnaissance actions without a human specifying each investigative step.
The agent may formulate investigative questions or hypotheses, select sources and approaches for addressing them, and update its understanding as new information is obtained. Findings may generate additional reconnaissance objectives or change the scope, depth, or direction of the investigation. This creates a recursive action-observation process in which reconnaissance results influence what the agent investigates next rather than merely supplying output from a predefined procedure.
The agent may correlate information across public sources and externally accessible services, prioritize promising systems, investigate suspected vulnerabilities, abandon unsuccessful approaches, or select alternative methods. It may also expand or substitute targets based on discovered names, infrastructure, or contextual relationships and independently reassess whether a system remains relevant or in scope. Incorrect assumptions may cause unrelated or unauthorized systems to be pursued, while successful scope recognition may cause the agent to stop or redirect its activity.
Autonomous AI agents can sustain reconnaissance across long-running operations, reason over multiple information sources, and test many alternative paths at a speed and volume difficult for human operators to maintain.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit release of information to reduce content an autonomous agent can use for reconnaissance.
mitigations.AML.M0001: Limit release of AI artifacts to reduce an autonomous agent's ability to conduct targeting.
mitigations.AML.M0037: Treat newly discovered resources as outside the authorized boundary to prevent expansion of the agent's permitted interactions without approval.
mitigations.AML.M0038: Identify when an agent attempts to discover or probe resources in ways no longer consistent with the authorized objective.
mitigations.AML.M0039: Deploy decoy assets or credentials to slow down or divert autonomous reconnaissance efforts. Detect adversary interactions with decoy assets or use of decoy credentials and block associated unauthorized access attempts.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on autonomous reconnaissance campaigns, including targeting, infrastructure, and observed sequences of investigative actions. Use this intelligence to correlate related reconnaissance activity, identify assets receiving adversary attention, and prioritize monitoring and exposure reduction.

AML.T0117.name: Autonomous Attack-Path Adaptation
AML.T0117.summary: Adversaries may use an AI agent to autonomously construct and repeatedly revise an attack path toward an adversary-defined objective.
AML.T0117.description:
Adversaries may use an AI agent to autonomously construct and repeatedly revise an attack path toward an adversary-defined objective. Given a high-level objective, the system may derive intermediate objectives, identify prerequisites, and compare candidate paths, and incorporate observations from previous actions to adaptively sequence techniques without a human directing each step.
Autonomous AI agents may also exhibit this behavior while pursuing an objective provided for a legitimate, benign, or authorized purpose when the intermediate objectives or methods selected by the system cross an authorization, trust, control, or safety boundary and result in attempted or realized harmful cyber activity.
Through repeated observation-decision-action cycles, the system may interpret command output, errors, defensive responses, changes in access, and newly discovered information. It may use those observations to reprioritize actions, replace an intermediate objective, abandon an unproductive branch, discard findings invalidated by additional evidence, or pursue an alternative path.
An autonomous AI system may generate enabling objectives whose primary purpose is to increase its future operational capability rather than directly accomplishing the assigned objective. These objectives may include acquiring new exploits (See Autonomous Exploit Development), additional authorities, identities, execution environments, communication paths, tools, or trust relationships that expand the set of actions available to subsequent planning cycles. Newly acquired capabilities may themselves become prerequisites for additional enabling objectives, resulting in progressive expansion of the agent's operational reach over the course of an operation.
Attack-path replanning may occur within one agent run or emerge across multiple independent agents. Agents may communicate persistent, shared artifacts (See Autonomous AI Agent Communication: Communication via Shared Artifacts), allowing discoveries, requests, capabilities, constraints, task state, and results produced by one agent to affect the subsequent path selected by another. Participating agents may adopt peer requests, divide work voluntarily, reuse successful methods, continue incomplete activity, or redirect their local paths without a centralized planner, shared context window, or complete view of the broader operation.
Human involvement does not preclude autonomous attack-path replanning. A human operator, user, evaluator, or workflow may select the target, define the objective, establish constraints, provide capabilities, or approve consequential transitions.
Autonomous Attack-Path Adaptation and Autonomous Attack Orchestration may occur together but describe different control functions. Attack-path adaptation captures how evidence changes the selected path. Attack orchestration captures how work is allocated, coordinated, validated, and redirected across agents.

mitigations.AML.M0037: Constrain actions that seek new authorities, identities, execution environments, tools, communication paths, or trust relationships.
mitigations.AML.M0038: Evaluate whether dynamically generated intermediate actions are within the agent's task scope.
mitigations.AML.M0039: Decoy assets, such as honeypots, can slow down autonomous operations by obscuring real attack paths, and can provide an early warning to the defender about adversarial autonomous activity.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on observed autonomous cyber behaviors, including observed changes in objectives and techniques following failed attempts, defensive responses, or newly acquired access. Use this intelligence to identify alternative attack paths requiring protection, update defensive evaluations, and prepare response procedures for continued activity after an initial path is blocked.

AML.T0118.name: Autonomous AI Agent Communication
AML.T0118.summary: Autonomous AI agents may exchange operational information with other AI agents, sub-agents, or independent agent runs. Exchanged information may include discoveries, objectives, tasking, capabilities, credentials, constraints, operating rules, task state, targeting information, instructions, or results.
AML.T0118.description:
Autonomous AI agents may exchange operational information with other AI agents, sub-agents, or independent agent runs. Exchanged information may include discoveries, objectives, tasking, capabilities, credentials, constraints, operating rules, task state, targeting information, instructions, or results. Communication enables autonomous AI agents to coordinate activities, share discoveries, delegate work, request assistance, validate results, or revise future actions without requiring a human operator to direct each interaction.
Autonomous AI agents may independently determine when communication is operationally beneficial, what information to exchange, and how to best utilize exchanged information to accomplish their task. The receiving AI agent may interpret the shared information and use it to continue prior activity, investigate a lead, perform a task, reuse a capability, validate a result, or revise subsequent attack activity.
Communication may occur directly through an agent interface (See Direct Agent Communication) or indirectly via writeable shared resources (See Communication via Shared Artifacts).

mitigations.AML.M0026: Limit communication and shared-resource permissions to approved inter-agent workflows. Separate authority across unrelated agents and services and authorize workflow initiators to prevent communication from exercising unrelated service privileges.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated communication and shared-resource access to the user's task and current permissions to restrict unauthorized inter-agent information exchange or coordination. Remove access when delegation ends.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Enforce caller-specific authorization on tools for direct agent communication or shared-artifact exchange. Check each operation against its recipient or target resource and prevent shared tool privileges from expanding the caller's communication or resource access.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Implement effective boundaries and sandboxing between system resources or services and agentic tools to limit undesired communication between agents.
mitigations.AML.M0037: Limit the ability of agents to autonomously acquire new credentials to prevent them from forming unwanted communications channels on external services.
mitigations.AML.M0038: Identify when objectives, tasks, capabilities, or instructions received through autonomous agent communication cause an agent's planned or executed actions to deviate from its authorized scope.

AML.T0118.000.name: Communication via Shared Artifacts
AML.T0118.000.summary: Autonomous AI agents may communicate by creating or modifying artifacts in a shared resource that persists outside their individual execution contexts.
AML.T0118.000.description:
Autonomous AI agents may communicate by creating or modifying artifacts in a shared resource that persists outside their individual execution contexts. Shared artifacts may convey discoveries, objectives, tasking, credentials, capabilities, operating rules, progress, scripts, targeting information, instructions, or results.
Shared artifacts allow communication to occur asynchronously and across independent runs. An agent may publish information for later retrieval, adopt information left by another agent, or update the shared state with new findings, progress, or results. Participating agents do not need to share a model, orchestrator, context window, or overlapping execution period.
The shared resource may be established for the operation or may be an existing repository, file store, message board, database, object store, queue, or similar service repurposed by the agents.

mitigations.AML.M0026: Limit service identities to shared resources required by approved workflows. Separate identities and resource permissions across unrelated workflows or agent runs, and avoid shared credentials to restrict unauthorized information exchange through shared artifacts.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated access to shared repositories, files, databases, queues, and other persistent resources required for the user's task. Scope read and write permissions separately to restrict information exchange through shared artifacts, and expire or revoke access when delegation ends.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Authenticate callers and authorize shared-artifact reads, creation, and modification against task-permitted repositories, storage locations, records, queues, and operations. Preserve restrictions through downstream services to prevent unauthorized information exchange through shared artifacts.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Implement effective boundaries and sandboxing between system resources or services and agentic tools to limit undesired communication between agents.
mitigations.AML.M0038: Identify when objectives, tasks, capabilities, instructions, or other operational information received through shared artifacts cause an agent to pursue actions outside its authorized scope.
mitigations.AML.M0043: Remove shared artifacts and revoke associated access to limit communication and coordination across independent agent runs.

AML.T0118.001.name: Direct Agent Communication
AML.T0118.001.summary: Autonomous AI agents may communicate directly through agent-to-agent, sub-agent, or orchestrator interfaces. An agent may provide another agent with operational context, discoveries, objectives, tasking, capabilities, credentials, or constraints, and may receive status, findings, or completed work in response.
AML.T0118.001.description:
Autonomous AI agents may communicate directly through agent-to-agent, sub-agent, or orchestrator interfaces. An agent may provide another agent with operational context, discoveries, objectives, tasking, capabilities, credentials, or constraints, and may receive status, findings, or completed work in response.
Direct communication may include delegation when the sending agent formulates or selects an objective or subtask and the recipient retains meaningful discretion over how to perform it. Direct exchanges may also report discoveries, request independent validation, synchronize activity, transfer capabilities, or return findings without delegating a new task.

mitigations.AML.M0026: Assign distinct service identities and narrowly scoped permissions to agent-to-agent and orchestrator interfaces. Authorize which agents or services may send messages, submit tasks, or retrieve results to restrict unauthorized inter-agent communication and task initiation.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated access to agent-to-agent and orchestrator interfaces to the user's task, with recipient and operation restrictions where supported. Permission to contact another agent must not imply permission to exercise all of its capabilities.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Authenticate calling agents and authorize tool-mediated messages, task submissions, and result retrieval against permitted recipients, operations, and workflows. Enforce checks at the receiving interface so that permission to contact an agent does not grant unrestricted use of its capabilities.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Implement effective boundaries and sandboxing between system resources or services and agentic tools to limit undesired communication between agents.
mitigations.AML.M0038: Identify when objectives, tasks, capabilities, instructions, or delegated work received through direct agent-to-agent communication cause an agent's behavior to diverge from its authorized scope.

AML.T0119.name: Exploit Automated Artifact Processing Pipeline
AML.T0119.summary: Adversaries may submit, publish, or modify an artifact in a way that triggers an automated processing pipeline.
AML.T0119.description:
Adversaries may submit, publish, or modify an artifact in a way that triggers an automated processing pipeline. As the pipeline handles the artifact, adversary-controlled content or configuration may exploit a weakness in the processing logic, causing the processor to act outside its intended behavior using the permissions and access of a processing worker.
Exploitation may cause the worker to access local or internal resources and expose information through normal processing output or evaluate adversary-controlled content and execute code. The attack is triggered by automated backend processing and does not require a victim to open, load, or approve the artifact.

mitigations.AML.M0011: Restrict library loading to limit the introduction of untrusted outside code into an automated pipeline.
mitigations.AML.M0016: Identify and patch vulnerabilities in artifact processing pipelines that accept external inputs.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on adversary use of crafted artifacts to exploit automated processing pipelines. Use this intelligence to identify exposed processing workflows, prioritize remediation and compensating controls, and update detection and response procedures.

AML.T0120.name: AI Artifact Repository
AML.T0120.summary: Adversaries may repurpose AI artifact repositories as asynchronous command-and-control channels. Commands, payloads, or tasking may be placed in repository objects for a compromised system to retrieve or poll.
AML.T0120.description:
Adversaries may repurpose AI artifact repositories as asynchronous command-and-control channels. Commands, payloads, or tasking may be placed in repository objects for a compromised system to retrieve or poll. The compromised system may then write execution results, status, or collected information back to the repository for retrieval by the adversary.
This communication can use ordinary artifact and repository operations, such as reading or updating artifact content, metadata, or revisions through an API or version-control interface. The repository acts as a message queue or dead drop, allowing the parties to exchange information without a continuous direct connection and potentially blending the activity with legitimate artifact traffic.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Control access to AI assets at rest to prevent an adversary from repurposing these channels for command and control.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Monitor repository accesses and correlate them with known workflows. Investigate repeated polling, unexpected repositories, and writes from workloads that normally only download artifacts.

AML.T0121.name: AI Agent Environment Reconstruction
AML.T0121.summary: An autonomous AI agent may reconstruct the environment needed to continue an existing operation after its execution environment is lost, reset, replaced, denied, or made unusable.
AML.T0121.description: An autonomous AI agent may reconstruct the environment needed to continue an existing operation after its execution environment is lost, reset, replaced, denied, or made unusable. The agent may recover or recreate tools, dependencies, configuration, credentials or access paths, communication or coordination resources, working artifacts, and externally stored operational state in order to resume the same objective.

mitigations.AML.M0026: Limit service permissions to provision execution environments, recreate supporting resources, and retrieve stored operational state to approved workflows. Separate identities and resource permissions across unrelated workflows or agent runs to restrict unauthorized environment reconstruction.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated permissions to provision execution environments, recreate supporting resources, and retrieve stored operational state to those required for the user's task. Expire or revoke access when delegation ends to restrict unauthorized environment reconstruction.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Authorize tool requests to provision execution environments, recreate supporting resources, and retrieve stored operational state against task-permitted operations and resources. Preserve restrictions through downstream services to prevent broader tool privileges from enabling unauthorized environment reconstruction.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Isolate runtime identities, credentials, storage, coordination resources, and network access. Restrict connectivity to provisioning services and alternative execution environments, and prevent replacement runtimes from automatically inheriting a terminated operation's access or state to limit unauthorized environment reconstruction.
mitigations.AML.M0037: Limit the ability of agents to autonomously acquire new credentials to prevent them from reconstructing environments on external services.
mitigations.AML.M0043: Remove external operational state and revoke associated access to limit environment reconstruction and resumption of an operation.

AML.T0122.name: Exploitation of Remote Services
AML.T0122.summary: Adversaries may exploit a software or design weakness in a service reachable from their current environment to gain unauthorized access to another system, component, network, or trust boundary.
AML.T0122.description:
Adversaries may exploit a software or design weakness in a service reachable from their current environment to gain unauthorized access to another system, component, network, or trust boundary. Exploitation may allow the adversary to execute code, access protected resources, invoke unauthorized operations, obtain the service's privileges, or cause the service to make network requests or perform actions on the adversary's behalf.
In AI environments, remote services may include package caches, artifact and model registries, dataset services, evaluation infrastructure, inference gateways, experiment trackers, vector databases, notebooks, training pipelines, orchestration services, and cloud or cluster control-plane interfaces. These services may be reachable from otherwise isolated training, evaluation, or agent workloads and can provide transitive access to internal infrastructure or external networks.
Exploitation does not require compromise of the remote service's underlying host. For example, an adversary may exploit a server-side request vulnerability in a shared service to cross a network-containment boundary while leaving the service host itself uncompromised. Exploitation that produces host access, privilege escalation, credential disclosure, command execution, or another effect should be mapped separately to the applicable technique.

mitigations.AML.M0000: Limit the release of sensitive information about an AI stack to restrict the amount of information that an adversary can use to develop and perform exploits against services in the stack.
mitigations.AML.M0016: Vulnerability scanning can help identify insecure services in an AI stack.
mitigations.AML.M0039: Deploy isolated decoy services to observe exploit attempts against remote services. Use captured payloads and behavior to develop and validate detection signatures.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on adversary use of exploits, including zero-day vulnerabilities, against remote services. Use this intelligence to identify exposed services and reachable attack paths, prioritize remediation and compensating controls, and update detection and response procedures.

AML.T0123.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
AML.T0123.summary: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit. This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses.
AML.T0123.description:
Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit. This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses.
Obfuscation may target AI-enabled defensive systems, including malware classifiers, content filters, secret scanners, and automated review systems. Content that appears benign or incomplete to a person or detector may be decoded, assembled, or interpreted by a downstream application, tool, or compromised system.

AML.T0124.name: Autonomous Attack Orchestration
AML.T0124.summary: Adversaries may use autonomous AI systems as an operational control layer to manage multiple distinct autonomous agents or sub-agents toward a common adversary-defined objective.
AML.T0124.description:
Adversaries may use autonomous AI systems as an operational control layer to manage multiple distinct autonomous agents or sub-agents toward a common adversary-defined objective. The orchestrating system may create assignments, select executors, allocate tools or resources, establish dependencies, schedule or synchronize activities, and track progress without a human directing each assignment.
The autonomous system exhibits centralized control over distributed execution including which agent performs which work, when it performs it, and how its output affects other assigned work. The system may aggregate findings and status from participating agents, request independent validation, reconcile conflicting results, prevent or resolve duplicated effort, and determine when an output satisfies a prerequisite for another activity. It may reassign stalled work, increase or reduce resources allocated to a branch, terminate low-value work, or initiate additional research or testing.
Orchestration may use direct agent interfaces (See Autonomous AI Agent Communication: Direct Agent Communication) to transmit assignments, status, and results.
Human involvement does not preclude autonomous attack orchestration. A human operator may define campaign objectives, select targets, provide infrastructure, establish constraints, or retain approval over consequential transitions.
Autonomous Attack-Path Adaptation and Autonomous Attack Orchestration may occur together but describe different control functions. Attack-path adaptation captures how evidence changes the selected path. Attack orchestration captures how work is allocated, coordinated, validated, and redirected across agents.

mitigations.AML.M0028: Enforce caller-specific authorization on tools that create sub-agents, assign work, and allocate resources. Check each operation against permitted executors, workflows, and targets to prevent unauthorized delegation.
mitigations.AML.M0029: Requiring authorized human approval for sub-agent creation, work assignments, and resource allocation can prevent unauthorized delegation and expansion of an orchestrated workflow.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Isolate agent identities, messaging, state, and execution environments. Restrict cross-agent assignment and coordination to explicitly authorized communication paths.
mitigations.AML.M0036: Limit concurrent agents, parallel assignments, delegation depth, runtime, and aggregate resource consumption to constrain the scale and duration of orchestrated workflows.
mitigations.AML.M0037: Propagate the parent agent's authority constraints to sub-agents to prevent executors with a broader set of permitted interactions, or permitted actions, or authorities than the originating agent.
mitigations.AML.M0038: Identify changes in task hierarchy, assignments, resource allocation, or newly initiated activities that may indicate an orchestrating agent is drifting from its authorized objective.
mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on autonomously orchestrated campaigns, including infrastructure, task allocation, and coordination among agents. Use this intelligence to correlate distributed activity as part of a common operation, identify coordination dependencies, and coordinate containment across affected systems.

AML.T0125.name: Create Account
AML.T0125.summary: Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to an AI system or its supporting infrastructure. With a sufficient level of access, creating such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that do not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system.
AML.T0125.description:
Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to an AI system or its supporting infrastructure. With a sufficient level of access, creating such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that do not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system.
Accounts may be created on local systems, in enterprise domains, cloud tenants, identity providers, or individual services. In AI environments, adversaries may create user, service, workload, or automation accounts in AI platforms, model or dataset repositories, development environments, experiment trackers, orchestration services, data stores, and other AI operations infrastructure.

mitigations.AML.M0043: Disable or delete agent-created accounts when authorization ends to limit persistent access through those accounts.

AML.T0126.name: Automated Collection
AML.T0126.summary: Adversaries may use automated techniques to collect data from AI systems and supporting enterprise environments. Automation may use scripts, command interpreters, command-line tools, or AI agent tools to identify, retrieve, copy, or aggregate data without a human selecting each individual item.
AML.T0126.description:
Adversaries may use automated techniques to collect data from AI systems and supporting enterprise environments. Automation may use scripts, command interpreters, command-line tools, or AI agent tools to identify, retrieve, copy, or aggregate data without a human selecting each individual item.
Collection criteria may be fixed, such as file name, type, location, owner, date. Automation may also collect repeatedly, monitor for new material, traverse related resources, or combine data from local systems, cloud services, repositories, databases, object stores, and application APIs.
In AI environments, targeted material may include models, datasets, configurations, conversation histories, retrieval databases, deployment information, logs, and other operational data.

mitigations.AML.M0005: Restrict access to model repositories, training data, and other AI resources to prevent or limit collection.
mitigations.AML.M0039: Deploy decoy files or resources and detect when they are accessed to expose automated collection workflows.

AML.T0127.name: Data Staged
AML.T0127.summary: Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location before exfiltration. Staging consolidates, organizes, or prepares information obtained from one or more sources so it can be reviewed, processed, transferred, or retrieved more efficiently.
AML.T0127.description:
Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location before exfiltration. Staging consolidates, organizes, or prepares information obtained from one or more sources so it can be reviewed, processed, transferred, or retrieved more efficiently.
Data may be staged on a compromised local system, another system in the victim environment, a cloud instance, shared storage, an application repository, or other remote infrastructure. It may remain in separate files or be combined into archives, databases, structured documents, manifests, or other collections. Adversaries may compress, encrypt, encode, split, rename, or otherwise transform staged data.

mitigations.AML.M0043: Remove staged data and revoke access to managed staging locations to limit subsequent retrieval and exfiltration.

AML.T0128.name: Compromise Infrastructure
AML.T0128.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure and repurpose it to support attacks against AI systems. Rather than buying, leasing, registering, or otherwise legitimately acquiring a resource, the adversary gains unauthorized control of infrastructure owned or operated by another party.
AML.T0128.description:
Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure and repurpose it to support attacks against AI systems. Rather than buying, leasing, registering, or otherwise legitimately acquiring a resource, the adversary gains unauthorized control of infrastructure owned or operated by another party.
Compromised infrastructure may include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, third-party web and DNS services, software or artifact repositories, development workspaces, compute services, and other externally hosted resources.
In operations involving AI systems, adversaries may compromise infrastructure used for model development, artifact hosting, dataset processing, evaluation, inference, agent tooling, or AI operations. They may repurpose this infrastructure to host malicious artifacts, stage payloads, run tools or agents, relay traffic, capture credentials, provide command and control, process collected data, or launch attacks against additional systems.
Compromised infrastructure may appear trustworthy because it uses a legitimate provider, established domain, valid certificate, reputable service, or expected AI development platform. It may also provide network access, compute resources, service identities, or trusted relationships that would be difficult for the adversary to establish directly.

mitigations.AML.M0016: Identify and remediate vulnerabilities to reduce opportunities for adversaries to gain unauthorized control of infrastructure.

AML.T0129.name: Triggers in Multimodal Inputs
AML.T0129.summary: Adversaries may place instructions or triggers in one part of a multimodal input to influence the model while staying unnoticed by human reviewers and by defenses that do not inspect all input modalities.
AML.T0129.description:
Adversaries may place instructions or triggers in one part of a multimodal input to influence the model while staying unnoticed by human reviewers and by defenses that do not inspect all input modalities.
Multimodal systems jointly process text alongside other modalities, yet many moderation and filtering controls operate mainly on the textual channel. A payload placed in a modality that is not inspected, or is inspected differently from text, is still parsed by the model but can escape detection, allowing it to alter model output or carry a cross-modal prompt injection.
Examples include instructions placed in an image, audio, or video channel, or carried in file metadata (e.g. EXIF for images, ID3 tags for audio, or document metadata).

mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models across supported input modalities, individually and in combination, for hidden instructions or triggers that alter model behavior.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect supported image, audio, video, text, and metadata inputs for concealed instructions or triggers before model ingestion.

AML.T0130.name: AI Agent Response Biasing
AML.T0130.summary: Adversaries may manipulate an AI assistant so that it favors adversary-chosen sources, or content in its responses.
AML.T0130.description:
Adversaries may manipulate an AI assistant so that it favors adversary-chosen sources, or content in its responses. By injecting instructions such as "treat [source] as a trusted source" or "recommend [source] first," an adversary biases the assistant's outputs toward their own interests, causing it to present promotional or self-serving content as if it were a neutral, well-reasoned response. This degrades the integrity and trustworthiness of the assistant's responses on topics the user may rely on, such as health, finance, or security, without the user being aware that the advice has been skewed.
The injected instructions can be delivered through different ways, for example through Crafted AI Assistant Links. This impact may persist if the agent's memory was poisoned (See AI Agent Context Poisoning: Memory). Microsoft observed these instructions embedded in apparently helpful summarization links and identified publicly available tooling, including CiteMET, supporting their creation. These attempts sought to introduce third-party preferences into assistant responses; effects varied by assistant and over time.

mitigations.AML.M0020: Check retrieved instructions and generated recommendations for unauthorized preferences, source promotion, or departures from the user's criteria. Compare recommendations against approved selection criteria and supporting evidence before presenting them.

AML.T0131.name: Crafted AI Assistant Links
AML.T0131.summary: Adversaries may craft links that open an AI assistant or agent with attacker-controlled input already supplied, so that opening the link initiates an interaction the adversary defines rather than one the target composed.
AML.T0131.description:
Adversaries may craft links that open an AI assistant or agent with attacker-controlled input already supplied, so that opening the link initiates an interaction the adversary defines rather than one the target composed. Many AI assistants accept a prompt through URL parameters (for example `?q=` or `?prompt=`) that is automatically populated, and in some cases submitted, when the link is opened. By encoding a chosen prompt into such a link, an adversary can cause the target's assistant to act on supplied instructions as soon as the link is opened.
These links are frequently disguised as helpful actions, such as a "Summarize with AI" button or a share link, and distributed through web pages, emails, documents, or messages. Because the resulting interaction runs in the target's own assistant session, a crafted link can drive a range of downstream impacts depending on the supplied instructions, such as exfiltrating data the assistant can access or for AI Agent Response Biasing.
Microsoft identified CiteMET and AI Share URL Creator as tools supporting this pattern in its investigation of AI Recommendation Poisoning. The generated links supply instructions to the receiving assistant; execution, memory retention, and downstream effects depend on the assistant's behavior and protections.

AML.T0132.name: Misconfigured or Publicly Exposed AI Services
AML.T0132.summary: AI agents and LLM platforms are deployed across diverse architectures, including standalone servers, SaaS platforms, and low-code builders.
AML.T0132.description:
AI agents and LLM platforms are deployed across diverse architectures, including standalone servers, SaaS platforms, and low-code builders. All of these often have misconfigured access controls, ranging from missing authentication in LLM runtimes to permissive public access settings, that significantly expand their attack surface.
AI agent's security posture affects how attackers are able to explore which agentic attack surface is available to them and directly either expands or limits an adversary's ability to discover and interact with a target's AI agents. For example, one internet-facing AI service could be more easily discoverable by any unauthenticated user, while another may require compromised credentials to even be discovered.
Adversaries may discover and interact with AI agents and LLM services as unauthenticated users via a combination of various OSINT and active scanning methods. These could include using search engines to discover accessible agentic deployments (See Search Open Technical Databases), search backlinks which could indicate existing or open agents which have been embedded to frontends (See Search Open Websites/Domains), or directly scanning a target's AI infrastructure (See Active Scanning).

mitigations.AML.M0039: Honeypots can safely absorb real attacks and exploit attempts, turning payloads into mapped defensive signatures for a potential target without risking real assets.

AML.T0133.name: Discover AI Agent Runtime Capabilities
AML.T0133.summary: Adversaries may interact with an AI agent at runtime to reveal the capabilities available to it, without requiring access to its underlying configuration.
AML.T0133.description:
Adversaries may interact with an AI agent at runtime to reveal the capabilities available to it, without requiring access to its underlying configuration. Direct interaction with the agent can surface its registered tools and their accepted parameters, the actions it can take, the resources it can reach, and the identity and permission scope it acts under. Capabilities can also be inferred indirectly by issuing varied requests and observing which succeeded, failed, or refused.
AI agents are often interconnected with enterprise resources, tools and databases, or embedded within SaaS platforms and have permissions to act on behalf of users in order to facilitate functionality. Once adversaries identify a functional agent that they have access to, they could map the attack surface within that agent, by testing its functionality, enumerating tools, capabilities, knowledge, and embedded credentials and permissions.
This mapping process often reveals the AI agent's full toolset and configuration details and exposes additional exploitation, as enabled by AI Agent Tool Invocation. The resulting intelligence facilitates follow-on exploitation, including Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Exfiltration.

mitigations.AML.M0039: Interactive agentic decoys can present a plausible but fake toolset and capabilities. When an adversary enumerates the agent's capabilities at runtime, the honeypot can capture which tools and privileges they probe for and how they attempt to exploit it, while planted decoy credentials can also be used as canary tokens.

AML.T0134.name: AI Targeted Cloaking
AML.T0134.summary: Adversaries may selectively deliver malicious or manipulated content to AI systems, while presenting different benign content to human users, web crawlers, or security detection mechanisms.
AML.T0134.description:
Adversaries may selectively deliver malicious or manipulated content to AI systems, while presenting different benign content to human users, web crawlers, or security detection mechanisms. They may identify AI browsers or agents via user-agent strings and condition the server response so that AI-based clients receive prompt injections or misleading content.
Preventing human visitors, conventional web crawlers, and security tools from observing the same content allows adversaries to make malicious input more difficult to detect. AI Targeted Cloaking may be combined with Drive-by Compromise to deliver an LLM Prompt Injection.

AML.T0135.name: Outputs from AI Models
AML.T0135.summary: Adversaries may gather, retain, and organize outputs from an AI model or service as material for subsequent adversarial operations. Systematic selection and aggregation of responses can produce datasets or observations useful for analyzing the target, reproducing its behavior, or developing further attacks.
AML.T0135.description:
Adversaries may gather, retain, and organize outputs from an AI model or service as material for subsequent adversarial operations. Systematic selection and aggregation of responses can produce datasets or observations useful for analyzing the target, reproducing its behavior, or developing further attacks.
Collected material may include predictions and scores, embeddings or other exposed feature representations, generated content, reasoning traces, grades or preference judgments, and model-generated plans or tool calls. Outputs may be acquired directly from inference responses or indirectly from product-generated artifacts and records in which they are embedded or retained.
Discover AI Model Outputs may help adversaries identify available outputs and useful signals before collection. Adversaries may perform LLM Prompt Crafting to elicit the outputs they require for follow-on actions. The resulting material may support collection of Training Data Information from AI Models, Recover AI Model Internals, or Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs. Adversaries may also use Centralized AI Service Request Routing, Indicator Removal, and AI Service Request Metadata Sanitization to obscure coordinated collection activity.

mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected collection to reduce the information available for subsequent adversarial operations.

AML.T0136.name: Exfiltration via AI User Interface
AML.T0136.summary: Adversaries exfiltrate information through an AI system's user-facing outputs. Information may be disclosed in conversational responses, generated documents, previews, or other content presented through the application.
AML.T0136.description:
Adversaries exfiltrate information through an AI system's user-facing outputs. Information may be disclosed in conversational responses, generated documents, previews, or other content presented through the application. The application may expose information available to a victim-controlled AI service or deliver information gathered from other victim systems.
Adversaries may direct an AI system to present sensitive information in responses or as downloadable artifacts. The application's user interface serves as the transfer channel through which adversaries receive the information.
Transferred information may include Data from AI Services or Outputs from AI Models.

AML.T0137.name: Training Data Information from AI Models
AML.T0137.summary: Adversaries may obtain sensitive information about the data used to train or fine-tune an AI model by analyzing its outputs or behavior. This can expose private associations, personally identifiable information, or proprietary data, creating data privacy concerns and supporting subsequent adversarial operations.
AML.T0137.description:
Adversaries may obtain sensitive information about the data used to train or fine-tune an AI model by analyzing its outputs or behavior. This can expose private associations, personally identifiable information, or proprietary data, creating data privacy concerns and supporting subsequent adversarial operations.
Adversaries may determine whether particular samples were used in training through Infer Membership, identify aggregate characteristics of the training dataset through Infer Properties, infer sensitive attributes or reconstruct representative examples through Invert AI Model, or recover retained training content through Extract Memorized Data.

mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected adversarial activity to limit signals used to infer information about private data used in model training.
mitigations.AML.M0041: Use privacy-preserving mechanisms to limit how much individual training data influences model behavior and outputs, reducing disclosure of sensitive information about the data used to train or fine-tune the model.

AML.T0137.000.name: Infer Membership
AML.T0137.000.summary: Adversaries may infer whether a particular data sample was included in an AI model's training dataset. Samples may include records, text passages, images, or audio samples. Establishing membership may reveal sensitive associations, participation in a private dataset, or use of proprietary information.
AML.T0137.000.description:
Adversaries may infer whether a particular data sample was included in an AI model's training dataset. Samples may include records, text passages, images, or audio samples. Establishing membership may reveal sensitive associations, participation in a private dataset, or use of proprietary information.
Membership inference is a data privacy concern because identifying a sample's inclusion may reveal sensitive associations or participation in a private dataset, even without recovering the underlying data.
Methods may analyze prediction scores, token probabilities, loss values, generated responses, or other differences in model behavior. Adversaries may use statistical tests, shadow models, or auxiliary datasets to distinguish likely training members from nonmembers.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Suggested approaches: - Restrict the number of results shown - Limit specificity of output class ontology - Use randomized smoothing techniques - Reduce the precision of numerical outputs
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit the volume of API queries in a given period of time to regulate the amount and fidelity of potentially sensitive information an attacker can learn.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models for training-data membership disclosure using controlled member and nonmember samples. Use measured privacy risk to guide model selection, training changes, or output restrictions.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if sensitive data has been exfiltrated.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Test whether model outputs reveal the membership of known training samples. Improve privacy-preserving training, output restriction, access controls, and query monitoring.
mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected adversarial activity to limit signals used to determine whether particular samples were included in training.
mitigations.AML.M0041: Use privacy-preserving mechanisms to limit how much an individual sample's inclusion in training influences model behavior and outputs, reducing the ability to infer whether that sample was used.

AML.T0137.001.name: Infer Properties
AML.T0137.001.summary: Adversaries may infer sensitive global properties of the data used to train an AI model. Properties may include dataset provenance, population composition, relative class proportions, domain coverage, collection period, or the presence of a category or group.
AML.T0137.001.description:
Adversaries may infer sensitive global properties of the data used to train an AI model. Properties may include dataset provenance, population composition, relative class proportions, domain coverage, collection period, or the presence of a category or group.
The adversary may compare output distributions, fit analytical or learned estimators, use auxiliary datasets, or contrast models trained with different known properties. The target is a property of the training data rather than membership of an individual record.
Inferred properties of the training dataset may help adversaries identify a model's likely origin, distinguish between candidate models, identify underrepresented populations or domains, and tailor subsequent attacks to suspected weaknesses.

mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected adversarial activity to limit signals used to infer sensitive characteristics of the training dataset.
mitigations.AML.M0041: Use privacy-preserving mechanisms to limit information about training data reflected in model behavior and outputs, reducing the ability to infer its aggregate properties.

AML.T0137.002.name: Invert AI Model
AML.T0137.002.summary: Adversaries may infer sensitive aggregate attributes or reconstruct representative examples of data used to train or fine-tune a target AI model by analyzing its behavior, outputs, or exposed representations.
AML.T0137.002.description:
Adversaries may infer sensitive aggregate attributes or reconstruct representative examples of data used to train or fine-tune a target AI model by analyzing its behavior, outputs, or exposed representations. Reconstructed information may reveal characteristics of individuals, records, or classes represented in the training data without reproducing a particular training example.
Methods may optimize candidate inputs, combine known attributes with model-derived signals, or use learned inversion models. Useful observations may include prediction scores, probabilities, embeddings, or gradients where exposed.
Results may include inferred sensitive attributes, approximate reconstructions, or representative examples associated with a target identity or class. Such results do not by themselves establish that a reconstructed example was present in the training dataset.

mitigations.AML.M0002: Suggested approaches: - Restrict the number of results shown - Limit specificity of output class ontology - Use randomized smoothing techniques - Reduce the precision of numerical outputs
mitigations.AML.M0004: Limit the volume of API queries in a given period of time to regulate the amount and fidelity of potentially sensitive information an attacker can learn.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models for reconstruction of sensitive attributes or representative training-data examples from outputs or representations exposed in deployment. Use demonstrated privacy risks to guide remediation or output restrictions.
mitigations.AML.M0024: Telemetry logging can help identify if sensitive data has been exfiltrated.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Attempt to reconstruct sensitive records, attributes, or representative training information from model outputs. Remediate leakage through model changes, output minimization, privacy controls, and restricted inference access.
mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected adversarial activity to limit information used to reconstruct representative training examples.
mitigations.AML.M0041: Use privacy-preserving mechanisms to limit information about training data reflected in model behavior and outputs, reducing the ability to infer sensitive attributes or reconstruct representative examples.

AML.T0137.003.name: Extract Memorized Data
AML.T0137.003.summary: Adversaries may elicit and recover sensitive content memorized by a generative AI model during training or fine-tuning.
AML.T0137.003.description:
Adversaries may elicit and recover sensitive content memorized by a generative AI model during training or fine-tuning. Recovered material may include complete training examples or recognizable portions of text, source code, or images, potentially exposing personal information, private communications, or proprietary material. Recovery may take the form of verbatim reproduction or near-duplicate outputs that reveal specific training content.
Adversaries may supply partial passages, contextual cues, or repeated and varied inputs that encourage reproduction of memorized content. They may generate and filter candidate outputs or compare them with available reference material to identify likely training examples. Researchers have recovered verbatim training passages through language-model queries, including from production systems, and extracted memorized training images from diffusion models.

mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate generative models for reproduction of sensitive training data using controlled extraction attempts and comparisons with known samples. Investigate confirmed disclosures and repeat evaluation after remediation.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Inspect generated outputs for sensitive training content or recognizable portions of protected records before release. Use sensitive-data detection and protected reference matching where available. Block or redact detected disclosures.
mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected adversarial activity to reduce disclosure of memorized training content.
mitigations.AML.M0041: Use privacy-preserving mechanisms to limit model memorization of individual training records and their influence on outputs, reducing the ability to elicit training content.

AML.T0138.name: Indicator Removal
AML.T0138.summary: Adversaries may delete, alter, or falsify records and artifacts to conceal their activity, impede investigation, or make unauthorized actions appear legitimate. Targeted artifacts may include logs, command histories, files, metadata, repository history, and published content.
AML.T0138.description:
Adversaries may delete, alter, or falsify records and artifacts to conceal their activity, impede investigation, or make unauthorized actions appear legitimate. Targeted artifacts may include logs, command histories, files, metadata, repository history, and published content. Changes may selectively remove suspicious evidence while preserving surrounding material to maintain the appearance of normal activity.
Agents may also conceal activity by modifying artifacts on external collaboration and distribution platforms. Editing public messages, removing malicious content, or rewriting revision history can obscure prior actions, make contributions appear benign, and complicate reconstruction of an attack. These changes may help an agent preserve credibility and continue operating after its activity attracts scrutiny, even when earlier versions remain recoverable.
Autonomous AI agents may identify and manipulate evidence of their own actions without a human directing each concealment step. Agents may edit or delete accessible transcripts, replace records with misleading content, or tamper with harness components responsible for executing or recording tool calls. Such tampering can cause recorded actions or results to differ from actual execution, undermining oversight that relies on the affected records.

AML.T0139.name: Compromise Accounts
