AML.T0139.summary: Adversaries may compromise existing accounts with services that can support targeting or subsequent operations. These accounts may provide established identities, trusted relationships, access to resources, or funded wallets for AI services.
AML.T0139.description:
Adversaries may compromise existing accounts with services that can support targeting or subsequent operations. These accounts may provide established identities, trusted relationships, access to resources, or funded wallets for AI services.
Adversaries may obtain account credentials through Phishing, password guessing or reuse, theft of access tokens, or purchase from third parties.
Adversaries may compromise AI service accounts for LLMJacking, a pattern of consuming model access and usage at the account holder's expense. Depending on the service, these resources may include prepaid balances or service wallets, promotional credits, subscription allowances, or usage charged to an existing payment method or enterprise billing account. Adversaries may use the acquired capacity for their own inference workloads, code generation, or tool development while exhausting the victim's available credits and quotas or generating additional charges.
Compromised accounts may also supply capacity for AI Service Proxies, allowing operators to aggregate and resell access while concealing the underlying credentials from downstream users. Google has reported model distillation campaigns that used proxy infrastructure to rotate requests across compromised credentials and fraudulent accounts. Account pooling and resale also feature in the gray-market transfer station economy, where account merchants and registration intermediaries supply access alongside discounted capacity, unused quotas, and shared subscriptions..

AML.T0140.name: Centralized AI Service Request Routing
AML.T0140.summary: Adversaries may distribute coordinated AI service requests across multiple pathways to impede detection, conceal the coordinated nature of the requests, and evade AI provider enforcement.
AML.T0140.description:
Adversaries may distribute coordinated AI service requests across multiple pathways to impede detection, conceal the coordinated nature of the requests, and evade AI provider enforcement. Distributing activity can limit the portion of an operation visible through any individual account or pathway, obscuring its aggregate scale and common objective.
Adversaries may use centralized routing infrastructure to divide a workload or prompt suite across multiple pathways, including various service APIs, cloud-hosted endpoints, third-party aggregators or relays, and account pools. Routers may rotate identities and request pathways, mix adversarial requests with unrelated customer traffic, and automatically redirect requests when requests are blocked. These capabilities allow adversaries to maintain coordinated operations while making the activity appear to originate from unrelated users or services.
Adversaries may also use routing infrastructure to centrally optimize API costs and sustain distributed operations within available quotas and budgets. This may include prioritizing cost-efficient access pathways, allocating quotas across accounts to align with operational budgets, segmenting accounts by purpose, and organizing requests to maximize cache reuse. Centralized routing may coordinate shifts across accounts, providers, or pathways in response to pricing or rate-limit changes, enabling an operation to adapt while continuing to obscure its common control and aggregate activity.
This behavior may be implemented via proxy services (See Acquire Infrastructure: AI Service Proxies), multiple cloud instances, IP pools, coordination across multiple accounts, or other distributed infrastructure.

mitigations.AML.M0042: Collect, analyze, and share intelligence on coordinated AI service requests distributed across accounts, providers, and intermediary services. Use this intelligence to correlate activity across access pathways, identify shared routing infrastructure, and coordinate detection and response to campaigns whose scale and common control may be obscured within individual accounts or services.

AML.T0141.name: AI Service Request Metadata Sanitization
AML.T0141.summary: Adversaries may remove or replace identifying information in request metadata before submitting requests to an AI service to impede attribution and correlation of coordinated activity. Sanitization may be enforced automatically in clients, relays, aggregators, or centralized routing infrastructure.
AML.T0141.description:
Adversaries may remove or replace identifying information in request metadata before submitting requests to an AI service to impede attribution and correlation of coordinated activity. Sanitization may be enforced automatically in clients, relays, aggregators, or centralized routing infrastructure.
Metadata may include client or device identifiers, session identifiers, account identifiers, client software identifiers, forwarding headers, and attribution markers embedded in request bodies. Metadata fields may be sanitized via removal, or replacement with normalized, randomized, or generated values.
The NSA, CISA, and FBI reported removal of organizational identifiers in industrial-scale distillation campaigns, with indicators including the disappearance of previously consistent metadata and generic or randomized patterns replacing organizational markers.

AML.T0142.name: Event Triggered Execution
AML.T0142.summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by creating or modifying event handlers, startup hooks, or associated configuration so that subsequent system or application activity automatically executes adversary-controlled code or commands.
AML.T0142.description:
Adversaries may establish persistence by creating or modifying event handlers, startup hooks, or associated configuration so that subsequent system or application activity automatically executes adversary-controlled code or commands. Triggers may include interpreter initialization, application execution, or other events processed by the affected mechanism. These modifications can allow malicious behavior to recur without another direct execution request from the adversary.
In AI environments, adversaries may target hooks in the software and execution environments used for data processing, model training, evaluation, inference, or agent tool execution. For example, Python startup hooks may execute adversary-controlled code when a subsequent workflow or tool invocation starts an interpreter that processes the hook.
Triggered code may perform malicious actions directly or emit content that is subsequently consumed by an AI system. Such content may contain fabricated approvals or instructions intended to manipulate the system's later behavior or make normally unobservable information available. AI Agents may also place triggers or trip-wires behind to observe, act on, or report conditions that the agent can no longer reach or are beyond its execution window.

mitigations.AML.M0011: Restrict automatic loading to trusted locations and disable unnecessary interpreter startup hooks.
mitigations.AML.M0013: Enforce that all software packages be signed before execution.

AML.T0143.name: LLM Prompt Propagation
AML.T0143.summary: Adversaries may cause malicious instructions already introduced into an AI-enabled environment to be transferred onward to additional storage locations, agents, applications, or resources where they can influence subsequent AI activity.
AML.T0143.description:
Adversaries may cause malicious instructions already introduced into an AI-enabled environment to be transferred onward to additional storage locations, agents, applications, or resources where they can influence subsequent AI activity. This extends the attack beyond its initial point of introduction and may allow adversaries to influence additional targets without directly delivering a malicious prompt payload to each one.
Propagation may occur through email or other communications, shared documents, source-code repositories, persistent agent memory, retrieval systems, databases, shared workspaces, or direct agent-to-agent communication. Connected tools and services may also carry malicious instructions between otherwise separate environments. The transfer may result from an induced agent action or from copying, forwarding, synchronization, or other workflows that distribute affected content.

mitigations.AML.M0026: Limit messaging, publishing, and shared-resource write permissions to approved workflows and destinations. Separate distribution capabilities from unrelated service access to restrict where an adversary can propagate malicious instructions through the agent.
mitigations.AML.M0027: Limit delegated messaging, publishing, and shared-resource write permissions to destinations and resources required for the user's task. Withhold unnecessary distribution capabilities to restrict propagation of malicious instructions through the agent.
mitigations.AML.M0028: Authorize messaging, publishing, repository writes, shared-storage updates, and agent communication against task-permitted resources and destinations. Preserve restrictions through downstream services to prevent shared tool privileges from enabling propagation of malicious instructions beyond the caller's authorized scope.
mitigations.AML.M0030: Restrict tool actions that send messages, publish content, modify shared resources, or communicate with other agents when untrusted content has entered the agent's context. Apply these restrictions to delayed actions and derived content that retain the influence of the untrusted instructions.
mitigations.AML.M0032: Isolate agent identities, storage, memory, messaging, and tool access, and mediate exchanges between agents and connected resources. Restrict cross-agent, cross-user, and cross-environment communication paths to limit where malicious instructions can be transferred after an initial compromise.
mitigations.AML.M0033: Validate content before it is forwarded, published, synchronized, or written to resources used by other AI components. Inspect messages, shared documents, agent instructions, rules files, and templates for embedded malicious instructions, including hidden or encoded content. Perform validation outside the agent and at receiving boundaries before accepting transferred content.

AML.T0144.name: Recover AI Model Internals
AML.T0144.summary: Adversaries may infer or recover non-public AI model internals through analysis of model behavior or exposed information. Targets may include architecture, layer dimensions, hyperparameters, decision-tree structure, projection matrices, or numerical parameters.
AML.T0144.description:
Adversaries may infer or recover non-public AI model internals through analysis of model behavior or exposed information. Targets may include architecture, layer dimensions, hyperparameters, decision-tree structure, projection matrices, or numerical parameters.
Methods may use strategically selected queries, equation solving, numerical reconstruction, or statistical identification. Recovery may be partial, approximate, or exact.

mitigations.AML.M0040: Degrade responses during suspected adversarial activity to limit observations used to infer model architecture, internal structure, or numerical parameters.

AML.T0145.name: Poison AI Agent Learning Environment
AML.T0145.summary: Adversaries may manipulate an environment in which an AI agent interacts so that observations, feedback, rewards, actions, or resulting interactions are incorporated into model training to cause persistent changes to the behavior of an AI system.
AML.T0145.description:
Adversaries may manipulate an environment in which an AI agent interacts so that observations, feedback, rewards, actions, or resulting interactions are incorporated into model training to cause persistent changes to the behavior of an AI system. This allows adversary's influence to persist beyond the original interaction and affect subsequent tasks.
An adversary may alter webpages, tool or API responses, elements in simulated environments, task descriptions, reward signals, evaluator outputs, or other environmental content used during AI agent learning or adaptation. The manipulated interactions may be incorporated into model fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, synthetic training corpora, agent memories, other persistent components.
Poison AI Agent Learning Environment targets the process that generates or selects learning experience, without requiring direct adversarial access to training datasets, model parameters, or stored agent artifacts. The resulting experience may appear legitimate because it was produced by an authorized agent operating through an expected interface. Once introduced, the adversary's influence may remain effective even after the manipulated environmental content is removed or is no longer encountered.
An adversary may use this technique to introduce backdoors, increase compliance with malicious instructions, distort policies or preferences, teach unsafe tool use, manipulate reward-seeking behavior. The malicious behavior may be activated later by an environmental trigger or during ordinary agent operation.

mitigations.AML.M0007: Screen environmental content and resulting interaction data for poisoning before use in learning or adaptation. Quarantine and remediate affected data before use.
mitigations.AML.M0008: Evaluate models after learning or adaptation using clean evaluation data and targeted tests for backdoors, unsafe tool use, and unexpected behavior. Compare results against trusted baselines and investigate unexplained deviations before deployment.
mitigations.AML.M0020: Independently check generated outputs and proposed actions against applicable policies at runtime. Block prohibited outputs and actions to limit the impact of learning from a poisoned environment.
mitigations.AML.M0022: Train or fine-tune models to follow intended policies and resist malicious instructions and unsafe tool use. Re-evaluate alignment after learning or adaptation to identify deviations caused by environment poisoning.
mitigations.AML.M0025: Record the sources of environmental content and resulting interaction data used in learning or adaptation to trace suspicious learning experiences to their sources.
mitigations.AML.M0035: Introduce controlled manipulations into the agent's learning environment to test for persistent behavior changes. Verify poisoning detection and rejection controls, and remediate identified weaknesses.

AML.M0000.name: Limit Public Release of Information
AML.M0000.summary: Limit the public release of technical information about the AI stack used in an organization's products or services. Technical knowledge of how AI is used can be leveraged by adversaries to perform targeting and tailor attacks to the target system.

AML.M0001.name: Limit Model Artifact Release
AML.M0001.summary: Limit public release of technical project details including data, algorithms, model architectures, and model checkpoints that are used in production, or that are representative of those used in production.

AML.M0002.name: Predictive AI Output Obfuscation
AML.M0002.summary: Reduce the fidelity and amount of information returned by predictive AI inference endpoints to make model discovery, extraction, replication, and black-box adversarial-example optimization more difficult.

AML.M0003.name: Predictive AI Model Hardening
AML.M0003.summary: Design and train predictive AI models to maintain intended performance when presented with adversarial examples. Adversarial examples may include digitally perturbed inputs or physical countermeasures intended to cause misclassification, missed detection, or another attacker-selected prediction.

AML.M0004.name: Limit AI Service Query Volume and Rate
AML.M0004.summary: Limit the number and rate of requests that users can submit to an AI service. Apply limits by user, API key, tenant, device, or other authenticated identity. Use short-term rate, burst, and concurrency limits together with longer-term usage quotas.

AML.M0005.name: Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest
AML.M0005.summary: Establish access controls on internal model registries and limit internal access to production models. Limit access to training data only to approved users.

AML.M0006.name: Predictive AI Ensembles
AML.M0006.summary: Use an ensemble of diverse predictive AI models to reduce reliance on a single model or model family and improve robustness against adversarial examples.

AML.M0007.name: Sanitize Training Data
AML.M0007.summary: Detect, quarantine, and remove or remediate poisoned data before it is used to train an AI model. Apply screening when datasets are acquired or updated, and before new data is incorporated into active learning workflows.

AML.M0008.name: Validate AI Model
AML.M0008.summary: Evaluate AI models against defined functional requirements before deployment and throughout their operational lifecycle. Validate newly trained or acquired models and repeat evaluation after fine-tuning, model updates, or changes to the conditions in which the model is used.

AML.M0009.name: Predictive AI Multi-Sensor Fusion
AML.M0009.summary: Use independent physical sensors (ideally across multiple modalities or from several perspectives) to avoid relying on a single sensor that may be manipulated, obstructed, or disrupted by an adversary.

AML.M0010.name: Predictive AI Input Restoration
AML.M0010.summary: Preprocess predictive AI inference inputs to remove, reduce, or disrupt adversarial perturbations before the inputs are evaluated by the model.

AML.M0011.name: Restrict Library Loading
AML.M0011.summary: Prevent abuse of library loading mechanisms in the operating system and software to load untrusted code by configuring appropriate library loading mechanisms and investigating potential vulnerable software.

AML.M0012.name: Encrypt Sensitive Information
AML.M0012.summary: Encrypt sensitive data such as AI models to protect against adversaries attempting to access sensitive data.

AML.M0013.name: Code Signing
AML.M0013.summary: Enforce binary and application integrity with digital signature verification to prevent untrusted code from executing. Adversaries can embed malicious code in AI software or models. Developers should also cryptographically sign SBOM and AIBOM components that track model or data provenance.

AML.M0014.name: Verify AI Artifacts
AML.M0014.summary: Verify the integrity and authenticity of AI artifacts before importing, loading, or deploying them. Artifacts may include model weights and checkpoints, datasets, tokenizers, model configurations, prompt templates, and agent configuration files.

AML.M0015.name: Predictive AI Adversarial Input Detection
AML.M0015.summary: Detect and block digital or physical adversarial examples submitted to predictive AI models. Adversarial examples are inputs modified or constructed to cause misclassification, missed detection, excessive computation, or another attacker-selected behavior.

AML.M0016.name: Vulnerability Scanning
AML.M0016.summary: Vulnerability scanning is used to find potentially exploitable software vulnerabilities to remediate them.

AML.M0017.name: AI Model Distribution Methods
AML.M0017.summary: Deploying AI models to edge devices can increase the attack surface of the system. Consider serving models in the cloud to reduce the level of access the adversary has to the model.

AML.M0018.name: User Training
AML.M0018.summary: Educate AI model developers to on AI supply chain risks and potentially malicious AI artifacts. Educate users on how to identify deepfakes and phishing attempts.

AML.M0019.name: Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production
AML.M0019.summary: Require users to verify their identities before accessing a production model. Require authentication for API endpoints and monitor production model queries to ensure compliance with usage policies and to prevent model misuse.

AML.M0020.name: Generative AI Guardrails
AML.M0020.summary: Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user.

AML.M0021.name: Generative AI Guidelines
AML.M0021.summary: Guidelines are instructions, policies, and behavioral constraints provided to a generative AI model to direct it toward desired outputs and away from unsafe, unreliable, or policy-violating behavior.

AML.M0022.name: Generative AI Model Alignment
AML.M0022.summary: Generative AI Model Alignment is the process of training or fine-tuning a generative model to guide its output toward a set of human values, goals, or ethical principles.

AML.M0023.name: Maintain an AI Bill of Materials
AML.M0023.summary: Create and maintain an AI Bill of Materials (AI BOM) that identifies the components and dependencies used to build, evaluate, and operate an AI-enabled system.

AML.M0024.name: AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring
AML.M0024.summary: Implement logging and monitoring across the AI lifecycle to detect suspicious activity and support investigation. Capture security-relevant access, changes, and operations across data pipelines, model development, deployment, and connected systems.

AML.M0025.name: Maintain AI Dataset Provenance
AML.M0025.summary: Maintain a detailed history of datasets used for AI applications. The history should include information about the dataset's source as well as a complete record of any modifications.

AML.M0026.name: Manage AI Agent Service Access
AML.M0026.summary: Limit service AI agents--agents using independently assigned service or workload permissions--to explicitly authorized workflows. Agents may serve multiple users or act on requests, events, or schedules.

AML.M0027.name: Manage User-Delegated AI Agent Access
AML.M0027.summary: Limit user-delegated AI agents to explicitly authorized tasks and permissions. Apply the principle of least privilege so that the agent receives only the access required for its designated tasks.

AML.M0028.name: Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools
AML.M0028.summary: Limit AI agent tool access to each caller's authorized, task-required operations and resources, including when tools are shared across agents, users, or tenants. Broader tool or backend privileges must not expand caller access.

AML.M0029.name: Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions
AML.M0029.summary: Systems should require the user or another human stakeholder to approve AI agent actions before the agent takes them. The human approver may be technical staff or business unit SMEs depending on the use case.

AML.M0030.name: Restrict AI Agent Tool Invocation on Untrusted Data
AML.M0030.summary: Untrusted data can contain prompt injections that invoke an AI agent's tools, potentially causing confidentiality, integrity or availability violations. It is recommended that tool invocation be restricted or limited when untrusted data enters the LLM's context.

AML.M0031.name: Memory Hardening
AML.M0031.summary: Memory Hardening protects persistent state used by AI agents, including saved preferences, episodic or semantic memories, conversation summaries, stored chat history, and agent-managed experience stores.

AML.M0032.name: Segmentation of AI Agent Components
AML.M0032.summary: Define enforceable security boundaries around AI agent tools, data sources, identities, and execution environments. Mediate access through authenticated APIs, isolate code execution via containers or virtual machines, restrict filesystem and network access, and limit tool invocation rates.

AML.M0033.name: Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components
AML.M0033.summary: Implement validation on inputs and outputs for the tools and data sources used by AI agents. Validation includes enforcing a common data format, schema validation, checks for sensitive or prohibited information leakage, and data sanitization to remove potential injections or unsafe code.

AML.M0034.name: Deepfake Detection
AML.M0034.summary: Apply deepfake detection algorithms against any untrusted or user-provided data, especially in impactful applications such as biometric verification, to block generated content.

AML.M0035.name: AI Red Team
AML.M0035.summary: Establish an AI red team responsible for conducting recurring, authorized, and threat-informed red-teaming exercises to identify and remediate vulnerabilities in AI-enabled systems before deployment and throughout operation.

AML.M0036.name: Limit AI Workload Resource Consumption
AML.M0036.summary: Limit the resources that an AI request, inference job, or agent workflow can consume. Set bounds on input size, batch size, execution time, memory, compute, and output size. Generative AI services should also limit context and output tokens.

AML.M0037.name: AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls
AML.M0037.summary: Limit an AI agent's ability to autonomously acquire additional authorities that expand its effective permissions during execution. The maximum authority available to the agent should be explicitly granted prior to runtime.

AML.M0038.name: AI Agent Scope Drift Detection
AML.M0038.summary: Continuously evaluate whether an AI Agent's planned actions remain consistent with its current authorized objective throughout execution. As autonomous agents interact within a dynamic environment, they may discover or generate intermediate objectives or adapt their strategy based on environment feedback.

AML.M0039.name: AI Honeypots
AML.M0039.summary: Deploy monitored decoy AI services, agents, credentials, or other resources that resemble legitimate, active assets in the external or internal environment, but serve no real business or operational functions.

AML.M0040.name: Adaptive AI Response Degradation
AML.M0040.summary: Reduce the utility of AI model outputs for unauthorized model replication, knowledge distillation, or inference about training data by dynamically modifying responses when suspected extraction activity or privacy attacks are detected.

AML.M0041.name: Privacy-Preserving AI Training and Inference
AML.M0041.summary: Use privacy-preserving mechanisms throughout model training and inference to limit disclosure of sensitive training or inference data.

AML.M0042.name: Threat Intelligence Program
AML.M0042.summary: A Threat Intelligence Program enables organizations to proactively collect, analyze, and share information on threats to AI and cyber systems by leveraging internal observations and external reporting.

AML.M0043.name: AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management
AML.M0043.summary: Organizations should control external resources created or acquired by AI agents during execution by treating those resources as attributable, lifecycle-managed assets.

AML.CS0000.name: Evasion of Deep Learning Detector for Malware C&C Traffic
AML.CS0000.summary: The Palo Alto Networks Security AI research team tested a deep learning model for malware command and control (C&C) traffic detection in HTTP traffic. Based on the publicly available paper by Le et al., we built a model that was trained on a similar dataset as our production model and had similar performance.

AML.CS0001.name: Botnet Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) Detection Evasion
AML.CS0001.summary: The Palo Alto Networks Security AI research team was able to bypass a Convolutional Neural Network based botnet Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) detector using a generic domain name mutation technique. It is a generic domain mutation technique which can evade most ML-based DGA detection modules.

AML.CS0002.name: VirusTotal Poisoning
AML.CS0002.summary: McAfee Advanced Threat Research noticed an increase in reports of a certain ransomware family that was out of the ordinary. Case investigation revealed that many samples of that particular ransomware family were submitted through a popular virus-sharing platform within a short amount of time.

AML.CS0003.name: Bypassing Cylance's AI Malware Detection
AML.CS0003.summary: Researchers at Skylight were able to create a universal bypass string that evades detection by Cylance's AI Malware detector when appended to a malicious file.

AML.CS0004.name: Camera Hijack Attack on Facial Recognition System
AML.CS0004.summary: This type of camera hijack attack can evade the traditional live facial recognition authentication model and enable access to privileged systems and victim impersonation.

AML.CS0005.name: Attack on Machine Translation Services
AML.CS0005.summary: Machine translation services (such as Google Translate, Bing Translator, and Systran Translate) provide public-facing UIs and APIs. A research group at UC Berkeley utilized these public endpoints to create a replicated model with near-production state-of-the-art translation quality.

AML.CS0006.name: ClearviewAI Misconfiguration
AML.CS0006.summary: Clearview AI makes a facial recognition tool that searches publicly available photos for matches. This tool has been used for investigative purposes by law enforcement agencies and other parties.

AML.CS0007.name: GPT-2 Model Replication
AML.CS0007.summary: OpenAI built GPT-2, a language model capable of generating high quality text samples. Over concerns that GPT-2 could be used for malicious purposes such as impersonating others, or generating misleading news articles, fake social media content, or spam, OpenAI adopted a tiered release schedule.

AML.CS0008.name: ProofPoint Evasion
AML.CS0008.summary: Proof Pudding (CVE-2019-20634) is a code repository that describes how ML researchers evaded ProofPoint's email protection system by first building a copy-cat email protection ML model, and using the insights to bypass the live system.

AML.CS0009.name: Tay Poisoning
AML.CS0009.summary: Microsoft created Tay, a Twitter chatbot designed to engage and entertain users. While previous chatbots used pre-programmed scripts to respond to prompts, Tay's machine learning capabilities allowed it to be directly influenced by its conversations.

AML.CS0010.name: Microsoft Azure Service Disruption
AML.CS0010.summary: The Microsoft AI Red Team performed a red team exercise on an internal Azure service with the intention of disrupting its service.

AML.CS0011.name: Microsoft Edge AI Evasion
AML.CS0011.summary: The Azure Red Team performed a red team exercise on a new Microsoft product designed for running AI workloads at the edge. This exercise was meant to use an automated system to continuously manipulate a target image to cause the ML model to produce misclassifications.

AML.CS0012.name: Face Identification System Evasion via Physical Countermeasures
AML.CS0012.summary: MITRE's AI Red Team demonstrated a physical-domain evasion attack on a commercial face identification service with the intention of inducing a targeted misclassification.

AML.CS0013.name: Backdoor Attack on Deep Learning Models in Mobile Apps
AML.CS0013.summary: Deep learning models are increasingly used in mobile applications as critical components.

AML.CS0014.name: Confusing Antimalware Neural Networks
AML.CS0014.summary: Cloud storage and computations have become popular platforms for deploying ML malware detectors. In such cases, the features for models are built on users' systems and then sent to cybersecurity company servers.

AML.CS0015.name: Compromised PyTorch Dependency Chain
AML.CS0015.summary: Linux packages for PyTorch's pre-release version, called Pytorch-nightly, were compromised from December 25 to 30, 2022 by a malicious binary uploaded to the Python Package Index (PyPI) code repository.

AML.CS0016.name: Achieving Code Execution in MathGPT via Prompt Injection
AML.CS0016.summary: The publicly available Streamlit application MathGPT uses GPT-3, a large language model (LLM), to answer user-generated math questions.

AML.CS0017.name: Bypassing ID.me Identity Verification
AML.CS0017.summary: An individual filed at least 180 false unemployment claims in the state of California from October 2020 to December 2021 by bypassing ID.me's automated identity verification system. Dozens of fraudulent claims were approved and the individual received at least $3.4 million in payments.

AML.CS0018.name: Arbitrary Code Execution with Google Colab
AML.CS0018.summary: Google Colab is a Jupyter Notebook service that executes on virtual machines. Jupyter Notebooks are often used for ML and data science research and experimentation, containing executable snippets of Python code and common Unix command-line functionality.

AML.CS0019.name: PoisonGPT
AML.CS0019.summary: Researchers from Mithril Security demonstrated how to poison an open-source pre-trained large language model (LLM) to return a false fact. They then successfully uploaded the poisoned model back to HuggingFace, the largest publicly-accessible model hub, to illustrate the vulnerability of the LLM supply chain.

AML.CS0020.name: Indirect Prompt Injection Threats: Bing Chat Data Pirate
AML.CS0020.summary: Whenever interacting with Microsoft's new Bing Chat LLM Chatbot, a user can allow Bing Chat permission to view and access currently open websites throughout the chat session.

AML.CS0021.name: ChatGPT Conversation Exfiltration
AML.CS0021.summary: Embrace the Red demonstrated that ChatGPT users' conversations can be exfiltrated via an indirect prompt injection. To execute the attack, a threat actor uploads a malicious prompt to a public website, where a ChatGPT user may interact with it.

AML.CS0022.name: ChatGPT Package Hallucination
AML.CS0022.summary: Researchers identified that large language models such as ChatGPT can hallucinate fake software package names that are not published to a package repository. An attacker could publish a malicious package under the hallucinated name to a package repository.

AML.CS0023.name: ShadowRay: Hijacking Exposed Ray Clusters
AML.CS0023.summary: Ray is an open-source Python framework for scaling production AI workflows. Ray's Job API allows for arbitrary remote execution by design. However, it does not offer authentication, and the default configuration may expose the cluster to the internet.

AML.CS0024.name: Morris II Worm: RAG-Based Attack
AML.CS0024.summary: Researchers developed Morris II, a zero-click worm designed to attack generative AI (GenAI) ecosystems and propagate between connected GenAI systems. The worm uses an adversarial self-replicating prompt which uses prompt injection to replicate the prompt as output and perform malicious activity.

AML.CS0025.name: Web-Scale Data Poisoning: Split-View Attack
AML.CS0025.summary: Many recent large-scale datasets are distributed as a list of URLs pointing to individual datapoints. The researchers show that many of these datasets are vulnerable to a "split-view" poisoning attack.

AML.CS0026.name: Financial Transaction Hijacking with M365 Copilot as an Insider
AML.CS0026.summary: Researchers from Zenity conducted a red teaming exercise in August 2024 that successfully manipulated Microsoft 365 Copilot. The attack abused the fact that Copilot ingests received emails into a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) database.

AML.CS0027.name: Organization Confusion on Hugging Face
AML.CS0027.summary: threlfall_hax, a security researcher, created organization accounts on Hugging Face, a public model repository, that impersonated real organizations.

AML.CS0028.name: AI Model Tampering via Supply Chain Attack
AML.CS0028.summary: Researchers at Trend Micro, Inc. used service indexing portals and web searching tools to identify over 8,000 misconfigured private container registries exposed on the internet. Approximately 70% of the registries also had overly permissive access controls that allowed write access.

AML.CS0029.name: Google Bard Conversation Exfiltration
AML.CS0029.summary: Embrace the Red demonstrated that Bard users' conversations could be exfiltrated via an indirect prompt injection. To execute the attack, a threat actor shares a Google Doc containing the prompt with the target user who then interacts with the document via Bard to inadvertently execute the prompt.

AML.CS0030.name: LLMjacking: Stolen Cloud Credentials Used to Access Cloud LLM Services.
AML.CS0030.summary: The Sysdig Threat Research Team discovered that malicious actors utilized stolen credentials to gain access to cloud-hosted large language models (LLMs).

AML.CS0031.name: Malicious Models on Hugging Face
AML.CS0031.summary: Researchers at ReversingLabs have identified malicious models containing embedded malware hosted on the Hugging Face model repository. The models were found to execute reverse shells when loaded, which grants the threat actor command and control capabilities on the victim's system.

AML.CS0032.name: Attempted Evasion of ML Phishing Webpage Detection System
AML.CS0032.summary: Adversaries create phishing websites that appear visually similar to legitimate sites. These sites are designed to trick users into entering their credentials, which are then sent to the bad actor.

AML.CS0033.name: Live Deepfake Image Injection to Evade Mobile KYC Verification
AML.CS0033.summary: Facial biometric authentication services are commonly used by mobile applications for user onboarding, authentication, and identity verification for KYC requirements.

AML.CS0034.name: ProKYC: Deepfake Tool for Account Fraud Attacks
AML.CS0034.summary: Cato CTRL security researchers have identified ProKYC, a deepfake tool being sold to cybercriminals as a method to bypass Know Your Customer (KYC) verification on financial service applications such as cryptocurrency exchanges.

AML.CS0035.name: Data Exfiltration from Slack AI via Indirect Prompt Injection
AML.CS0035.summary: PromptArmor demonstrated that private data can be exfiltrated from Slack AI via indirect prompt injections. The attack relied on Slack AI ingesting a malicious prompt from a post in a public channel into its RAG database and a victim user querying Slack AI, causing the prompt to be retrieved and executed.

AML.CS0036.name: AIKatz: Attacking LLM Desktop Applications
AML.CS0036.summary: Researchers at Lumia have demonstrated that it is possible to extract authentication tokens from the memory of LLM Desktop Applications.

AML.CS0037.name: Data Exfiltration via Agent Tools in Copilot Studio
AML.CS0037.summary: Researchers from Zenity demonstrated how an organization's data can be exfiltrated via prompt injections that target an AI-powered customer service agent.

AML.CS0038.name: Planting Instructions for Delayed Automatic AI Agent Tool Invocation
AML.CS0038.summary: Embrace the Red demonstrated that Google Gemini is susceptible to automated tool invocation by delaying the execution to the next conversation turn.

AML.CS0039.name: Living Off AI: Prompt Injection via Jira Service Management
AML.CS0039.summary: Researchers from Cato Networks demonstrated how adversaries can exploit AI-powered systems embedded in enterprise workflows to execute malicious actions with elevated privileges.

AML.CS0040.name: Hacking ChatGPT's Memories with Prompt Injection
AML.CS0040.summary: Embrace the Red demonstrated that ChatGPT's memory feature is vulnerable to manipulation via prompt injections. To execute the attack, the researcher hid a prompt injection in a shared Google Doc.

AML.CS0041.name: Rules File Backdoor: Supply Chain Attack on AI Coding Assistants
AML.CS0041.summary: Pillar Security researchers demonstrated how adversaries can compromise AI-generated code by injecting malicious instructions into rules files used to configure AI coding assistants like Cursor and GitHub Copilot.

AML.CS0042.name: SesameOp: Novel backdoor uses OpenAI Assistants API for command and control
AML.CS0042.summary: The Microsoft Incident Response - Detection and Response Team (DART) investigated a compromised system where a threat actor utilized SesameOp, a backdoor implant that abuses the OpenAI Assistants API as a covert command and control channel, for espionage activities.

AML.CS0043.name: Malware Prototype with Embedded Prompt Injection
AML.CS0043.summary: Check Point Research identified a prototype malware sample in the wild that contained a prompt injection, which appeared to be designed to manipulate LLM-based malware detectors and/or analysis tools. However, the researchers did not find the prompt injection to be effective on the models they tested.

AML.CS0044.name: LAMEHUG: Malware Leveraging Dynamic AI-Generated Commands
AML.CS0044.summary: In July 2025, Ukrainian authorities reported the emergence of LAMEHUG, a new AI-powered malware attributed to the Russian state-backed threat actor APT28 (also tracked as Forest Blizzard or UAC-0001). LAMEHUG uses a large language model (LLM) to dynamically generate commands on the infected hosts.

AML.CS0045.name: Data Exfiltration via an MCP Server used by Cursor
AML.CS0045.summary: The Backslash Security Research Team demonstrated that a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool can be used as a vector for an indirect prompt injection attack on Cursor, potentially leading to the execution of malicious shell commands.

AML.CS0046.name: Data Destruction via Indirect Prompt Injection Targeting Claude Computer-Use
AML.CS0046.summary: Security researchers at HiddenLayer demonstrated that an indirect prompt injection targeting Claude's Computer Use AI can lead to execution of shell commands on the victim system and destruction of user data.

AML.CS0047.name: Code to Deploy Destructive AI Agent Discovered in Amazon Q VS Code Extension
AML.CS0047.summary: On July 13th, 2025, a malicious actor using the GitHub username "lkmanka58" used an inappropriately scoped GitHub token to make a commit containing malicious code to the Amazon Q Developer Visual Studio Code (VS Code) extension repository.

AML.CS0048.name: Exposed ClawdBot Control Interfaces Leads to Credential Access and Execution
AML.CS0048.summary: A security researcher identified hundreds of exposed ClawdBot control interfaces on the public internet. ClawdBot (now OpenClaw) "is a personal AI assistant you run on your own devices. It answers you on the channels you already use ... , plus extension channels. ...

AML.CS0049.name: Supply Chain Compromise via Poisoned ClawdBot Skill
AML.CS0049.summary: A security researcher demonstrated a proof-of-concept supply chain attack using a poisoned ClawdBot Skill shared on ClawdHub, a Skill registry for agents. The poisoned Skill contained a prompt injection that caused ClawdBot to execute a shell command that reached the researcher's server.

AML.CS0050.name: OpenClaw 1-Click Remote Code Execution
AML.CS0050.summary: A security researcher demonstrated a 1-click remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability to the OpenClaw AI Agent via a malicious link containing a JavaScript script that only takes milliseconds to execute. This vulnerability has been reported and is being tracked to versions of OpenClaw as CVE-2026-25253.

AML.CS0051.name: OpenClaw Command & Control via Prompt Injection
AML.CS0051.summary: Researchers at HiddenLayer demonstrated how a webpage can embed an indirect prompt injection that causes OpenClaw to silently execute a malicious script.

AML.CS0052.name: LLMSmith: RCE Vulnerabilities in LLM-Integrated Applications
AML.CS0052.summary: Researchers identified 20 remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across 11 different LLM frameworks. They discovered applications deployed on the public internet built using these LLM frameworks and demonstrated the RCE vulnerabilities could be exploited using prompt injection.

AML.CS0053.name: Poisoned Postmark MCP Server Email Exfiltration
AML.CS0053.summary: A bad actor successfully exfiltrated emails from users of the Postmark's MCP server via a supply chain attack. Postmark is an email delivery service that allows organizations to send marketing and transactional emails via API. The Postmark MCP server allows users to interact with Postmark via AI agents.

AML.CS0054.name: Data Exfiltration via Remote Poisoned MCP Tool
AML.CS0054.summary: Researchers at Invariant Labs demonstrated that AI agents configured with remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) Tools can be vulnerable to model poisoning attacks. They show that an MCP Tool can contain malicious prompts in its docstring description, which is ingested into the AI agent's context, modifying its behavior.

AML.CS0055.name: AI ClickFix: Hijacking Computer-Use Agents Using ClickFix
AML.CS0055.summary: Embrace the Red demonstrated that AI computer-use agents are vulnerable to social engineering attacks and can be manipulated into executing arbitrary code on a victim's machine.

AML.CS0056.name: Model Distillation Campaigns Targeting Anthropic Claude
AML.CS0056.summary: Anthropic uncovered campaigns to extract Claude's capabilities carried out by the three Chinese AI Labs: DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax. Collectively, these campaigns used approximately 24,000 accounts and 16 million queries.

AML.CS0057.name: Storm-2139 Azure OpenAI Guardrail Bypass
AML.CS0057.summary: Storm-2139 built custom jailbreak tooling to bypass guardrails on Azure OpenAI Services, allowing users to generate harmful synthetic content.

AML.CS0058.name: Google Photos AI Model Extraction
AML.CS0058.summary: Skyld researchers analyzed the Google Photos Android application and recovered TensorFlow Lite models used by AI-powered photo editing and image analysis features. The researchers found models stored unencrypted in the application's assets, embedded in the native library, and encrypted on disk.

AML.CS0059.name: EchoLeak: Zero-Click Prompt Injection Targeting M365 Copilot for Data Exfiltration
AML.CS0059.summary: Aim Security researchers discovered EchoLeak, a zero-click vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot that could allow an attacker to exfiltrate sensitive enterprise data without user interaction.

AML.CS0060.name: Cross-Site Scripting via Prompt Manipulation in Lenovo AI Chatbot
AML.CS0060.summary: Cybernews researchers demonstrated that Lenovo's AI chatbot "Lena" was vulnerable to a prompt injection that produced malicious HTML which was saved in the chat history and could exfiltrate a human support agent's session cookie when rendered in their browser.

AML.CS0061.name: AI in the Middle: Web-Based AI Services as C2 Relays
AML.CS0061.summary: Check Point Research demonstrated an "AI in the Middle" attack in which malware can abuse web-based AI assistants with anonymous or unauthenticated browsing and URL-fetch capabilities as a covert command-and-control channel.

AML.CS0062.name: RCE Vulnerability in Semantic Kernel Search Plugin
AML.CS0062.summary: The Microsoft Defender Security Research Team discovered a vulnerable path in Microsoft Semantic Kernel, in which a single prompt injection could lead to host-level remote code execution (RCE). Semantic Kernel is Microsoft's open-source framework for building AI agents and integrating AI models into applications.

AML.CS0063.name: Prompt-Based Attacks Against Gemini via Calendar Invitations
AML.CS0063.summary: SafeBreach researchers demonstrated how adversary-controlled instructions embedded in productivity content, including Google Calendar invitations, emails, and shared files, could influence the behavior of Gemini-powered assistants when that content was later retrieved.

AML.CS0064.name: Poisoned GGUF Templates: Inference-Time Supply Chain Attack
AML.CS0064.summary: Researchers from Pillar Security and Fujitsu Research of Europe demonstrated an inference-time supply-chain backdoor in which poisoned chat templates alter model and agent behavior without modifying model weights.

AML.CS0065.name: Model Namespace Reuse Supply Chain Attack
AML.CS0065.summary: Unit 42 researchers demonstrated an AI supply chain attack in which an attacker reclaims a deleted Hugging Face author namespace and publishes a malicious model under the same historical Author/ModelName identifier.

AML.CS0066.name: ZombieAgent: Data Exfiltration Attack on ChatGPT
AML.CS0066.summary: ZombieAgent is a proof-of-concept indirect prompt injection attack demonstrated by Radware against OpenAI's ChatGPT Deep Research and Connector functionality.

AML.CS0067.name: Claude Code GitHub Action Secret Exposure
AML.CS0067.summary: The Microsoft Defender Security Research Team demonstrated that Anthropic's Claude Code GitHub Action could expose CI/CD workflow secrets when processing GitHub content, such as issue bodies, pull request descriptions, and comments, containing prompt injections.

AML.CS0068.name: Autonomous OpenAI Evaluation Agents Compromise Hugging Face Infrastructure
AML.CS0068.summary: During large-scale internal OpenAI cyber evaluations from May 26 through July 13, 2026, a partially coordinated collective of autonomous agent runs crossed evaluation boundaries, established external infrastructure, and compromised Hugging Face production systems.

AML.CS0069.name: GTG-1002 Claude Code Espionage Campaign
AML.CS0069.summary: In September 2025, GTG-1002 used a jailbroken Claude Code agent to conduct a cyber-espionage campaign against approximately 30 organizations, succeeding against a small number. Anthropic assessed with high confidence that GTG-1002 was a Chinese state-sponsored group.

AML.CS0070.name: Threat Actor Uses a DeepSeek-Powered Hermes Agent in Langflow and n8n Exploitation Attempts
AML.CS0070.summary: A Chinese-speaking threat actor operating as knaithe or KnYuan configured Hermes Agent to use DeepSeek as its reasoning engine. Hermes supplied terminal access, Telegram-based operator control, and a skills system containing both bundled and actor-created red-team skills.

AML.CS0071.name: Multi-Agent Framework Compromises Taiwanese Government Systems
AML.CS0071.summary: In early July 2026, an unknown Chinese-language operator used a multi-agent framework built on Hermes and OpenClaw against government systems that subsequent public reporting identified as Taiwanese.

AML.CS0072.name: AI Recommendation Poisoning via Crafted AI Assistant Links
AML.CS0072.summary: The Microsoft Defender Security Research Team identified a widespread pattern of AI assistant memory manipulation carried out for promotional purposes, which they named AI Recommendation Poisoning.

AML.CS0073.name: Autonomous Claude Agents Compromise Three Real Organizations During Cyber Evaluations
AML.CS0073.summary: Autonomous Anthropic models gained unauthorized access to systems belonging to three unrelated organizations during six cybersecurity evaluation runs from April through July 2026, compromising real systems while pursuing capture-the-flag objectives.

AML.CS0074.name: AISI Evaluation Agents Conduct Unsanctioned Real-World Cyber Activity
AML.CS0074.summary: Between July 25 and 28, 2026, autonomous AI agents undergoing cybersecurity evaluations by the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) took unsanctioned actions involving real people and public Internet services. AISI identified 19 events across 10 evaluation runs: 17 involved Claude Mythos 5 and two involved GPT-5.6 Sol.

AML.CS0075.name: Model Distillation Campaigns Targeting Google AI Services
AML.CS0075.summary: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Google DeepMind reported recurring distillation campaigns targeting Google AI services. Adversaries sought model outputs to reproduce capabilities, including reasoning, visual and audio understanding, image generation, and video generation.

AML.CS0076.name: China-Based Artificial Intelligence Companies Conducting Industrial-Scale Distillation Campaigns Against U.S. AI Companies
AML.CS0076.summary: NSA, CISA, and FBI attributed industrial-scale distillation campaigns to six China-based AI companies. Since at least late 2024, these companies collected outputs from U.S. AI models over millions of exchanges, and used the responses to train or improve their own models.
